articles.title: Fire at nursing home in Chile kills 16
articles.summary: SANTIAGO, Chile – A fire at a nursing home in Chile that had previously violated regulations has killed 16 elderly residents and left others hospitalized, authorities said Saturday. The blaze…

blocks.text: SANTIAGO, Chile – A fire at a nursing home in Chile that had previously violated regulations has killed 16 elderly residents and left others hospitalized, authorities said Saturday.
The blaze began on Friday night at the single-story care home in the Araucania region, 640 kilometers (400 miles) south of the capital Santiago, and was extinguished early Saturday.
Images shared on social media showed massive flames rising above the building in the darkness, while a fire truck sprayed water to tackle the flames.
“We express our sorrow and dismay at the deaths of 16 elderly people in this tragedy,” authorities in the municipality of Pitrufquen said in a statement.
A total of 26 elderly residents were in the nursing home. Ten of them survived and were taken to the local hospital, the statement said.
On Saturday, firefighters were still clearing debris and removing collapsed corrugated metal roofing. Police cordoned off the area for safety.

“It is a situation that fills our souls with great sorrow and pain. We have been… providing support to the families,” said local mayor Jacqueline Romero, who said that municipal health and public safety teams, firefighters and police were deployed.
The cause of the fire remained unclear.

“We are currently carrying out investigative procedures, including examining the scene and conducting inquiries, to determine the origin and cause of the fire, as well as to rule out third-party involvement,” Jorge Granada, the prosecutor assigned to the case, told local media.
The owners of the private care home were summoned to give statements.
An official at the regional health secretariat said there had been previous operational problems at the care home.
“It was an unregulated facility; it had faced administrative proceedings and fines since 2019, and was a repeat offender,” the official, Jose Bravo, said.

“In February, the municipality had sent a letter specifically calling for an inspection because the facility was not in compliance with regulations — it was subject to sanitary enforcement proceedings,” Romero told local networks.

On his X account, Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast demanded that the truth be uncovered and “necessary corrections be made to do everything possible to prevent a tragedy like this from happening again.”
He said he had ordered “urgent measures” to review conditions at nursing homes across the country.

articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte lawyers’ bid to have charges refiled opposed
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The prosecution and lawyers of the victims of the drug war of then President Rodrigo Duterte objected to a motion by his lawyers before the International Criminal Court (ICC)…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The prosecution and lawyers of the victims of the drug war of then President Rodrigo Duterte objected to a motion by his lawyers before the International Criminal Court (ICC) seeking to have the charges against him refiled, saying they cannot revisit that matter at the trial stage.
In a filing on Aug. 31, Duterte’s lawyers asked Trial Chamber (TC) III to have the charges “properly inform…the accused of the case he needs to meet.”

The defense said it wants the scope of the charges defined in terms of how many counts they constitute. It also seeks an “exhaustive list of underpinning acts” to represent the entirety of the charges. The former president faces three counts of crimes of humanity of murder.

Duterte’s lawyers were referring to the prosecution’s document containing the charges, which accused Duterte of being criminally responsible for the killing of 76 individuals in 49 incidents during the drug war.
Reopening the charges?

In separate filings dated Sept. 10, the prosecution and the common legal representative of victims (CLRVs) opposed the defense’ motion, saying that questions on the “adequacy” posed by the defense were already determined and affirmed by Pre-Trial Chamber (PTC) I.

“To the contrary, the three counts each have a clear temporal, geographical and material scope, and this is consistent with the requirements of article 74(2) of the [Rome] Statute,” the prosecution said in its 10-page response, referring to the 2002 treaty which established the court.
It added “The…mere disagreement [of the defense] with the analysis of the [PTC] is insufficient to show any defect.”
The CLRVs sought the outright rejection of the motion for being “procedurally misconceived.”
They said the defense cannot just ask TC III to reopen the issue “under the guise of a motion concerning the ‘form’ of the charges.”

“[S]hould the Chamber consider that the defence genuinely seeks to challenge defects in the [document containing the charges], such objections belong to the pre-confirmation stage and cannot now be raised before the trial chamber,” they said in a 10-page response.
They said the defense merely reiterated its disagreement with PTC’s earlier decision and “advance[d] no argument” to warrant a reversal.
Another defense motion
The trial of Duterte, who is detained in The Hague, is scheduled to begin on Nov. 30 and is seen to continue until next year.
A third status conference will be held on Sept. 16 to discuss the prosecution’s list of witnesses and evidence, the number of hours it needs to present its case and its disclosure of evidence.

The prosecution last week also opposed a proposal by the defense to authenticate its evidence from open source and user-generated materials, saying this step is “unnecessary and burdensome” and even risks delaying the start of the trial.

It said the prosecution should have the discretion to determine whether a certain piece of evidence from open source or user-generated materials should be accompanied by a certification from an expert.

It cited as an example information from open sources that are credible sources—such as the United Nations, nongovernment organizations and government websites—and should not require authentication by experts. /cb

articles.title: Expectations high ahead of historic BARMM polls
articles.summary: WAO, LANAO DEL SUR, Philippines — Expectations are high that Monday’s first regular parliamentary election in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) will be peaceful, orderly and…

blocks.text: WAO, LANAO DEL SUR, Philippines — Expectations are high that Monday’s first regular parliamentary election in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) will be peaceful, orderly and less marred by fraud, even as polling officials contend with logistical problems, including weak internet signals that have slowed final testing of voting machines.

The Sept. 14 polls mark the first time BARMM voters will elect a regional parliament, a key milestone in the implementation of the 2014 Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro between the government and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF).
Postponed four times, the election is being closely watched as the final major step in the political track of the peace agreement that ended decades of armed conflict in Mindanao.

Peace advocates, church leaders and election monitors said extensive government preparations, particularly the deployment of security forces, should help ensure credible polls and deter intimidation, vote-buying and other irregularities.

“We expect that the elaborate security preparations of the national government translates to a peaceful, orderly, and credible conduct of the BARMM regional elections,” Bishop Felixberto Calang, convenor of the Initiatives for Peace in Mindanao (InPeace), told the Inquirer on Saturday.
Calang said the heavy security presence should protect voters and curb irregularities rather than create fear.
“We should not be hearing reports of vote-buying and voter harassment given the widespread law enforcement presence,” he said.
But some voters remain skeptical.
Extensive security preparations
In this frontier town, residents said “ulan-ulan,” a euphemism for vote-buying, could still take place despite heightened security.
“There will definitely be ulan-ulan in the (residential) compounds,” said Aaron Baligod, who said some voters would likely rely on sample ballots distributed by political supporters.
Levy Garduce, 40, said he expected money to be offered during the campaign and voting period.
“I don’t really know anyone running, but I’ll still vote,” Garduce said, unfazed by the unfamiliar names seeking parliamentary seats.
He added that he expected no major trouble in the community.

About 10,000 Philippine National Police personnel and 30,000 soldiers from the Armed Forces of the Philippines have been deployed across the region, particularly in areas classified “red” because of serious security threats and a history of election-related violence. The police are on full alert until Sept. 30.

Commission on Elections (Comelec) Chair George Erwin Garcia warned voters and political groups that vigilance should continue after Election Day, noting that some losing candidates or their supporters may refuse to accept the results.
“Vigilance shouldn’t end on Monday,” Garcia said.
Election materials and equipment were delivered early Saturday to designated schools serving as voting centers.
In Basilan, Explosive Ordnance Disposal teams and K9 units inspected Lamitan City Central Elementary School in Barangay Maganda.
Weak internet slows testing
The final preparations were not without glitches.

Two days before the vote, weak internet signals slowed final testing procedures for automated counting machines inseveral precincts at Lamitan City Central School. Election workers continued manual checks and system diagnostics despite the connectivity problems.
In Cotabato City, at least 86 teachers on election duty failed to report for final testing and sealing, according to Garcia. They were replaced by trained police personnel serving as poll managers.
Comelec officials said final testing and sealing of the counting machines and other election paraphernalia were being completed across 5,212 clustered precincts.

Garcia said the machines had been sealed and packed for deployment, with safeguards preventing any single election officer from controlling their operation. Two election officers must insert their cards before a machine can be operated.
2.39M voters
About 2.393 million registered voters are expected to cast ballots at 1,186 voting centers across the BARMM.
The election will determine the 80 members of the Bangsamoro Parliament, the legislative body created under the Bangsamoro Organic Law, or Republic Act No. 11054.
Voters will make eight choices: one regional political party, one parliamentary district representative and six sectoral representatives.
The parliament will have 40 regional party representatives, 32 district representatives and eight sectoral representatives.

For the regional seats, voters will select a political party rather than an individual candidate. Seats will be allocated according to each party’s share of the vote, with its nominees filling the seats won.

Voters will also elect one district representative. The 32 district seats are distributed as follows: four in Basilan, nine in Lanao del Sur, five in Maguindanao del Norte, five in Maguindanao del Sur, four in Tawi-Tawi, three in Cotabato City and two in the Special Geographic Area.
The six sectoral seats will represent settler communities, women, youth, traditional leaders and the “ulama,” with two seats for settler communities and one each for the other four sectors.
Peace and disinformation
Bishop-Prelate Leo Dalmao of the Diocese of Isabela de Basilan urged candidates, voters, election personnel, security forces and political leaders to protect the gains of peace.
“Basilan has known the cost of conflict. Today, we have the opportunity to show what peace can make possible,” Dalmao said.

He urged candidates and supporters to reject violence, intimidation, vote-buying, threats, misinformation and other forms of electoral dishonesty. He also reminded voters not to sell their votes, and appealed to Muslim and Christian communities “not (to) allow political differences to divide our families and our communities. We may choose different candidates, but we remain one people.”
Election monitors are also warning of a surge in online disinformation as voting day approaches.

The Independent Election Monitoring Center (IEMC) said it had monitored misleading social media posts invoking the MILF and its armed wing, doctored or miscontextualized photographs, and artificial intelligence (AI)-generated images depicting bogus events.
“The closer we get to the ballot box, the louder the digital noise becomes,” said Sheila Algabre, IEMC head of operations.
Moro Ako delisted

Days before the vote, the Comelec en banc issued a resolution disqualifying the Moro Ako Party. It denied the group’s motion for reconsideration after earlier granting a petition by Aladin Abdul to cancel the party’s registration for alleged misrepresentation.

The petition alleged that Moro Ako declared nonexistent chapters in Cotabato City, Lamitan City, Maguindanao del Norte and Maguindanao del Sur. But the party maintained that the discrepancies were just typo errors.
Comelec officials said winners are expected to be proclaimed by Sept. 15.

Those elected will serve from noon Oct. 30, 2026, to June 30, 2031. Beginning in 2031, regular Bangsamoro elections will be synchronized with the national and local elections and held every three years. —With reports from Edwin Fernandez, Holly Bacay, and Inquirer Research

articles.title: Swimming pigs draw tourists to Greek island
articles.summary: GREECE — On a beach at the small Greek island of Atokos in the Ionian Sea, tourists frolic in the azure waters like most visitors do in the popular Mediterranean country at this time of year. The…

blocks.text: GREECE — On a beach at the small Greek island of Atokos in the Ionian Sea, tourists frolic in the azure waters like most visitors do in the popular Mediterranean country at this time of year. The difference is that they are surrounded by a herd of black pigs.

The island lies a short distance from Ithaca, the island home and kingdom of the hero Odysseus in Homer’s epic poem “The Odyssey.” And like Ithaca, Atokos has become a social media sensation, drawing visitors from around the world who come to swim alongside, and even feed, the docile animals.
The pigs mostly mind their own business as they scour the sand for anything edible, before taking short dips in the sea to cool off.
‘Piggy Island’
“They seem to be in their [environment], and they don’t try to bite if you don’t touch them,” said Francesco Ferrari, a 22-year-old tattoo artist from Italy.
The visitors have been ferried over by tour operator Renato Bisha, who makes several such trips over from Ithaca every day.
With the “Piggy Island” experience gaining popularity over social media, similar day trips are organized from the nearby islands of Lefkada and Kefalonia.
“The island has become viral because of the pigs. Many people actively ask to come to Atokos,” said Bisha, throwing fruit to attract the animals to his boat.
“This is so amazing, I recommend it to anyone,” said American visitor Jamie Jackson. “Never in my life had I ever thought I’d be doing this.”
Little known before images of the swimming pigs went viral on Instagram and TikTok, Atokos now has thousands of visitors, especially during the busy summer months.
“I think [the pigs] are having as much fun as we are,” said another American visitor, Michael Mcanelly.
“It’s something unique, worth coming over to see,” added Simos Gleridis, a 33-year-old accountant from Thessaloniki. /cb

articles.title: Marcos seeks India expertise for PH railway, space projects
articles.summary: NEW DELHI, India — President Marcos is seeking India’s technical expertise and cooperation on major railway projects and space technology development in the Philippines. On the sidelines of his…

blocks.text: NEW DELHI, India — President Marcos is seeking India’s technical expertise and cooperation on major railway projects and space technology development in the Philippines.

On the sidelines of his participation in the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India on Saturday, Marcos held separate meetings with Rail India Technical and Economic Service Ltd. (RITES) and the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO).
The summit is ending on Sunday, Sept. 13, which also happens to be the President’s 69th birthday.
Presidential Communications Office (PCO) Acting Secretary Dave Gomez said Marcos met with RITES representatives to explore possible cooperation on at least three railway projects.

The priority projects being considered by RITES are the Mindanao Railway Project, a mass rail system in Cebu and the extension of the Philippine National Railways (PNR) system from Tutuban commercial center in Tondo, Manila.
Gomez said RITES could participate in the projects as a consultant or through a public-private partnership (PPP), while also helping the Philippines explore official development assistance (ODA).
“They will look into them and we will study them),” he said after the meeting.
RITES, a Government of India Enterprise under the Ministry of Railways, provides consultancy services in the fields of transport, infrastructure and related technologies.
It has been listed as among the top 500 Indian companies, establishing itself as a preferred choice for clients in over 55 countries across Asia, Africa, Latin America and the Middle East.
Marcos also met with ISRO officials to discuss cooperation with the Philippine Space Agency (PhilSA) in support of the country’s long-term goal of launching its own satellite. —Philippine News Agency

articles.title: Trump's comments on a united Ireland may have targeted audience across the Atlantic
articles.summary: Nobody could have predicted that today's main global headline would be Trump's desire to see a unified Ireland.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
US President Donald Trump is visiting Ireland
ByCaitriona Perry
Chief PresenterReporting fromin Dublin
When another world leader meets US President Donald Trump the only certainty about what might happen is the uncertainty about what might happen.
This was exactly the case ahead of President Trump's two-day visit to Ireland.
Nobody could have predicted that by the end of the first day, the main global headline would be his desire to see a unified Ireland.

As the shockwaves of his remarks rippled through this island and Great Britain, it was unclear whether this represented a new US administration policy, or an off-the-cuff remark from a president who likes to take questions from reporters, and likes to give answers.

blocks.caption: Image caption, President Trump with the Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin

blocks.text: President Trump with the Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin
Former Republican Congressman Mick Mulvaney was Trump's special envoy to Northern Ireland in his first term in office.
He cautioned against anyone reading too much into the president's remarks.
"This does not represent a shift in US foreign policy," he said.
"We're still very much committed to the Good Friday Agreement."
Democratic Congressman Brendan Boyle agreed.
"There is bipartisan support for that deal, and that is not going to change."
Although both agreed that Donald Trump was probably right to say that "eventually" unification would happen, that did not mean the US was about to start pushing for it.
Watch: President Trump says he would 'love' to see Ireland unified

Giving an answer to a question that is asked at a free-flowing press conference is one thing, but Donald Trump repeated his sentiments a short time later when he was delivering a speech to an invited audience at the US Ambassador's residence.
In fact it was almost the first thing he mentioned, hinting that maybe he realised he had kicked over a can of worms at his earlier appearance.
The rest of that speech was curious. It was billed as a 20-minute address to Irish and Irish American business leaders, but was about twice that and strayed largely into domestic US matters.
President Trump has a speaking style that he describes himself as "the weave".
He can bounce from topic to topic during any speaking engagement, veering off the script and then returning to the matter at hand.
Today he lauded his own achievements, as he sees them, such as clamping down on illegal immigration, doing deals and boosting defence production.
He repeated his criticisms once again of what he views as the UK's lack of support for his military operation in Iran.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Donald Trump meets Irish President Catherine Connolly

blocks.text: Donald Trump meets Irish President Catherine Connolly
Midterm elections fast approaching
But who was his target audience? The gathered business leaders in Dublin or a US audience tuning in before it was even dawn in much of that country?
This November's crunch midterm elections are fast approaching and the Republican party is under intense pressure because of the president's policies.
They may lose control of one or both houses of Congress.
About one tenth of the US population claim Irish heritage but they are not a homogeneous voting bloc.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Bill Clinton alongside former Irish President Mary Robinson in 1995

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Bill Clinton alongside former Irish President Mary Robinson in 1995
Was he trying to target Irish-American independent or swing voters in the US, of which there are many who have flip-flopped between the Republican and Democratic party in recent years?
Some of them do support a unified Ireland and so in this time of chasing every vote, perhaps that played a part.
Bill Clinton secured a lot of Irish-American support when he was running for president, by promising to get engaged in the peace process.
They voted for him and he followed through on his promise and much of that work led to the foundations of the Good Friday Agreement.
But, Irish America is a different place now. Indeed, America is a different place now as politics have become more polarised.
The November election campaigns show no indication that will change anytime soon.
But political leaders in Ireland will be hoping the only debate tomorrow is about the play on the golf course.

articles.title: Sustaining the Pisa results
articles.summary: The improved performance in the 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) is a much-needed boost to the country’s morale after years of being in the news for a worsening and…

blocks.text: The improved performance in the 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) is a much-needed boost to the country’s morale after years of being in the news for a worsening and deepening learning crisis.

But while these gains are a reason to celebrate, many more challenges lie ahead, and the crisis is far from resolved. It continues to threaten future generations unless problems—like teacher and classroom shortages—among others, are addressed.

The country scored 373 in science, 371 in mathematics, and 367 in reading, up 17, 16, and 20 points, respectively, from its 2022 results. It ranked 77th out of 91 countries and economies in science, 74th out of 90 in mathematics, and 72nd out of 90 in reading. These figures were also the country’s best Pisa performance since participating in the assessment in 2018.

However, it is sobering to note that while the Philippines was heralded as the “fastest-improving” country in reading literacy, the results were still below the average scores of 482 in science, 463 in mathematics, and 461 in reading in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) nations.
Baseline level

The official OECD report showed that more Filipino students reached Level 2 or higher, considered the baseline level of proficiency. At level 2 in science, students are expected to recognize explanations for familiar scientific phenomena and at least determine whether available data support a conclusion. In mathematics, they should recognize how simple situations can be represented mathematically; while in reading, they should identify the main idea of a moderately long text and identify information based on explicit criteria.

The share of Filipino students reaching at least level 2 went up to 32 percent in 2025 from 23 percent in 2022 for science; 21 percent from 16 percent for mathematics; and 31 percent from 24 percent in reading. However, OECD data showed that most Filipino 15-year-olds remained below minimum proficiency.
To compare, the average for the OECD was 74 percent for science, 65 percent for mathematics, and 69 percent for reading.
In addition, top-level performance remained extremely rare, with no Filipino students reaching Level 5 or 6 in science and mathematics, or Level 5 or higher in reading.

Education Secretary Sonny Angara noted that the country’s scores should also be taken in the context of how other Southeast Asian nations have improved their ranking. Vietnam, for example, which spends 20 percent of its national budget on education, with a focus on teachers’ welfare and training, has performed closer to the OECD average.

The Marcos administration has touted the P1.35 trillion it allocated to the education sector this year as a record-high. But think tank Ibon Foundation pointed out that the increase does not take into account the projected growth in enrolment, nor does it provide enough funding to close the classroom gap.

A look at next year’s proposed National Expenditure Program also raises red flags. For one, no budget has been earmarked for the Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning (Aral) program under Republic Act No. 12028 enacted in October 2024. The Department of Education’s (DepEd) official remedial program meant to address students’ skills gap in reading, mathematics, and science, received P9 billion this year. Leaving it with zero budget in 2027 is tantamount to abandoning a crucial program that came about as a direct result of the country’s previously dismal Pisa performance.

Angara told the House committee on appropriations this week that 4.5 million out of the 6.7 million students it admitted under Aral were no longer considered struggling readers. The DepEd has proposed almost P16 billion for the program to sustain these gains.
On the right track

The Bayang Bumabasa initiative has also not received any budget for next year. Angara has sought a P50 million budget for the campaign, which the DepEd launched last year together with the Second Congressional Commission on Education (Edcom 2) to address foundational reading and literacy crises among early-grade students.

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian, a former cochair of the Edcom 2, said the latest Pisa results should help the government craft policies and shape next year’s education budget. He named the Aral program, hiring of new teachers, and early child development as among the items that should be given budget priority. “We must sustain the momentum to ensure that these gains translate into lasting improvements in learning outcomes,” he said.
But words mean nothing if crucial initiatives and personnel and infrastructure backlogs are not fully funded. Indeed, there is still so much to be done in addressing the country’s learning crisis.
The country’s performance in the latest Pisa proves it is on the right track, but the government must now put its money where its mouth is to sustain the momentum.

articles.title: Justice by attrition
articles.summary: In November 2001, the late Sandiganbayan Presiding Justice Francis Garchitorena was indefinitely suspended by the Supreme Court and fined P20,000 for gross negligence of duty. Of 198 cases raffled to…

blocks.text: In November 2001, the late Sandiganbayan Presiding Justice Francis Garchitorena was indefinitely suspended by the Supreme Court and fined P20,000 for gross negligence of duty. Of 198 cases raffled to his division, 138 had long been submitted for decision. He was given six months to clear the backlog, which included the Marcos cases.

Garchitorena, a bright lawyer with a sharp tongue, had been active in the anti-dictatorship movement, and was appointed by then President Cory Aquino soon after Edsa. Few could accuse him of stalling the Marcos cases. Asked about his suspension, he said some had been handled by other justices. “All of these is not a product of sloth,” he said.

Years earlier I had put the same question to him: why was it taking so long? Many Marcos associates had by then surrendered assets and turned state witness. It was not that simple, he said. The Marcoses had retained the country’s most experienced lawyer, Estelito P. Mendoza, solicitor general for 14 years under Marcos. He had complete mastery of court procedure, and the officials now across the table had once been his subordinates.

There was, Garchitorena believed, a deliberate strategy of delay across some 32 cases. Through pleadings and repeated postponements, the cases dragged on; original documents went missing; changes in the Presidential Commission on Good Government (PCGG) leadership meant custody of evidence was not always consistent. But what struck me most was his final observation: that with enough time, the fate of a case could change completely, once a less adversarial administration came into power.
He was describing, 35 years in advance, what happened this month.

On Sept. 9, the Supreme Court released a decision its first division had promulgated on June 10, reversing former first lady Imelda Marcos’ 2018 conviction on seven counts of graft. It rests on three grounds. In four of the cases, the information accused her of holding a prohibited interest as a member of the Interim Batasang Pambansa, while she was convicted under a constitutional restriction applying to Cabinet members. The charges were never amended.

Second, the Swiss documents linking her to the foundations were treated as private documents requiring authentication, and the witnesses could establish how these papers reached government hands but not their genuineness or due execution. Third, the prosecution failed to establish that the foundations were “businesses” within the meaning of the statute.
Not one of these grounds pertains to whether the money was stolen.

That question was answered years ago, in a civil case. In 2003 the Supreme Court ordered the forfeiture of $658 million held in those same foundations, declaring the deposits ill-gotten. That judgment stands. Our legal system therefore holds, without contradiction, that the money was unlawfully acquired and that no one may be convicted of having had an interest in it. The standards of proof differ: preponderance of evidence in the civil case, proof beyond reasonable doubt in the criminal one.

Technicality, it is tempting to say, is the last refuge of the guilty. But these rules, that no conviction may rest on a charge never made, that documents must be authenticated, that penal statutes are read strictly, protect ordinary defendants every day. The rigor cannot be faulted, and yet it reads as a favor.

Which returns us to Garchitorena. Delay rewards those who can afford to wait, converting wealth and expert counsel into time, and time into acquittal. It came from three directions at once: a defense using the accused’s procedural rights with great skill, a prosecution worn down by time, and a court that could not keep up.

I suspect there is more to it than law following its own logic; a family restored to Malacañang is not a neutral fact for the courts. I cannot prove that it influenced the ruling, and will not pretend otherwise. But the structural explanation is actually the more disturbing one. If someone from the Palace did make a call to the high court, then there is someone to identify. But, if these outcomes followed instead from sloppy prosecution and a defense that outlasted decades of prosecutors and judges—then the next cases are bound to end the same way.

Perhaps a more telling proof of this sad reality came eight days before the reversal, and was barely reported. On June 2 the Sandiganbayan’s special division dismissed what remained of Civil Case No. 0141, the omnibus forfeiture petition the PCGG filed in December 1991, after the government manifested it would present no further evidence. Most of its personnel, the commission had told the court, were already retired. The case was not lost. It was abandoned for want of anyone left to try it. Thirty-five years ended in a seven-page resolution no one thought worth reporting.

articles.title: Be still...
articles.summary: Who is the least stressed driver in the world? The funeral car driver. Why? He is not in a hurry, he is not bothered by traffic, and, best of all, he does not carry a backseat driver.…

blocks.text: Who is the least stressed driver in the world? The funeral car driver. Why? He is not in a hurry, he is not bothered by traffic, and, best of all, he does not carry a backseat driver.

In today’s Gospel (Matthew 18:21–35), Jesus teaches us about forgiveness and reconciliation. Forgiveness is one of the most difficult, yet most freeing, lessons we can learn in life. It is a journey of the heart that often calls us to let go, again and again. As Martin Luther King Jr. once said, “Forgiveness is not an occasional act; it is a constant attitude.” How true. Forgiveness is not always a single act that happens once and is finished forever. Sometimes, we have to forgive again and again, especially when the memory of the hurt returns, again and again.

There is a saying that reminds us of what anger can do: “Anger does more damage to the vessel in which it is stored than to the vessel on which it is poured.” When we keep anger inside us, we may think we are punishing the person who hurt us. But often, we are the ones who suffer. Lewis B. Smedes wrote, “To forgive is to set a prisoner free and discover that the prisoner was you.” We have a choice: to forgive and become free, or to refuse to forgive and remain trapped in anger, stress, bitterness, and sadness.

Mahatma Gandhi said, “The weak can never forgive. Forgiveness is the attribute of the strong.” Indeed, forgiveness is not weakness. It takes strength to forgive when we have been deeply hurt. It takes humility to set aside our pride. And it takes faith to surrender to God what we cannot change. Perhaps this is the prayer we need to make: “Lord, You have forgiven me so many times. Help me to do likewise.”

Think for a moment of the person who has hurt you the most. Perhaps there is someone you dislike so deeply that even hearing that person’s name disturbs your peace. Perhaps the wound is still fresh. Perhaps it happened many years ago, but the pain remains. What should we do? Offer that person to God. Leave that person in God’s heart. Pray, if you can, for that person’s conversion and healing. Release the matter from your hands. You do not have to carry it forever. Surrender. Let God take over.

Forgiveness does not mean saying, “It did not happen.” Neither does it mean saying, “It did not hurt.” What happened may have been real, and the pain may have been deep. But forgiveness means choosing not to allow that pain to control you anymore. Get rid of the “backseat driver”!

There is a story of a monk who saw a scorpion on a leaf drifting along a river. Wanting to save it, the monk reached out to lift the scorpion from the water. But each time he tried, the scorpion stung him. Someone watching asked, “Why do you keep trying to save it when it keeps hurting you?” The monk replied, “It is the nature of the scorpion to sting. It is my nature to love. Why should I give up my nature to love simply because it is the scorpion’s nature to sting?”

“Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart.” (Matthew 11:29). Gentleness is the way, and humility is the key to true peace and reconciliation. Gentleness softens hearts, while humility helps us recognize that we, too, have made mistakes and have needed forgiveness. Let us take—and remain on—the road of gentleness and humility.

Allow me to share my simple prayer of forgiveness: “Lord, forgive me for all my sins. I forgive all who have hurt me. I ask forgiveness from and pray for all those I have hurt. With humility and gratitude, I joyfully accept Your unconditional love and forgiveness. Amen.” And whenever the burdens of anger, resentment, worldly worries, and personal struggles become too heavy, let us return to the One who is always merciful. Let us pray often: “Jesus, I trust in You. Mama Mary, I love you.”

“Be still and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10) The lessons come when you are calm. When you listen more to the Lord, and less on your feelings, hurts, and disappointments, then you are growing, you are moving on, again.
A moment with the Lord:
Lord, forgive us our sins as we forgive those who have sinned against us. Amen.

articles.title: Cayetanos back from Singapore trip: 'We just wanted to rest'
articles.summary: Senator Alan Peter Cayetano said he and his family traveled to Singapore simply to take a break, amid questions over their trip abroad.

blocks.text: Published September 13, 2026 4:51am
Senator Alan Peter Cayetano on Sunday said he and his family traveled to Singapore simply to take a break, amid questions over their trip abroad.
In a Facebook Live early Sunday, Cayetano said the trip was private and that there was no reason why they could not travel.
“Private yun at gusto lang magpahinga (It was a private trip and we just wanted to rest),” Cayetano said.
The Cayetano siblings were seen arriving at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport early Sunday.
He said “responsible” public officials, including those from the Bureau of Immigration and the Office of the Ombudsman, had said there was no reason why they could not travel.

Cayetano said he was surprised that their “routine, quiet and short” trip became an issue, which he attributed to what he described as the country’s increasingly “toxic” political environment, where people are quick to create conflict and controversy.
The Senate minority leader’s trip abroad raised questions amid reports linking him to the controversy over the construction of the cauldron, or “kaldero,” used during the 2019 Southeast Asian Games.

Senator Panfilo Lacson has also submitted to the Ombudsman case studies, supported by official documents, detailing the supposed “systemic anomalies” in flood control infrastructure projects in Taguig City, the political bailiwick of the Cayetanos.
Cayetano also referred to what he described as Lacson’s “persecution” of him and his family, as well as Taguig.
“Pinapaubaya ko na sa Panginoon (I leave it to the Lord),” he said.
He said threatened cases, investigations and what he described as constantly changing accusations were part of the cost of fighting for the country.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: The Stunt Driver star Jay Baruchel says Canadians in film industry can 'punch above our weight'
articles.summary: As tensions between Canada and the U.S. creep into the film industry, Jay Baruchel is more than confident his country can stand toe to toe with its southern neighbour. He's one of a number of…

image.caption: The cast and director of The Stunt Driver on the red carpet for the film at the Toronto International Film Festival in on Friday. (Laura Proctor/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

As tensions between Canada and the U.S. creep into the film industry, Jay Baruchel is more than confident his country can stand toe to toe with its southern neighbour. He's one of a number of Canadian actors sharing their love of the country's film industry and Canada in general on the TIFF red carpet after the festival kicked off Thursday night.
Devon Bostick, Mary Walsh among other Canadians proudly championing homegrown art at TIFF
Jay Baruchel's film The Stunt Driver premieres at Toronto International Film Festival | Glasner-0800
As tensions between Canada and the U.S. creep into the film industry, Jay Baruchel is more than confident his country can stand toe to toe with its southern neighbour.
"We will be fine," the Ottawa-born actor said on the red carpet Friday ahead of the world premiere of The Stunt Driver at the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF).
"We have never done anything but punch above our weight, and our record is pretty bloody strong when it comes to that.… We always find a way through."
He's one of a number of Canadian actors sharing their love of the country's film industry and Canada in general on the TIFF red carpet after the festival kicked off Thursday night.
Baruchel, known for films such as BlackBerry and She's Out of My League, is in the driver's seat of the new underdog film, which is based on the true story of stuntman Ken Carter.

Baruchel portrays Carter, known as The Mad Canadian, who attempted to jump over the St. Lawrence River in a rocket-powered car in the 1970s — partially driven by a desire to outdo his American rival Evel Knievel.
The timing of the film's debut during the ongoing trade war between Canada and the U.S. "added an extra sense of urgency … and a vitality" to the film, Baruchel said.
"If you've ever been talked down to, if you've ever been dismissed ... you understand where this comes from," he added, calling the story "an indignant middle finger."

The trade war gained took on a cultural dimension ahead of TIFF when, earlier this month, U.S. President Donald Trump singled out Canada during the announcement of a proposed federal incentive to keep U.S. film productions in the U.S. rather than travelling abroad, stirring up concerns in the Canadian film industry.

items: The best-dressed stars at TIFF 2026
‘It’s Canada’s turn now’: TIFF market looks to capitalize on U.S. political climate, boost local film
The U.S. is considering a federal tax incentive for films. How might that affect Canada?

blocks.text: The two film industries have long been close.

"It's been over a hundred years that there's been a very solid bridge built between the entertainers and artists and business people of Canada and the U.S. when it comes to making movies," TIFF CEO Cameron Bailey told CBC News on Thursday, noting that the opening film at TIFF, Being Heumann, is a U.S. production that was shot in Toronto.
At TIFF, Canadian actors and artists say they aren't feeling cowed — but instead feel inspired to champion Canadian art.
"Art can reflect who we are as a country and … who we are as people," Canadian actress Laurence Leboeuf, who plays Carter's wife Gloria in The Stunt Driver, said on the red carpet Friday.
'Canadian renaissance'

Devon Bostick, a Toronto-born actor who co-wrote Closing Night — which also premiered at TIFF — added that he feels "we're part of a Canadian renaissance right now." The film tracks a movie star (Sarah Paulson) as she attempts to connect with her estranged family.

"I live in the States now and from afar I just think Canada's got it going on, and I feel like it's a beacon of light, that what is happening here is thriving and resisting," the Mile End Kicks actor said.
When asked if he had any concerns about the Canadian film industry amid trade tensions, he quipped, "I think I'm not afraid for Canada, I’m afraid for the States."
Mary Walsh, a comedian and actress known for her work with This Hour Has 22 Minutes, echoed those sentiments when she arrived on the red carpet for the upcoming Netflix miniseries Below on Thursday.
"The Canadian film industry is bigger than it's ever been, and it's growing. And the more Mr. Trump threatens to attack us, the more we pull together and become stronger," she said.
Trump's threats only make Canada's film industry stronger: Mary Walsh
Walsh, who hails from St. John's, plays the mayor of a small, shrinking town in Newfoundland in the new horror series.
She said the U.S. upping its aggression against Canada could be the "kick in the arse that the Canadian film industry needed," to back its own artistic works more fully.

"As a country we must support our own … culture, and we do a somewhat good job of that. But at times, you know, Canadians aren't always behind Canadian culture. They've sort of looked to the larger thing to the south, and so I think our eyes are sort of turning back to ourselves.
"If Mr. Trump did only one good thing, only one good thing, it would be that it made us realize that we are a country, and a country worth working together to save and to be."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alexandra Mae Jones is a senior writer for CBC News based in Toronto. She has written on a variety of topics, from health to pop culture to breaking news, and previously reported for CTV News and the Toronto Star. She joined CBC in 2024. You can reach her at alexandra.mae.jones@cbc.ca

articles.title: Fossilized 10,000-year-old mastodon tooth found by California scientist
articles.summary:
Molar from large mammal that once lived in North America is in ‘immaculate condition’ after discovery in Bay Area

A 10,000 year-old tooth in remarkable condition from an ancient Pacific…

blocks.text: A 10,000 year-old tooth in remarkable condition from an ancient Pacific mastodon, a large mammal that once inhabited North America, was recently discovered by a California scientist.
Brigid Lynch, a geomorphologist, was working at a preserve in San Mateo county, when she stumbled across a peculiar rock.
Paleontologists later confirmed it was not a stone, but an adult Pacific mastodon molar, according to a Wednesday news release from the Midpeninsula regional open space district (Midpen).

“The tooth itself is in immaculate condition. It’s the most complete mastodon molar from our area, and the most spectacular mastodon molar that I’ve ever seen. I had chills and shivers up and down my spine,” said paleontologist Wayne Thompson in a statement. “It’s another puzzle in the Ice Age saga that we can put into place.”

The pacific mastodon, related to modern-day elephants, were most prominent in the American west including what is now California, Oregon, the northern Rocky Mountain region and parts of Mexico. The herbivore mammal, which dates back about 2.5m years ago in North America, went extinct more than 10,000 years ago due to the climate crisis’s effects on their habitat coupled with overhunting from humans.
The fossilized tooth has been donated to Stanford University, where researchers at the school of sustainability will employ carbon dating to determine the molar’s exact age, according to Midpen.
“Fossils are our only opportunity to see into past biodiversity,” said Christine Garcia, a curator and manager of the geoscience specimen collection at Stanford.

“We can study fossils to better understand Earth’s past, past wildlife and the ecosystem they were a part of, and to help us make better predictions and better decisions about how to help our ecosystems and biodiversity thrive into the future.”
after newsletter promotion
Several ancient mastodon fossils have surfaced in recent years.

In 2024, a New York state resident found a mastodon jaw under the surface of their lawn. A year prior to that, a woman stumbled across a foot-long ancient mastodon tooth sticking out of the sand on a beach near California’s central coast.

articles.title: Gilas Pilipinas bounces back to set up key showdown vs rival China
articles.summary: SCHEDULE: Gilas Pilipinas men at Asian Games 2026 5×5 basketball The Philippines will face a huge obstacle in its bid to keep its title defense alive in the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games—a Great Wall, in…

blocks.text: The Philippines’ bench celebrates after a win against Kazakhstan. —SAMAHANG BASKETBOL NG PILIPINAS via Asian Games 2026
SCHEDULE: Gilas Pilipinas men at Asian Games 2026 5×5 basketball
The Philippines will face a huge obstacle in its bid to keep its title defense alive in the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games—a Great Wall, in fact.

Gilas Pilipinas kept its hopes afloat with a 109-78 victory over Kazakhstan on Saturday, but whether or not the Filipinos get to keep fighting for their crown will depend on the outcome against a familiar—and smarting—continental rival.
Robert Bolick delivered for Gilas, scoring 13 of his 20 points in the first half, when the Filipinos pulled away and bounced back after a shock 69-65 defeat to Bahrain in their opening tiff.

And the Gilas captain had every reason to feel good about himself after a sluggish showing during the two blowout losses against South Korea in Suwon prior to the Games and after failing to make an impact against Bahrain.
Bolick was a game-time decision after playing through a knee injury in the Bahrain matchup. Coach Tim Cone had said that Bolick got hurt during warmups.
Revenge in mind

Up next for the Philippines is China, which the country shamed in the last Asian Games in Hangzhou. China led by 20 on its home floor in the semifinal duel between the two Asian rivals, before Justin Brownlee sparked a comeback that resulted in a stunning Gilas win.

A win by the Philippines will assure the team a spot in the quarterfinals. A loss to China, which is aching for payback, could still leave a side door open for the Filipinos, who need to be the best third-placers to qualify.
The Philippines and Iran from Group B are currently at 1-1 while Saudi Arabia is at 0-2 in Group A.
Gilas, however, cannot afford a huge loss to China, which beat Bahrain, 105-59 earlier in the day. Bahrain takes on Kazakhstan on Monday.
Bolick wasn’t the only player who stepped up for the Philippines.
Jerrick Ahanmisi dropped three consecutive triples during a key stretch in the fourth that helped Gilas stretch its lead after Kazakhstan kept knocking on the door in the second half.
Ahanmisi added a fourth before the buzzer, ending as the game’s top scorer with 22 points.

Coach Tim Cone curiously handed the reins of the team to his assistant, Richard del Rosario, who had been one of those in charge of the Asian Games team while Cone was busy with the Fiba World Cup Asian Qualifiers.
And allowing Del Rosario to call the shots seemed to have worked well for Gilas. INQ

articles.title: UAAP: Behind solid core, host FEU looks to cause problems
articles.summary: UAAP SCHEDULE: Season 89 basketball tournament There’s a certain kind of pressure that comes with being the host school of the UAAP. And having the reigning MVP in your roster adds a little more…

blocks.text: Janrey Pasaol (left) and Jorick Bautista will lead the Tamaraws’ charge. —MARLO CUETO
UAAP SCHEDULE: Season 89 basketball tournament
There’s a certain kind of pressure that comes with being the host school of the UAAP. And having the reigning MVP in your roster adds a little more heat.
That doesn’t seem to bother Far Eastern University’s senior guard Jorick Bautista, who is graduating this school year.
In fact, he feels it might bother other schools.
“FEU’s going to be a problem. That’s all I can say,” Bautista told the Inquirer. “It’s exciting. We’re a bit nervous but that’s a part of it. I think we’ll enjoy this coming UAAP.”
“We don’t think about us hosting. Our focus now is the team. That’s it.”

That team will be led by Janrey Pasaol, Bautista’s backcourt running mate who won the MVP last season. Pasaol will have that extra burden on his shoulders as expectations on him rise, but coach Sean Chambers believes that the spitfire guard has the maturity to handle all of that.
“For Jan, I’m reminding him—and he’s taking it very well—that the expectations that we can put on ourselves should always be more than what anybody tries to put on us,” Chambers told the Inquirer.
“Whatever anybody else thinks outside our circle can never match what we’re going to put on ourselves.”

FEU is expected to be among the teams in contention for a spot in the Final Four—at the very least—in Season 89 of the men’s basketball tournament. After all, the Tamaraws barely made the semifinals last year after finishing with a 7-7 record, just one win behind fourth-seed and eventual champion La Salle (8-6).
And the team only got better this year. Pasaol certainly will be better.

The 23-year-old guard posted averages of 15.43 points, 7.5 assists, 4.14 rebounds and 2.14 steals per game to zoom past UST’s Nic Cabañero, Green Archer Mike Phillips and National U’s Jake Figueroa for the MVP plum.
And he can start thinking about something bigger.

“We’re talking about legacy when we talk about Jan,” Chambers, the Gilas Pilipinas assistant coach, said. “One of the things my high school coaches taught me was, ‘What kind of legacy will you leave behind?’ I live with that motto.”
“The expectations we’re putting on Jan, or Jan puts on himself, can never [be at the level of] what people [have]. They should always be higher.”

FEU’s cohesion will be key to its campaign, with school athletic director and league president Mark Molina, a former Tamaraws coach, saying that out of the team’s 15 local players, 11 are from its own high school program.
“We can expect this team to fight as one,” Molina said.
Pasaol, Bautista and foreign student-athlete Mo Konateh will be at the forefront of FEU’s bid, which kicks off against Adamson at noon on Sunday at Smart Araneta Coliseum.
Among the rookies from FEU’s high school program who will reinforce the team are UAAP junior stars Cabs Cabonillas and Marc Burgos.
Chambers will also enter the season with a little coaching improvement, after gathering added know-how from his stint with the national team.
As an assistant to national coach Tim Cone, Chambers helped the Philippines defeat Jordan and Iran in the recent window of the Fiba World Cup Asian qualifiers.

“It’s like a cheat code when we got a chance to examine and study teams like Jordan, Iran, New Zealand and Australia,” said Chambers. “I got to see it live, up close and personal, so there are things I’ll be bringing to the table.
“But at the end of the day, we’ll stick to what we do as Tamaraws.”
Defending champion La Salle will take on last season’s top seed National U at 2:30 to be followed by a blockbuster affair between the University of Santo Tomas and State U at 6 p.m. INQ

articles.title: PH Open to go on as scheduled at Southwoods’ Masters
articles.summary: The National Golf Association of the Philippines (NGAP) on Saturday stressed that the Philippine Open—the oldest national championship in Asia—will push through as scheduled from Nov. 12 to 15 even…

blocks.text: Julien Sale (left) acknowledges cheers from the gallery before he was presented the championship trophy by Al Panlilio last year. NGAP PHOTO

The National Golf Association of the Philippines (NGAP) on Saturday stressed that the Philippine Open—the oldest national championship in Asia—will push through as scheduled from Nov. 12 to 15 even after the withdrawal of BingoPlus as the main presenter.

The Philippine Sports Commission and the Asian Tour have stepped in as the tournament’s new chief backers, even as NGAP president Al Panlilio assured that the 72-hole championship will be at least a $1-million (around P63 million) event that the Masters of Manila Southwoods will host.

“We are very grateful to Chair Pato (Gregorio of the PSC), Mr. Cho (Minn Thant of the Asian Tour) and of course, to Manila Southwoods, that we will still be able to hold the event as scheduled,” said Panlilio, who came out of a crucial meeting with Asian Tour officials recently and secured the commitment of several other firms as sponsors.

“There are several other entities from different businesses which are very willing to make this happen,” Panlilio said. “We are just ironing out the details of everything before we make the announcement.”
The Masters course, as early as two months ago, is being spruced up to championship shape to challenge the best in the region.

Frenchman Julien Sale is the defending champion, breaking through as a pro last year while at the same time becoming the first debutant to win the PH Open. He fired a final round five-under-par 65 for a 269 total to win by a shot over Thailand’s Sadom Kaewkanjana and Tomoyo Ikemura of Japan.

Miguel Tabuena was in that field and gave a gallant chase to end up the best Filipino finisher, winding up just four shots behind the champion in front of a big crowd that followed him the entire week.

articles.title: Do not call her a racist: anti-Pauline Hanson strategists tell campaigners character attacks won’t work in Victoria
articles.summary:
Exclusive: strategic rethink urges progressive activists to respectfully steer one-on-one conversations with One Nation supporters towards economic concerns

  • Get our…

blocks.text: The message from strategists was blunt: do not, however tempting, personally attack Pauline Hanson or call her a racist.
The request has been made to progressive campaigners and unionists who have been asked to start one-on-one conversations with One Nation supporters before the Victorian election in November.
It is also indicative of a strategic rethink in response to One Nation’s sustained surge in public support and the party’s recent wins in state and federal byelections and in South Australia.

Separate training sessions run by the peak body for unions in Victoria, the Trades Hall Council, and the progressive campaign group GetUp, have warned members they may be inadvertently pushing people to One Nation by not respectfully engaging with their legitimate economic concerns.
“As best as you can, I know it’s hard, don’t make it personal,” a GetUp strategist told hundreds of members on a Thursday night Zoom call.

“Going after Pauline Hanson personally and calling her a racist, or going after her character, although very tempting, just confirms what people already believe: that she is an outsider and the establishment is attacking her.”

This is a change of approach for the progressive group, which spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on ads personally attacking Hanson and her deputy leader, Barnaby Joyce, during the Farrer byelection. The ads, which linked the pair to Donald Trump, had little impact. One Nation comfortably won the seat.

The reset, based on research conducted by the polling company Redbridge after the Farrer byelection, brought GetUp in line with advice from Trades Hall, which has been hosting training sessions for major unions in recent weeks.

Oscar Kaspi-Crutchett, a senior researcher at Trades Hall, says people thinking about voting for One Nation shut down when they perceive personal attacks on the party’s leadership that do not acknowledge their legitimate concerns.
“For many people, simply ignoring her racism is not going to be possible or desirable,” Kaspi-Crutchett said. “It’s what drives them to get involved in the fight against One Nation.
“In these cases, we need to make it very clear that Hanson’s racism isn’t merely a character flaw but a sophisticated political device. It manufactures differences between groups which have none.”
GetUp has also told campaigners to not personally attack Hanson’s billionaire benefactor.
“Pauline Hanson is closely tied to Gina Rinehart, and it’s a problem, but it’s not what the research says should be in focus,” GetUp told campaigners.

“It can be effective if it is raised organically by the person you’re speaking to but leading with it reads as a standard partisan attack, which triggers the same defensiveness as going after her character directly.”

This advice marks another change for the group, which in the weeks after the Farrer byelection published ads describing Hanson as a “wannabe billionaire” flying around in “mummy Gina’s” private plane.

Senior state and federal Labor sources, who declined to be named so they could speak freely, say these changes makes sense. They argue the group’s personal attacks on rightwing figures, including Peter Dutton during the 2016 and 2019 federal elections, were not helpful.
after newsletter promotion

GetUp’s decision to unveil a banner behind Hanson during her National Press Club address in June caused disquiet among Labor ranks, with some arguing it was unproductive. While the banner’s message focused on her record on wages, it also included cartoon images of cash flying around her.
‘Listen to the beat, not the lyrics’

Kaspi-Crutchett and his colleagues at Trades Hall are telling unionists to listen carefully for any hint of economic concerns that may be underpinning opinions about immigration, crime or culture wars.

“Pauline Hanson’s greatest weaknesses and the policy areas where she is the most vulnerable are the ones where the Labor movement has the highest trust from the public: working conditions, entitlements, maternity leave,” he says.
He says campaigners should resist the urge to fact-check conspiracy theories. Instead, conversations should be respectfully redirected to the economy.

“Don’t listen to the lyrics, listen to the beat of what they are saying,” he says. “What is consistent is their dissatisfaction with the status quo so get them to tease out what that looks like and how it makes them feel.
“There might be a spiel about Bill Gates but, eventually, you get to them saying ‘my kid can’t afford a house’.”

In June, the head of Trades Hall Council, Luke Hilakari, rebuked 23 state Labor MPs and candidates for having “zero conversations” with their constituents in the past two weeks, saying they needed to “work their ass off” to stop One Nation.
Kaspi-Crutchett said one-on-one conversations are vital because the politicians that once persuaded people against voting for Hanson had “lost credibility with the people she is targeting”.
“A nurse on the doorstep can do infinitely more than a legion of cabinet ministers and press secretaries.” Kaspi-Crutchett said.
“The trust has been exhausted.”

articles.title: Labor has had 12 years to fix Victorian roads. Turning to ‘pothole populism’ now may be too late
articles.summary:
Potholed roads are ‘devastating political advertising’ for the Victorian government – but Ben Carrol’s made them the focus of his campaign

  • Get our

blocks.text: At a press conference to celebrate the sold-out NFL match played at Melbourne’s MCG on Friday, the Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, was heckled on one issue.
“Fix the potholes,” a punter called out as they walked past the Victorian premier’s press conference.

No matter where you’re driving in Victoria – be it a rural road, regional freeway or an inner-city street – you’re bound to encounter one. Then comes the split-second decision: swerve into another lane, or power through and hope your tyres survive the impact?

For regional Victorians it has been an issue for years. In 2024, the National party began collating images for its “Potholes for All Seasons” calendar, which was distributed to MPs at state parliament last year.
But now potholes have become so omnipresent they could become the defining symbol of the Victorian election in November.

At the Nepean byelection in May, the opposition leader, Jess Wilson, and her successful candidate, Anthony Marsh, made it a central issue of the campaign – going so far as to fill a pothole themselves, prompting an investigation by the transport department.
