This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

The headlines have kept coming. In July, the ABC reported that seven cars were forced off the Calder Freeway near Gisborne due to tyre damage from potholes. In August, the Herald Sun reported a dismal 23 Victorian drivers had received compensation from the Transport Accident Commission for pothole damage over the last two years – despite thousands of complaints.

AI-generated ads for the political lobby group Fix Victoria feature potholes prominently. On Thursday, the group stood outside Parliament station handing out bumper stickers that read: “Not drunk, avoiding potholes”. At the same time, the Insurance Council of Australia chief executive Andrew Hall was telling reporters they had been “more claims for tyres and rim blowouts” in Victoria than other states, because of potholes.

An auditor general report tabled in state parliament on Wednesday examined more than 23,000km of Victorian roads and found almost half (48%) were rated in poor or very poor condition. It also found they were deteriorating faster than the government could repair them: the gap between the number of road defects recorded and those repaired doubled between January 2025 and June 2026.

According to the auditor general, the Department of Transport told the government before the May budget it needed $3bn a year to maintain road pavement at existing levels while replacing ageing assets.
But the government allocated only $1.04bn in the budget for 2026-27. That same financial year, it is forecast to spend $8.9bn on interest payments on state debt.
Toby Ralph, a marketer and researcher who has worked on more than 50 elections worldwide, said potholes were “devastating political advertising” of the state’s poor financial situation.
“They’re omnipresent, impossible to spin, and while motorists don’t study the state budget when they hit a pothole, they ask: with all the money being spent, why can’t you fix this?
“Potholes are the symptom. The deeper problem is a government that needs to get its finances and priorities back in order.”
after newsletter promotion

Since becoming premier in July, Carroll has attempted a reset, promising to focus the government on the “basics”. He’s announced an additional $300m to fix 500,000 potholes by the end of January, using money saved from delaying infrastructure projects and with help from prisoners.

He’s committed to a review of TAC claims and promised to bring maintenance work back in-house, which is significant given the auditor general said most major repairs were conducted by four external contractors.
The Coalition has pledged $5bn over four years to fix a million potholes – a 25% increase on current spending.

Some senior Labor sources have described the party’s pothole plan as an attempt to “neutralise” the politically damaging issue, an approach questioned by Lissie Ratcliffe, chief of staff for Daniel Andrews when he was premier.

“If you are stuck in the issues that your opponents are stronger and more trusted on, it is very difficult to win from there,” she said on the Socially Democratic podcast. She urged Carroll to “change the debate and get it on to a ground where, ideally, we’ve got a new idea or two and people think we’re the best people to deliver”.

Others within the party have compared the strategy to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s “pothole populism”. The democratic socialist has made repairing potholes quickly part of his pitch to rebuild trust in government, telling reporters: “If you want someone to believe in the promise of a transformative vision … you have to first deliver on the thing that diminishes their faith on a daily basis.

“If you are driving your car or you’re riding your bike and you hit the same pothole every single day, why would you trust city government in its ability to deliver something that you have never seen at that scale, when it can’t even do this?” Mandani said.

But there’s a problem with that comparison. Mamdani is using potholes to prove his new style of government can deliver on its big, bold, progressive agenda. Carroll doesn’t have one. Instead, he’s pitching himself as fixing a problem his government has allowed to deteriorate over 12 years in office.

articles.title: NSW government paid for homeless man to be sent back to New Zealand instead of offering housing
articles.summary:
Local council and state government attempting to move on residents living in an encampment by the river in Wagga Wagga

  • Get our

blocks.text: The New South Wales government paid for a homeless man in Wagga Wagga to be sent back to New Zealand instead of offering him temporary accommodation, in an attempt to move on residents living in an encampment by a river.
The local council and state government have been attempting to clear out the encampment for several months after a newborn baby died in May when its mother gave birth to twins in a tent.

Residents of the encampment have faced increasing pressure to move on, including “compliance action” requests for them to leave or be fined up to $1,100. Advocates said at least four people have been fined about $110 for not moving on in time. The council has denied fining people “on the basis of where they are staying”.

Mark Hudson, 53, said he has permanent residency in Australia and is therefore entitled to temporary accommodation. He arrived 18 years ago, but does not have a ​​​​​​​​​​Visa Entitlement Verification Online – to prove permanent residency. Despite this, Homes NSW repeatedly offered him a flight back to New Zealand, where he has not lived for over 18 years.
“They kept pressuring me,” Hudson said. “[The Homes NSW officer] offered it to me first, like six, seven times. She just kept on … ‘You want the flight? You want the flight?’”

This week, they booked the flight to Sydney and then Auckland, at a cost to the taxpayer of $1,797. On Thursday the international flight was cancelled by the airline, and Hudson, who has a girlfriend in Wagga, and is about to take custody of his granddaughter, is still in Wagga. He also has a dog he does not want to leave.
“They were chasing me all day yesterday to try and sort it out. They were like, we’ll sort the tickets out, we’ll arrange it again … But I’ve got my granddaughter now.”
On Friday, after Guardian Australia contacted the NSW government, Hudson was offered accommodation, which he is expected to move into next week.
“I didn’t want to leave Wilks [Park],” Hudson said. “I wanted to stay in Wagga. And it was just the approach was always bully tactics,” he said.

A spokesperson for Homes NSW said it has been working with people facing housing insecurity in the area since April. It confirmed travel costs, including air fares, were one of the support options available.

“Where a person is not eligible for social housing or other support services in New South Wales and requests assistance to return to their home country, Homes NSW may assist with that request as part of an individual support plan,” the spokesperson said.
“Homes NSW have been working with Mark, a New Zealand citizen, who initiated discussions about returning to New Zealand where he has family.
“If he has decided not to return to New Zealand, Homes NSW will continue to work with him to identify alternative accommodation, noting he is not eligible for social housing.”

In April, a Guardian Australia investigation revealed that former international student, 32-year-old Nepali born Bikram Lama, Sydney’s “birdman”, died at central Sydney’s St James station in December where he had been sleeping rough.
His death exposed a gap in federal and state responses to homelessness for people who lose their visa status or are unable to prove permanent residency.
after newsletter promotion

NSW residents need to prove permanent residency to access social housing, normally through Centrelink payments. If permanent residents have been in Australia for more than 10 years, they can receive six months’ worth of payments. Hudson was previously receiving Centrelink payments for six months, before being cut off. New Zealand citizens on special category visas are also entitled to emergency housing.
Housing advocate Timothy Verhoef said it was a failure of the state government to offer Hudson a flight before offering him a home.
“It has been a failure because they’ve paid $1,700 and nothing’s happened. It’s pushing the problem around.”

Hudson has worked most of his life in Australia, as a truck driver and farm manager in Western Australia. He moved to Wagga to be closer to family in the area. He was not able to find work, so has been living in a tent by the river for almost two years, while getting help from family and eating at charities. Asked how he managed to survive, Hudson said “faith”.
“You just rely on [public] showers and Vinnie’s to get through, and mates.
“I would take temporary housing, but because I didn’t get on the plane, I guess they’ll hate me … I want to get some sort of housing first. Yeah, some sort of help.”
Verhoef said the council, state government and local authorities had failed to provide genuine solutions for the people living along the river encampment.
“The reality is that they haven’t worked together on anything substantial – they are just pushing a narrative to make it look like they are addressing the issue.”

articles.title: ‘Small price to pay’: The young homeowners welcoming falling house prices even as it hurts them
articles.summary:
Some buyers say they are ready to absorb the fallout of housing weakness if it means boosting home ownership across the board

  • Get our

blocks.text: Falling property prices have come at the worst possible time for Alex Hogan and his partner. They are now weighing up whether they can afford to have another child.
Locked out of the established housing market, the Queensland couple resorted to buying a block of land to build a family home.

Fast-rising construction costs are now limiting their options and the anticipated value of their finished home is sliding, as rising interest rates and the government’s property tax reforms drag down property prices.
Yet Hogan wants the government to go even further in tackling the housing affordability crisis.
“If you don’t seize that momentum when there’s a push for it, then things can just go back to bubbling away under the surface and nothing ever gets done about them,” the 41-year-old says.

blocks.caption: Alex Hogan is feeling the pain of a slowing property market, but argues it’s still better than having a two-tier society. Photograph: Rhett Wyman/The Guardian

blocks.text: Although falling prices are frustrating many property owners, and price falls leave Labor vulnerable to political attacks, there are some homeowners willing to accept lower valuations in order to make housing more accessible for others.
Hogan is among several recent property buyers Guardian Australia spoke to who is prepared to absorb the fallout if it helps close the growing divide between forever renters and their landlords.
“It might end up sucking,” Hogan says. “But it’s better than having a two-tier society.”
Prices could fall 10%
House prices are falling across the country amid higher borrowing costs, a weak economy, and a once-in-a-generation change in the tax treatment of property investors.
The government’s critics have blamed the downturn on Labor’s May budget reforms, which included getting rid of negative gearing for new investors, excluding new builds.

“Australian families already struggling to pay their bills are now sitting at the kitchen table watching the value of their biggest asset, their family home, fall through the floor,” Tim Wilson, the Liberal Treasury spokesman, said earlier this month.

Prices around Australia have fallen 3.6% from their peak earlier this year, according to Cotality data, led by steep declines in Sydney. The most expensive markets are falling the most, in a sign interest rates are a dominant cause.
Falls of more than 10% have been forecast by some analysts as elevated inflation makes a fourth rate hike more likely in coming months.

Most long-term home owners have enjoyed years of growth, which has included a 26% price surge in just the three years to March. Newer buyers who missed the boom are most affected by the recent weakness.
Eibhlinn Cassidy bought a Melbourne apartment two years ago. They know loan repayments could spike when they refinance next year if the value of the apartment falls.

Yet the 30-year-old junior doctor is stoic about the downturn if it makes housing more affordable because they remember the constant anxiety of grappling with soaring rents, weak tenant rights and losing bonds.
“I’d stress about it if it happened but, either way, I’ve got to be paying either rent or a mortgage and I’d rather be somewhere I can put paint on the walls,” Cassidy says.
“Even if I have to eat it, then big deal … I consider it a really small price to pay for a long overdue adjustment in the market that will let more people get in.”

Terry Rawnsley, a KPMG economist, says many recent buyers won’t have to refinance anytime soon and should be able to wait out the downturn. Prices are expected to rise again once the RBA starts cutting interest rates, likely in 2028.
after newsletter promotion
“If you’re in a situation where you bought in the last 12 or 18 months, or you come into refinancing, you might be felling a bit of stress,” Rawnsley says.
“But if you don’t have to sell at this point in time, that paper loss is just a theoretical one and you don’t have to worry about it.”
‘I do not want to be a landlord’
Australian homes were turned into unaffordable wealth-building assets after a surge in prices in the 90s and early 2000s, thanks largely to favourable tax settings for investors.

Experts expect the current downturn and the loss of those settings to push the Australian mentality back in the other direction – in part because those who played by the old rules could soon find themselves in financial pain.
Remy Coll, a 37-year-old business owner, has become an accidental property investor after the price falls made it impossible for him to sell his old house.

blocks.caption: Remy Coll bought a property in Canberra’s inner north earlier this year but has become an accidental landlord after being forced by the drop in prices to hold onto the outer suburbs home he had intended to immediately sell. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

blocks.text: When he bought in Canberra’s inner north earlier this year, he used his old home on the city’s outer fringe as collateral with a view to sell it soon after settling. The government announced its tax reforms the following week and, months later, the median Canberra home is now $44,000 cheaper.
Coll says he is now stuck with rising repayments on two mortgages, taking rent from tenants he doesn’t want.

“I do not want to be a landlord,” he says. “I do not want to contribute to the problem of rentals. But equally, now the house that I live in is contingent upon me getting a certain price for that house.”
Selling in the current market would mean he loses money on his first purchase, while potentially grappling with a higher interest rate on his second purchase as the bank revalues.
He and his partner are working extra hours and spending less time with their young children to hold on to their home as prices fall. He still believes the Albanese government did the right thing.
“That period of [price] reduction will be painful for probably a lot of people like me, and maybe some investors,” Coll says.
“But in the future, as long as real estate grows by a small amount [and] peoples’ wages grow more ... people will be able to, in their early 30s, start to afford a house again.”

articles.title: Fire at nursing home in Chile kills 16 residents
articles.summary: Ten people were evacuated from the home in Araucanía region in central Chile.

blocks.text: At least 16 elderly residents have died in a fire at a nursing home in Chile, according to authorities.
Ten others were evacuated after a blaze broke out at El Edén home in /idt2/d9cfcc9a-2842-463f-a4d8-4dd007ef9547, around 640km (400 miles) south of the capital Santiago, on Friday evening.
Jorge Granada, a prosecutor leading the case, said it was not clear at this stage what caused the incident.
Chile's President José Antonio Kast said he had ordered a review into the condition of nursing homes across the country.

"We will fully collaborate with the justice system to clarify what happened, determine where failures may have existed in oversight or prevention, identify what alerts were raised and what actions were taken in response to them," Kast said.
"We need to know the truth and, based on that, correct whatever is necessary to do everything possible to prevent a tragedy like this from happening again," thre president added.
The fire, which began at around 22:30 (01:30 GMT) was finally put out on Saturday morning.
On Saturday, firefighters were still clearing debris and removing collapsed corrugated metal roofing. Police cordoned off the area for safety.
"It is a situation that fills our souls with great sorrow and pain. We have been... providing support to the families," said local mayor Jacqueline Romero.

articles.title: Trump asks Smithsonian to install ‘Colossus statue’ of George Washington with exhibit
articles.summary:
Trump, again trying to curate museum, says exhibit would stay until 2032 for 300th anniversary of Washington’s birth

Donald…

blocks.text: Donald Trump asked the Smithsonian Institution to install a 30ft “Colossus statue” of George Washington outside the National Museum of American History, and a special exhibit honoring the nation’s first president, in a social media post late on Friday.
The president requested that the exhibit continue through February 2032, the 300th anniversary of Washington’s birth.
“He is easily America’s Greatest Hero. Without him, our Country and our Freedoms wouldn’t exist,” Trump posted on Truth Social as he flew to his golf course in Ireland.
The statue of Washington would replace the current Infinity sculpture by New York artist José de Rivera, commissioned by the federal government and installed in 1967.

Trump’s latest request underscores a perception that he sees himself as curator-in-chief of the nation’s national museum. His administration issued a 162-page report in March 2025 accusing the museum of focusing too much on oppression, social justice and division rather than shared national achievements.
In July, Trump ordered the interior department to display signs in front of the Smithsonian National Museum of American History that accuse the institution of inaccuracy.

The order declared signs outside the National Museum of American History “shall notify visitors that the museum exhibits should be renovated consistent with the findings in the report”. Those signs have yet to appear.

In Friday’s post, Trump complained that the Smithsonian currently doesn’t mention Washington’s fabled crossing of the Delaware River during the Revolutionary War, which he called “one of the greatest moments and turning points of the Revolution”.
Nor, he said, was Washington’s victory at Trenton mentioned. “Stories of the Americans who fought and died for our Independence, deserve far more attention,” he wrote.

Instead of a Center for Restorative History – a recently ended museum initiative to spotlight spotlights stories that have been excluded from the national historical narrative – Trump said the museum should have a “Center for American Heroes.”

But it is not clear that Trump has the power to order the museum to make the change. The Smithsonian operates outside the executive branch and its leadership is overseen by a board of regents that includes JD Vance, Chief Justice John Roberts, a bipartisan group of lawmakers and a group of citizens.
Last week, the Smithsonian’s secretary, Lonnie Bunch, announced he will step down by the end of the year, after seven years leading the institution.

“We’re at a time when people are challenging that independence,” Bunch earlier told the Washington Post. “but I feel very strongly that it is as independent as we were before, and that I will continue to fight – for as long as I’m in this chair – for the independence of the Smithsonian.”

The administration appears to be expanding its reach into arts and culture. For Constitution Day on 17 September, Trump asked the Smithsonian to install the 11ft statue of Washington featured at the recent Freedom 250 IndyCar race in the museum’s Flag Hall.

The board of the Kennedy Center, comprised largely of Trump appointees, recently removed Blue, a sculpture by the late New York artist Joel Shapiro, which had been on the grounds of the center since 2019. There had been no public announcement or consultation ahead of its removal.

Statues are a consistent theme in Trump’s many efforts to remake Washington – including a proposal for a “Garden of Heroes” along the Potomac River to display statues of 250 prominent Americans – and he has installed a statue of Washington in the recently remodeled Rose Garden patio.

But art in two dimensions is also included in the effort. Last month, the state department said it is contemplating selling a painting by Kehinde Wiley that it removed from the US embassy in the Dominican Republic.

The canvas, titled Young Artists after Siamesas 1960, features two young Dominican women standing, flanked by two seated male counterparts. It was commissioned from Wiley – who went on to paint Barack Obama’s official portrait – in 2013.
Erin Scavino, the director of Art in Embassies, called the painting “very woke”, adding that “it was by the gentleman who did Obama’s portrait, and it was aesthetically terrifying.”

articles.title: Former US detention officer charged with 20 counts of felony forgery
articles.summary:
Michael Diehl allegedly forged magistrates’ signatures in North Carolina to allow enough time for ICE to take custody of prisoners

A former Guilford county detention officer in North…

blocks.text: A former Guilford county detention officer in North Carolina faces forgery charges in connection to 20 alleged forged Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detainment documents, according to a Guilford county sheriff’s office (GCSO) news release.

Guilford county’s sheriff, Danny H Rogers, reported that on Friday the Guilford county magistrate’s office notified the GCSO of a potentially forged court document submitted by GCSO detention officer Michael Diehl, 40.

“The document, entitled ‘Order After Receipt of ICE Detainer and Administrative Warrant’, an AOC-CR-662 form, was associated with an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detainer issued for inmate Claudio Nepornuceno,” the statement read.

“Upon review, the Magistrate’s Office and GCSO Detention staff determined that the document contained the allegedly forged signature of a different magistrate who didn’t process Nepornuceno’s initial arrest,” the statement added.

Under North Carolina law, when inmates are subject to an ICE detainer, they must see a magistrate with a copy of the ICE detainer. Afterwards, the magistrate can issue an AOC-CR-662 form, which allows the detention center to hold the inmate for up to 48 hours beyond the time they would otherwise be entitled to be released from custody. The 48-hour window allows ICE an opportunity to take custody of the inmate.
However, the GCSO found that Nepornuceno was not presented before the magistrate with the detainer. Instead, the form containing the magistrate’s allegedly forged signature was submitted.
A further investigation into the GCSO’s jail booking records identified 19 additional AOC-CR-662 forms associated with 19 additional inmates that contained allegedly forged signatures of magistrates.
The investigation found that in each of these 20 cases, ICE had issued a detainer based on evidence that the inmate who was the subject of the detainer was in violation of US immigration law.
During the GCSO’s criminal investigation into the matter, Diehl’s employment with the sheriff’s office was terminated.
And as a result of the investigation, Diehl was arrested and charged with 20 counts of felony common law forgery.
He received a $5,000 secured bond and has since been released from custody.
The investigation remains ongoing and additional charges may follow.
The investigation into Diehl comes as the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown continues across the country.
Since Trump’s inauguration, a record number of individuals – more than 70,000 – have been detained by ICE.

articles.title: ‘Be productively paranoid,’ Globe CEO tells team
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — If there’s one thing that Globe Telecom Inc. president and CEO Carl Cruz does not shy away from, it’s subscribing to the telco’s perennial rival, Smart Communications Inc. of…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — If there’s one thing that Globe Telecom Inc. president and CEO Carl Cruz does not shy away from, it’s subscribing to the telco’s perennial rival, Smart Communications Inc. of PLDT Inc.
And it’s not just one subscription. Cruz keeps separate smartphones for Smart’s prepaid and postpaid services, plus another for duopoly challenger DITO Telecommunity.
Of course, he also has Globe prepaid and postpaid phones, along with one for the telco’s digital brand GOMO.

It is Cruz’s way of keeping tabs on the competition as he seeks to preserve Globe’s No. 1 spot in the Philippine mobile business, where it has nearly 70 million subscribers and which remains its top moneymaker, raking in more than P60 billion in the first half alone.

That Globe is already the market leader in mobile connectivity is no reason for complacency, if you ask Cruz. Even with the telco titan at the top, he still wants to know exactly what his competitors’ customers are experiencing.

“To my mind, and it’s proven, if you’re able to offer the best-in-class experience, customers would stay with you,” Cruz tells Sunday Biz in an interview in his office at the Globe Tower in Bonifacio Global City.
But that obsession—or being “anal,” as he describes it—with network experience does not mean Globe is losing sight of businesses where it does not yet have the edge.

Cruz knows all too well that the Philippine telco landscape is becoming far more than just about calls, texts and data. And as he settles into his second year at the helm, he is embarking on a mission to turn Globe’s sprawling digital assets into new engines of growth.
‘Digital orchestrator’

There is still a long runway, he believes, as many Philippine businesses have yet to fully embark on their digital transformation. Where corporate clients once came to Globe mainly for mobile lines, Cruz says they are increasingly looking for cybersecurity, cloud and other digital solutions.
Broadband presents another opportunity, although Cruz readily acknowledges that Globe remains in “catch-up mode” against larger rivals.

And then there are data centers, where demand has accelerated on the back of artificial intelligence (AI). Globe-backed STT GDC Philippines expects to have 30 to 32 megawatts of capacity by yearend, which Cruz says could already be fully utilized.
Rather than treating these businesses in isolation, Cruz wants Globe’s network, data centers, subsea cables and digital platforms to work as one ecosystem.
“We want to be the main digital orchestrator of the digital economy of the Philippines,” Cruz says.
A different world

It is an ambitious vision coming from someone who spent most of his career mastering another sector: fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG), where Cruz worked for three decades before making the big leap into the cutthroat telco business.

When he eventually entered telco through Airtel in Africa, the learning curve was steep. Three weeks into the job, Cruz reviewed the copious notes he had been taking and realized he still did not know what to do.
“So, I had to raise my hand and say, you know, I need help,” he recalls.
Cruz later found out that while telco could be simpler than FMCG in some respects, it is far more intense operationally because data —and customer feedback — come almost instantaneously.
But fret not, because that is exactly what Cruz had been looking for. “It’s music to my ears,” he says.
Into the trenches
By the time Cruz joined Globe in January 2025 and took over as CEO that April, he was no longer a stranger to telco after his stint at Airtel, now one of the world’s biggest telco brands.

Still, Globe was a different behemoth altogether. Apart from its core telco operations, Cruz inherited a growing portfolio of digital businesses, including fintech arm Mynt Inc., operator of GCash, which is now preparing for a landmark listing on the Philippine Stock Exchange in October.
More than a year into the job, Cruz says he is settling deeper into the role.

“I think I’m a bit more really in the trenches in terms of how we operate,” he says. “Whenever I move on to a new role, or a new market, or a new country, the first thing I always do is get myself immersed in operations.”
“Having been doing this for the last year and a half has given me that level of awareness in terms of where we really need to go,” he says.
“But I’m not at all being complacent,” he quickly adds.

That immersion can look like this: Mondays are largely reserved for meetings with his network team, where Cruz watches metrics such as video stall rates. At least once a week, he eats at the company canteen to hear what employees are dealing with and spot processes that can be simplified.
What’s next
Cruz is also looking far into the future.

As artificial intelligence (AI) changes how people use devices, Cruz says Globe is already studying a “future state architecture” capable of handling heavier data and latency requirements. That could mean peppering the country with smaller “edge” data centers closer to users as AI-powered devices and wearables become more commonplace.

Even Globe’s physical stores are being reconsidered. Cruz wants the company to be equally strong online and offline, with new flagship stores in the works that could eventually cater to enterprise customers as well as consumers.

Cruz says these are all part of his order to his team to be “productively paranoid.” This means constantly studying what global operators such as T-Mobile, Airtel, KDDI and Singtel are doing and measuring Globe against the best.
“Don’t get me wrong, we’re very good,” Cruz says. “But I always feel that someone is always going to be ahead.” INQ

articles.title: Legarda spox calls Ombudsman probe 'political persecution'
articles.summary: A spokesperson for Senator Loren Legarda has described the Ombudsman"s investigation into the senator and her son, Batangas Representative Leandro Leviste, as “lawfare” and “political persecution.”

blocks.text: A spokesperson for Senator Loren Legarda has described the Ombudsman’s investigation into the senator and her son, Batangas Representative Leandro Leviste, as “lawfare” and “political persecution.”
Legarda and Leviste are facing complaints before the Ombudsman over Leviste’s solar power firm.

In a statement on Friday, Atty. Antonio “Tony” La Viña said Legarda was facing “classic lawfare,” which he described as the weaponization of the law for political purposes and noted that it had traditionally been used against government critics and opposition figures.

“This is classic lawfare, the weaponization of the law for political purposes. Sadly, this is not the first time it has happened. Previous administrations have done it as well to opposition politicians, government critics, journalists, Supreme Court justices, and social and political activists,” said La Viña, a former dean of the Ateneo School of Government.

La Viña, who said he has worked with Legarda for three decades, cited the senator’s environmental legislation and said she had never been investigated or charged with corruption or similar offenses during her decades as a public official.

The Office of the Ombudsman announced in July that it had launched an investigation into Legarda and Leviste following allegations that Leviste’s renewable energy company failed to supply electricity as mandated by its legislative franchise.

Prior to the Ombudsman probe, the Department of Energy (DOE) filed a complaint with the Department of Justice (DOJ) against Leviste and five executives of Solar Para sa Bayan Corporation (SPBC) for alleged violations of the Public Service Act.

Ombudsman Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla claimed Legarda was linked to the case because her son’s company could not have secured its 2019 franchise without her influence as then-chairperson of the Senate finance committee.

La Viña defended Legarda, emphasizing that no formal charges have been filed against her or Leviste. He said, however, that the Ombudsman’s public pronouncements already conveyed an “unmistakable impression that liability has already been assumed,” even though the matters involving them remain at the preliminary investigation stage.
Both Legarda and Leviste have filed their counter-affidavits.
In his radio program on dzRH on Saturday, Remulla said it appeared that Legarda, who is currently on medical leave, did not want to return home from France.
La Viña, in response, said, “Walang sinabi na ganyan sa akin si Senator Loren (Senator Loren never told me anything like that).”
Timing
According to La Viña, Legarda’s inclusion in the Ombudsman’s probe and its timing raise questions about whether the scrutiny is based on evidence or driven by political motives.

“The subsequent inclusion of Senator Legarda in an Ombudsman preliminary investigation, and the timing with which that proceeding emerged, inevitably raise questions about whether the scrutiny against her is grounded in evidence of her own acts or is being driven by the wider political issues surrounding her son,” La Viña said.

He noted that Legarda does not own, run, or participate in SPBC or any Solar Philippines company, adding that being both a parent and a senator does not establish that she benefited, acted improperly, or committed a crime.
“Senator Legarda should not be shielded from scrutiny because Leviste is her son. But neither should motherhood become evidence against her,” he added.
La Viña said Legarda should only be scrutinized based on concrete evidence showing that she improperly intervened with government officials or benefited from the grant of the franchise.

“But the record establishes important facts: the franchise was non-exclusive, it did not provide for government subsidy, its implementation depended in part on regulatory actions assigned to the DOE, and Senator Legarda herself did not vote for its passage,” La Viña said.
‘Out-of-the-box entrepreneur’

La Viña also defended Leviste, maintaining that he did not commit any illegal acts and describing him as an “out-of-the-box entrepreneur” who introduced “new ideas and approaches to fast-track the energy transition.”

“In any case, Leandro introduced new ideas and approaches to fast-track the energy transition, and there may have been policy gaps that prevented the successful implementation of some of those ideas,” La Viña said.

“But that is not a criminal act. He should be praised, not punished, for that. In the same way, he should be lauded and not harassed for his crusade against corruption. Note that harassment against them started only in late 2025 when Leandro exposed corruption,” he added.
La Viña also pointed to the sequence of events leading up to the complaints against Leviste.

He said that after Leviste publicly exposed corruption in late 2025 and called for government-wide investigations, a steady stream of allegations and “investigations” targeting his projects began to surface.
“In conclusion, I reiterate my earlier point that lawfare—weaponization of the law for political ends and gain—is always wrong and in fact unlawful,” La Viña said.
“What is going on is clearly political persecution,” he added. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Portsmouth experiences second weekend of anti-immigration protests
articles.summary:
Rightwing activists faced a heavy police presence and counter-demonstrations to their march against small boat crossings

Two men and a teenage boy have been arrested in Portsmouth at a…

blocks.text: Two men and a teenage boy have been arrested in Portsmouth at a far-right protest against immigration.
Far-right activists have gathered in Portsmouth for a second weekend after a small boat with 140 people seeking asylum on board was intercepted last Sunday while heading towards the city.
They were greeted by counter-protesters as police warned they would not tolerate incitement of fear or violence.

One of the arrested, a 76-year-old man from Southampton, was detained on suspicion of concealing his identity at the Portsmouth protest. Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary had warned that protesters wearing face coverings could be arrested under powers in the Crime and Policing Act.

A 33-year-old man from Portsmouth was also arrested on suspicion of obstructing a highway and a 16-year-old boy, also from Portsmouth, was arrested on suspicion of violent disorder in relation to scenes last Sunday.

blocks.caption: Protesters gather for a counter-demonstration in Portsmouth on Saturday. Photograph: James Veysey/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Donna Jones, the police and crime commisioner for Hampshire and Isle of Wight, said that they “thankfully didn’t see repeated scenes of Sunday night with assaults on police officers and criminal damage to police vehicles and people’s property” and that “with the exception of a few people, it was peaceful and conducted in accordance with the new law calling for their faces to be uncovered”.
Jones added: “The people of Portsmouth deserve to go about their business without fear and disruption.
“While some may think it was arbitrary to use the new power directing people to remove face coverings, the police ensured it was implemented equally and impartially for everyone involved.
“I will ensure this power is used proportionately in the future for both sides of the spectrum of protesters.”

blocks.caption: Demonstrators at an anti-immigration march in Portsmouth on Saturday.  Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PA

blocks.text: In Portsmouth city centre, there was a large police presence where demonstrators assembled to march on Saturday.
Some protesters held union flags while some wearing Portsmouth patriot branded clothing gathered outside All Saints Church on Commercial Road.
A man with a megaphone got the crowd chanting “stop the boats”. He said the protest was against “illegal men invading the shores”.

In the neighbouring car park, demonstrators holding Stand Up to Racism (SUTR) and Refugees Welcome banners gathered. Signs included: “RNLI are heroes, no one is illegal” and “stop pretending your racism is patriotism”.
Hundreds of people also gathered in Glasgow for an anti-immigration rally and associated counter-protest.

blocks.caption: The Pink Ladies event in Glasgow. The event passed off peacefully amid a heavy police presence and segregation of opposing protesters. Photograph: Iain Masterton/Alamy Live News

blocks.text: The Pink Ladies movement organised their event at Glasgow Green, prompting opposing groups, including SUTR, to arrange a counter-protest.
The two groups were contained in separate areas on the eastern side of the park, with the People’s Palace and a heavy police presence between them.
Ch Supt Stevie Dolan warned of a “strong response” if there was any violence after flashpoints at a previous protest in the same park in July.
MSPs Alison Thewliss, a Scottish government minister, and Iris Duane were at the SUTR rally, with the Scottish Trades Union Congress general secretary Roz Foyer.

blocks.caption: Police officers contain counter-protesters against a Pink Ladies rally beside Glasgow’s People’s Palace. Photograph: Steve Welsh/PA

blocks.text: Prominent figures on the Scottish right, such as Reform UK’s deputy leader in Scotland, Thomas Kerr, and the Reform councillor Audrey Dempsey, attended the Pink Ladies event.

Saturday’s protests came after hundreds of far-right activists descended on Portsmouth last Sunday after a small boat crossing the Channel approached the city. The demonstrators tried to stop those onboard from being processed.
Hampshire police said: “We will support those who want to express their views peacefully and lawfully, but we will not tolerate those whose only aim is to create fear and incite violence.”

The opposing groups were allocated specific locations at which they could gather under protest conditions. Failure to comply with conditions could lead to arrest, police said. The anti-immigration protest marched to Guildhall Square and the counter-protest followed later on the same route.

blocks.caption: Lifejackets at Eastney abandoned by people seeking asylum who made the crossing from France on 6 September. Photograph: Ollie Thompson/Solent News & Photo Agency/Solent News

blocks.text: The incident with the small boat last Sunday is thought to be the first time such a large vessel containing asylum seekers has been brought to Portsmouth and the first time a significant group of anti-migrant protesters have tried to block newly arrived asylum seekers from being processed.

Small boat crossings have fallen by more than 40% compared with the same period last year. While the Home Office has disrupted the smugglers’ business model, their methods appear to have evolved by launching boats – such as the one that arrived on last Sunday – from different parts of the French coast much farther from the UK, making the crossings more dangerous.

Most small boat arrivals are rescued by Border Force and RNLI vessels on the English side of the Channel and brought ashore at Dover. RNLI volunteers and staff have faced abuse from protesters over their rescue work bringing some small boat migrants ashore.
The first man charged over last weekend’s anti-migrant demonstration in Portsmouth appeared in court on Saturday.

blocks.caption: Police officers at Eastney beach, Portsmouth, where hundreds of protesters gathered to meet a small boat arriving from France. Photograph: PA

blocks.text: Del Leon Somerville, 42, of Paulsgrove in Portsmouth, appeared before the city’s magistrates court charged with violent disorder and assaulting a police constable in the execution of their duty.

Assistant chief constable Tony Rowlinson said Somerville’s arrest was the “first of what we fully anticipate to be a number of arrests” and hoped it would send a “clear warning” to those planning future disruption and disorder.

The government condemned what it described as the “thuggish behaviour” of the protesters last Sunday. “We condemn the intimidating and thuggish behaviour we are seeing tonight,” a government spokesperson said. “The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but it must never cross a line into disorder.”

The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, met police on Thursday for reassurance they are ready to move quickly in dealing with “far-right groups” seeking to intimidate communities after last weekend’s events in Dover and Portsmouth. Official vehicles were damaged in Portsmouth and a small number of officers were injured, police said. In Dover, crowds of masked men blocked road access to the port in scenes that were condemned by politicians of all parties.

Mahmood said: “These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents.
“This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons.”

articles.title: Bulgaria investigates fire at weapons site that owner calls sabotage
articles.summary: Officials are not ruling out "outside interference", while the company says the blaze at its site was sabotage.

blocks.text: Bulgaria is investigating the cause of an overnight fire at an ammunition storage site run by a private defence company.

Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev said the authorities "are not ruling out outside interference" in the incident in central Bulgaria. No-one was injured in the blaze that triggered a series of explosions.

EMCO company, whose weapons are used by Ukraine against invading Russian forces, said the fire at its site was sabotage and that human error was "completely ruled out". It did not say who might be responsible.
The latest incident follows last month's fire and blasts at another EMCO ammunition warehouse in the area.

In a statement, EMCO said the storage facility that was burned this time - near the central village of Gorni Varpishta, some 170km (106 miles) east of the capital Sofia - had not been used for months and was inspected just 20 days ago, when full compliance with all regulations was confirmed.
It cited a number of similar incidents at Bulgarian defence firms since 2011, saying that the latest was "no exception to the series of acts of sabotage against the Bulgarian defence industry".
"As the EU and Nato member state most severely affected by such actions, Bulgaria must join the collective effort to prevent and neutralise these attacks," EMCO said.
The firm is run by Bulgarian arms dealer Emilian Gebrev, who Bulgarian prosecutors allege has already been targeted by Russian agents.
This includes a poisoning attempt in 2015 of Gebrev, his son and another company employee - three Russian nationals were later charged in absentia for attempted murder.
Bulgaria is a major weapons supplier to Ukraine, as it continues to repel a full-scale Russian invasion launched in 2022.
And although Sofia has recently halted state-owned arms supplies to Ukraine, Bulgarian private defence companies continue such transfers.
Russia appears to have recently escalated its sabotage campaign across Europe.
Last week, Germany said Russia was responsible for August's drone attack at Leipzig's airport - a claim denied by Moscow as "absurd".
There have also been a number of suspicious fires at defence facilities from Italy to Estonia, with some of the affected countries blaming Russia.

articles.title: Céline Dion fans prepare for comeback concert in Paris

blocks.text: Céline Dion greeted fans today as she left her hotel, hours before she kicked off her comeback concert in Paris.

The Canadian singer returns to the stage on Saturday for her first full concert in six years, to open a sell-out Paris residency after a battle with a rare neurological disorder put a pause in her career.
Some fans arrived as early as 06:00 to get a spot in front of LeRoyal Monceau hotel to catch a glimpse of the star before she left.
She is one of the best-selling music artists of all time and is due to perform a series of 26 concerts over the next eight months.

articles.title: Baghdad confirms attack on Saudi pipeline came from Iraq
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia has said it will not relatiate and wants Iraq to "take the necessary measures." Baghdad is under pressure from the United States to rein in Iran-backed militias.

image.caption: The Iraqi government is under US pressure to rein in Iran-backed militiasImage: Iraqi Prime Minister's Press Office/Handout/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Iraq's government confirmed on Saturday that Friday night attacks on a key Saudi oil pipeline had been launched from Iraqi territory.
Saudi Arabia said that it shut down the pipeline on Friday, calling it a "precautionary measure" over a drone attack that occurred the previous day.
Riyadh said that it would not retaliate, stressing that it wanted to give Baghdad "an opportunity to take the necessary measures."
Saudi oil pipeline attack could raise global gas prices
Who is behind the attacks on the Saudi pipeline?
No group has claimed responsibility for the attacks.
The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), an alliance of Iran-backed Iraqi militias, denied any involvement.
The militias are formally part of Iraq's security forces, but some of the groups occasionally act independently.

Also on Saturday, US President Donald Trump said Iran was "probably" responsible for the pipeline attack, while also seemingly downplaying the US and Saudi Arabia's conflict with the Houthis, an Iran-backed militia that control swathes of Yemen.
"The Houthis called us, and they don't want to fight with us," Trump said. "They would much prefer not having us involved, and they're letting most ships go through."

The Houthis and some of the Iraqi Shiite armed groups are part of what Tehran dubs the "Axis of Resistance," a group of Iran-backed militias in the Middle East that oppose the United States and Israel.
The Yemeni armed group has imposed a blockade on Saudi Arabia since July and seized the Red Sea port city of Mokha on Thursday.

The Houthis have previously targeted international shipping in the Red Sea, citing solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza amid Israel's offensive in the territory, but have said they do not intend to do so as part of their recent advances along Yemen's coast.

blocks.caption: The Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah militia group has said it will not comply with Baghdad's order to disarm by September 30 [FILE: September 2014]Image: dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Iraq under pressure to disband Iran-backed militias

Iraq has been under pressure from Washington to rein in Iran-aligned Shiite armed groups, as some of the militias have hit US-linked targets in the region since the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran on February 28.
While Baghdad has set a September 30 deadline for their disarmament, several militias have said they will not comply with the order,
The deadline coincides with the date set for the withdrawal of the remaining US-led coalition forces from Iraq.

One of the most influential militias, Kataib Hezbollah, has heavily criticized the disarmament plan and called for guarantees that US forces would never return and measures would be implemented to rid Iraq of US influence on political or economic decision-making.

articles.title: Mississippi police say more arrests to come in death of woman found hanging from tree
articles.summary:
Officials still investigating death of Tasia Fortune, a Black woman, a day after man’s arrest in relation to killing

Mississippi…

blocks.text: Mississippi police said on Saturday they were still investigating the death of Tasia Fortune, a Black woman found hanging from a tree last month, a day after a man was arrested in connection with the killing.
Loved ones also painted a picture of Fortune as a mother, athlete and woman of faith who they hoped would not solely be remembered for her horrific death.

Police sought and found Jarques Ratliff, 51, who is Black, and arrested him when they encountered him walking on the street, authorities said on Friday. Jackson’s police chief, RaShall Brackney, also said on Friday that additional arrests are expected in the case. Ratliff should appear in Jackson municipal court no later than Monday morning, said André de Gruy, Mississippi’s state defender.

Brackney said Ratliff had an “association” with Fortune but would not elaborate on their relationship. She said police arrested Ratliff on a homicide charge and called that “an important development” in the investigation.

“But it is not the conclusion. This case remains active, and additional arrests will be pending as our investigators continue to follow the evidence wherever it leads,” Brackney said on Friday. “We understand that this case has received media attention from across the globe, and across this community.”
The state medical examiner’s office determined on Thursday evening that the death was a homicide, Brackney said, allowing police to execute the warrants they already had on hand.
Police did not respond to calls and messages from the Associated Press on Saturday about potential updates to the investigation beyond confirming it was still going on.

Ratliff also did not appear in Hinds county jail records on Saturday. It couldn’t immediately be determined if he had a lawyer, and a message was left for the public defender’s office. If represented by a public defender, it would be the Hinds county public defender, de Gruy said.
Christy Spivey, Fortune’s mother, said on Friday after police told her of the arrest: “I just started crying and told them, ‘Thank you, thank you, thank you.’”

Spivey said police did not share a motive or whether DNA led them to the arrest. Spivey said she did not know the man who had been arrested, but she was asking her daughter’s friends if they knew him. Spivey described the family as “in disbelief” and “shock”.
“We still don’t have a lot of answers,” Spivey said.
Police discovered Fortune’s body hanging in the backyard of an abandoned home in Jackson on 3 August.
Spivey said she was certain that her daughter, 29, would not have killed herself.
“Absolutely not. Even if she could climb that tree, no, no, she would never, ever, ever,” Spivey said.

An obituary about Fortune posted on the website of Tucker funeral home in Central City, Kentucky, in August stated that Fortune’s “path was not always easy, and there were highs and lows”. It also stated that she skipped her junior year of high school, was a star cross-country runner, and had a strong faith in God. Services were held last month in Kentucky.
“She leaves behind a powerful legacy of resilience, rooted deeply in her unwavering faith. Even in her darkest hours, she never stopped believing in her Savior,” the obituary stated.

Fortune was also the mother of four children, but she rarely saw two of them, Spivey said. The last time Spivey saw her daughter was in late July for a planned family reunion in Kentucky that was canceled, but her daughter came to see her anyway.
“When she was there, there was this pull, like a spiritual pull to her. I needed her. I guess God knew that was going to be it,” Spivey said.
Spivey said she and Fortune’s father faced racism and violence as a mixed-race couple in Crittenden county, Kentucky, before Fortune was born.

Fortune was taken from her parents and placed in foster care as a child. During her high school years, she moved around among group homes and eventually ran away to Mississippi. The obituary stated that she had lived in Jackson for 10 years.

Spivey wasn’t sure where Fortune was living at the time of her death but said her daughter had been struggling with homelessness in recent years. Fortune had two sisters and was close with them. The father of one of her children was verbally and physically abusive to Fortune, Spivey said.
Before she died, Fortune had talked about starting a cleaning business and was trying to get her life in order.
“Say her name. Keep it going,” Spivey said. “Because I’m not going to stop until I get answers.”

articles.title: Uganda's King Oyo buried amid calls for unity over his successor
articles.summary: A TV news presenter has been named as the traditional kingdom of Tooro's new monarch but the late king's family claim he chose an heir.

blocks.text: Uganda's King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, once the world's youngest reigning monarch, was buried on Saturday, days after a row broke out over who would succeed him.
Oyo, 34, who had ruled the traditional kingdom of Tooro in western Uganda since the age of three, died last month while undergoing cancer treatment in the US.

Tooro is one of Uganda's traditional kingdoms. They were abolished in 1967 but restored in the 1990s under President Museveni. Their monarchs are recognised as cultural leaders rather than political rulers.
Thousands of mourners lined the streets as the king's casket was transported to the royal tombs in Fort Portal where a private ceremony took place.
Oyo was just a toddler when he was named as Tooro's king and, according to Guinness World Records, was the world's youngest monarch while he reigned.

TV news presenter Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, 56, who was named as the next monarch by clan elders, reportedly cast nine coffee beans into Oyo's grave, a ritual signifying the end of one reign and the start of another.
But days earlier, Oyo's family rejected Kijanangoma, the late monarch's cousin, as Tooro's new king.
Oyo's sister, Princess Ruth Komuntale, said the late king had left a will, written in 2022, naming his young son as his successor.
The boy's identity has never been disclosed.

Meanwhile, his mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, said royal guards had been withdrawn from the palace and soldiers deployed. This, she said, restricted the royal family's movement and their ability to receive visitors, describing it as "house arrest".
On Saturday, the Archbishop of the Church of Uganda, Stephen Kazimba Mugalu, urged unity.
"Words spoken in grief can cause pain, division and conflict. It can even destroy the legacy of the king we are mourning," he told mourners.
Uganda's President Yoweri Museveni also called for the matter to be resolved "and to favour unity over division".
The clan overseeing the succession defended its choice of Kijanangoma.
Omusuuga Charles Karumasi, head of the Babiito royal clan, said: "We have done everything in observance of the culture and traditions of Tooro. We must all preserve peace and serenity."

articles.title: Trump's call for united Ireland draws swift rejection from pro-British unionists
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump said on Saturday that he would "love" to see British-run Northern Ireland unify with Ireland, remarks made during a visit to Dublin that drew a sharp response from…

image.caption: Demonstrators carry a banner during a protest against the visit of U.S. President Donald Trump in Dublin, the capital of Ireland, on Saturday. (Natalia Campos/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

U.S. President Donald Trump said on Saturday that he would "love" to see British-run Northern Ireland unify with Ireland, remarks made during a visit to Dublin that drew a sharp response from pro-British unionists in Northern Ireland.
Reunification would mean 'destruction of our country,' says Democratic Unionist Party

Trump's comments come weeks after new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said a referendum on Northern Ireland leaving the United Kingdom was "off the table," a position Downing Street on Saturday said remained unchanged.

"Well, I don't want to cause any problems, but I will tell you, I'd love to see it unified," Trump told reporters as he sat next to Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin after the pair met in Dublin. "It's going to happen eventually.... I think it would be a fantastic thing."
He added: "Now the U.K. will have something to say about it ... but I think it would be a great thing."
Trump later said that there "was no good answer" to the question on Irish unity but repeated that he thought it would be "a very cool thing."
Break with neutral stance of previous presidents
Under the terms of the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, which then-U.S. president Bill Clinton played a key role in brokering, a referendum can be held only at the discretion of the British government.

The accord ended three decades of violence between Irish nationalists seeking a united Ireland and unionists who wanted Northern Ireland to remain in the U.K. Unlike England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, the Republic of Ireland is not part of the United Kingdom.

While polls show a comfortable majority in Northern Ireland favour remaining in the U.K., the gap has narrowed slightly since Britain's departure from the European Union pushed unity higher up the political agenda.

The leader of the Democratic Unionist Party, Northern Ireland's largest party advocating continued union with Britain, rejected Trump's prediction, saying unification with Ireland would lead to "the destruction of our country."

"Northern Ireland's constitutional future will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington," Gavin Robinson, who has publicly supported Trump in the past, wrote on social media platform X.

items: Your guide to the U.S. midterms, and why they're crucial for Donald Trump
Carney says he's still regularly speaking with Trump despite latest trade rift

blocks.text: In Belfast, supporters of Irish unity gave a guarded response.

"I think it's just headline grabbing.... I don't think he gives a toss whether there is a United Ireland or not," said Eamon Hanna, a supporter of the nationalist Social Democratic and Labour Party, which has been a strong critic of Trump's policies.

Previous U.S. presidents, including those with strong Irish heritage like Joe Biden, have been careful to remain neutral on Irish unification. The U.S. government played a key role in brokering the 1998 peace deal.

Shortly after Trump left to watch a golf tournament at one of his resorts in the west of Ireland, thousands of protesters, some holding posters calling the U.S. president a warmonger and chanting "Free free Palestine," marched through central Dublin.
It was one of the country's largest anti-war protests in recent years.

articles.title: 13 seen as voting threshold in Sara Duterte impeachment trial
articles.summary: Thirteen votes could be enough to convict Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment trial if only 20 senators are considered active and eligible to participate in the proceedings, law professor…

blocks.text: Published September 13, 2026 12:27am

Thirteen votes could be enough to convict Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment trial if only 20 senators are considered active and eligible to participate in the proceedings, law professor and litigation lawyer Howard Calleja said on Saturday.

Calleja said the two-thirds voting threshold for conviction should be based on the number of senators who are present and able to perform their functions, rather than automatically using the full 24-member Senate.
“If 20 na lang ang natira, I think the 2/3 of 20 is 13 point something, so 13 din ang gagamitin natin as the number for conviction,” Calleja said at the Saturday News Forum.
(If only 20 remain, I think two-thirds of 20 is 13-point-something, so we would use 13 as the number of votes needed for conviction.)
Calleja said the 1987 Constitution does not specifically require 16 votes for conviction, noting that it requires the “concurrence of two-thirds of all the members” of the Senate.
“The Constitution didn't state ‘16’ or ‘24’ — it admits to the moving number of members of the Senate,” he said.
Calleja made the assertion as the Senate impeachment court seeks the opinion of amici curiae before deciding on the voting threshold for Duterte's conviction in the ongoing impeachment trial.
According to Calleja, the term “concurrence” means senators must be capable of participating in the proceedings.
He said senators who are suspended, unavailable or otherwise unable to perform their legislative functions should not automatically be included in determining the threshold.
Calleja cited suspended senators Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta, saying their suspensions remove their rights, functions, obligations, responsibilities and privileges as members of the Senate.

He also questioned whether Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa should be included in the count, citing his status as a fugitive and questions over whether he took the oath required to serve as a senator-judge after the 2025 elections.
If the three senators are excluded, 21 senators would remain for purposes of computing the two-thirds requirement, Calleja said.
He also raised the case of Senator Loren Legarda, who is on medical leave abroad.
If Legarda returns and participates in the proceedings, Calleja said she should be included in the count. If she does not return, however, he said she should not be counted.
This would leave 20 senators, resulting in a two-thirds threshold of 13 votes, according to Calleja.

Calleja maintained that his interpretation would not amount to changing the rules in the middle of the impeachment trial, saying the Constitution itself does not fix the number of senators to be counted at 24.
He said the number could change depending on which senators are present and capable of participating in the impeachment proceedings.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Number of UK anti-migrant vigilante groups surges in last 18 months
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Many ‘use community protection as a cover for racist thuggery’, raising concerns about fresh disorder

At least 28 anti-migrant vigilante groups have formed in the UK in the last…

blocks.text: At least 28 anti-migrant vigilante groups have formed in the UK in the last 18 months, ranging from unauthorised street patrols claiming to protect women and children to groups harassing migrants in France and blocking ports.

From Belfast to the south coast of England, the number of active groups has surged since the summer of 2025, according to analysis by the Guardian, amid widespread concerns over fresh disorder after black-clad vigilantes, many of them wearing balaclavas, blocked roads in Portsmouth and Dover last weekend.

Often arguing that they are filling gaps left by the police or taking action on migration that the government is unable to, the groups range from small-scale community patrols near asylum-seeker accommodation to those attempting to stop migrants crossing the Channel from France.

They include Scots Active, which conducts late-night patrols around Glasgow city centre claiming to protect the public from migrants, sometimes wearing balaclavas and stab-proof vests. It says its activities help ensure the safety of women and girls. It was one of two groups banned from TikTok earlier this year after reportedly sharing footage claiming to expose migrant hotels.

Another is the British Security Project, a self-styled civilian safety group that has described itself as the “tip of the spear in mass deportation under a Rupert Lowe government”. It recruits “visible deterrent patrol” volunteers via its website and social media platforms, and responds to reports from the public about incidents claiming to involve migrants. It aims to “provide 124,000 security personnel to public spaces by 2035”, according to its Facebook page.

When the Guardian contacted the group for comment, a spokesperson said it was neither vigilante nor anti-migrant. “The British Security Project is a developing non-profit community protection organisation committed to lawful, peaceful and accountable volunteer action,” they said. “It has no police or immigration-enforcement powers, does not permit people to be targeted because of their nationality or immigration status, and expressly prohibits vigilantism, intimidation, racism and unlawful discrimination.”

Members of another group, Raise the Colours, made several trips to France in 2025 to try to stop migrants crossing the Channel in small boats. They filmed themselves claiming to have slashed dinghies on French beaches. France subsequently banned 10 members from the country.

Members of far-right Patriot Platform blocked roads near Dover for several hours last Saturday, disrupting traffic to and from the port. Kent police initially said they had received no warning, but later admitted officers had failed to act on calls made on Friday evening.

On Sunday, about 200 black-clad men gathered in Portsmouth after 120 asylum seekers rescued from a dinghy were brought ashore there. They blocked roads and allegedly assaulted several police officers.
The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, urged police on Thursday to curb the activities of such groups, telling senior officers to make full use of their powers.

The rise in vigilante groups is a recent phenomenon, overwhelmingly happening in the last year. Of the 31 active groups the Guardian was able to establish initiation dates for, 28 were set up since last summer, with a spike in August 2025 after Raise the Colours’ flag operation and unrest at an asylum hotel in Epping. Setup dates were taken from online activity on Facebook and Instagram, domain name registrations and media reports.

To classify as anti-migrant vigilantes, the Guardian considers that a group must have taken the law into its own hands in the name of opposing migrants or asylum seekers. Groups limited to more conventional protests and far-right political parties were not included.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Anti-migrant demonstrators march in Epping, Essex, in September 2025.  Photograph: Ian Davidson/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.

blocks.text: In a campaign of intimidation last summer, a vigilante group called the Belfast Nightwatch First Division was involved in targeting dark-skinned males in the city, challenging them to produce identification documents.
Dr Julia Ebner, an expert on extremism at the University of Oxford, said the figures showed a rapid shift in the ways anti-migrant activists were mobilising which was particularly striking.

“At the heart of most vigilante groups is the claim that the authorities are incapable or unwilling to protect a country’s citizens,” she said. “This is a dangerous dynamic, because when trust in authorities is undermined this can quickly translate into justifications of running their own policing operations or even violent campaigns – all supposedly for a good cause.

“Another underlying narrative that is not new but has been amplified across social media is the idea that ‘our’ women and children are threatened by men of migrant backgrounds. There is also a performative aspect of vigilante movements: uniforms, patrols and security equipment can project authority and legitimacy even when the groups themselves are relatively small.

blocks.caption: Patriot Platform hold a silent vigil at the RNLI station in Poole from where a volunteer crew rescued about 140 migrants last weekend. Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/Getty Images

blocks.text: “This can help far-right movements recruit new members and produce visually appealing social media content to increase their public profile and expand their followership.”

Alex MacKinnon, a researcher at Hope Not Hate, said vigilantism had long been part of far-right activism, but that there had been a dramatic increase in extremists’ grassroots efforts in the last 18 months.

“While vigilante groups typically purport to protect the wider community, the majority do not properly vet their members, resulting in several being exposed for their violent criminal histories,” he said.

“Furthermore, they regularly engage in intimidatory behaviour, as seen in Patriot Platform’s Dover demonstration. Vigilante groups of this type often promote aggressive anti-migrant agendas, using ‘community protection’ as a cover for racist thuggery.”
In response to the Guardian’s analysis, the National Police Chiefs’ Council said it was important for the public to report concerns about crime and safety.

“Police officers are specially trained to respond to a wide range of incidents safely and lawfully,” a spokesperson said. “While we understand people may want to protect their communities, taking enforcement into your own hands can be dangerous, and could compromise a police investigation.”

articles.title: CICC to lead ASEAN cooperation on online child safety
articles.summary: The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center vows to push for stronger cooperation among Southeast Asian countries to protect children from online threats, including grooming and other…

blocks.text: September 13, 2026 | 12:00am

CICC executive director Renato Paraiso made the commitment after ScamWatch officials urged the Philippines to use its 2026 chairmanship of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to establish a regional front against online threats.
Philstar.com / Irra Lising

MANILA, Philippines — The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center vows to push for stronger cooperation among Southeast Asian countries to protect children from online threats, including grooming and other malicious activities on social media and gaming platforms.
“I think we all agree also on the strategic approach and I commit that DICT and CICC will take a strong lead on the charge for ASEAN,” Paraiso said in a statement.

He said the initiative would go beyond child safety and include broader efforts to combat cybercrime, particularly as criminal groups involved in online child exploitation can operate across borders and exploit gaps between jurisdictions.

articles.title: DPWH boosts Oplan Kontra Baha initiatives
articles.summary: After floods submerged parts of the country during recent storms and the enhanced southwest monsoon, the Department of Public Works and Highways is strengthening its Oplan Kontra Baha initiatives in…

blocks.text: September 13, 2026 | 12:00am
Motorists and commuters were forced to make their way through floodwaters along UN Avenue corner Taft Avenue in Manila on September 9, 2026
Edd Gumban / The Philippine STAR

MANILA, Philippines — After floods submerged parts of the country during recent storms and the enhanced southwest monsoon, the Department of Public Works and Highways is strengthening its Oplan Kontra Baha initiatives in the country, on orders from President Marcos.

DPWH Secretary Vince Dizon said they are laying down long-term programs to reduce flooding not only in Metro Manila but in other parts of the country, such as Ilocos, Cagayan Valley, Tarlac and Naga City, Camarines Sur as well as parts of the Visayas and Mindanao.
Among these initiatives are cleaning and dredging of waterways in flood-prone and low-lying areas and construction and maintenance of pumping stations.
Meanwhile, repairs of the drainage system along Doña Remedios Trinidad Road in Baliwag, Bulacan are in full swing.
Dizon said the rehabilitation works along the road are meant to reduce flooding during heavy rains, which have affected motorists, commuters and residents of Bulacan.

articles.summary: Inclement weather did not stop the entrepreneurs of La Union from trooping to SM City La Union yesterday to participate in Go Negosyo’s Trabaho at Negosyo.

Hundreds of active and aspiring entrepreneurs and job applicants came to avail of the free job matching and entrepreneurship mentoring from Go Negosyo and its partners in the public and private sector.
