Also a standout athlete in sambo and wrestling, Chino Sy has shifted his focus to judo as he pursues an Olympic berth that would fulfill not only his dream, but also that of his family

items: Chino Sy, a Filipino judoka from Davao City, is focused on qualifying for the 2028 Olympics, drawing motivation from his family's sacrifices and his father's unfulfilled Olympic dream.
Sy has a strong background in combat sports, having won medals in sambo and wrestling, and is now concentrating on judo, where he has achieved significant success at the UAAP and SEA Games.

As he prepares for the upcoming Asian Games in Japan, Sy aims to win a judo medal for the Philippines, inspired by fellow athlete Kiyomi Watanabe, and is determined to honor the trust placed in him by his family and country.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Filipino judoka Chino Sy learned at an early age to make the most of every opportunity.

Hailing from Davao City, Sy developed a sense of responsibility to perform whenever he and his family traveled to Manila for combat sports competitions, knowing that they invested not only time and effort, but also money, just to be there.
As he embarks on his biggest challenge yet to make the Olympics, Sy is taking that same approach.

“I feel like those experiences shaped how I compete today and my mentality towards sports. Even when we were young, we were told that we couldn’t come home with a loss. For one, we already spent money on plane tickets. We also paid entry fees and covered all other expenses,” said Sy in a mix of Filipino and English.
Sy, 25, grew up immersed in combat disciplines.

His father, Paolo Tancontian, represented the Philippines in judo, winning medals in international competitions including the Southeast Asian Games and the Arafura Games, and now serves as the president of the Pilipinas Sambo Federation.

Sy’s older sister, Sydney, is currently the fifth-ranked sambo athlete in the world in the women’s +80kg division and has won medals in the last three Asia and Oceania Sambo Championships, including gold in 2025.
With martial arts deeply rooted in his family, it comes as little surprise that Sy found success in the field that he captured medals in three different sports in the SEA Games.
At 18 years old, Sy delivered a sambo gold when the country hosted the biennial showpiece in 2019. Four years later, he earned a wrestling silver in the 2023 edition in Cambodia.

But Sy has shifted his focus on judo, the sport in which he dominated the UAAP by winning gold medals in four seasons at UST and earning two MVP awards, as he sets his sights on qualifying for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
And he showed promise in that pursuit by striking a judo gold in the men’s -100kg division in the 2025 SEA Games in Thailand.

“Every athlete’s dream is the highest stage, the Olympics,” said Sy. “I feel like I’m at the peak of my career as an athlete. I’ll grab this opportunity and I’ll do everything I can to make it to the Olympics.”
Sy is not pursuing the Olympic dream for himself alone, but also for his family, revealing that his father once dreamed of competing in the 2000 Sydney Olympics — hence his sister’s name.
“This is not just my dream, it’s also my family’s dream. Papa may not have made it to the Olympics, but he’s doing everything he can to help me achieve our dream,” said Sy.
“If all goes well, this will truly be a milestone for our family.”

And with an Olympic dream in sight, Sy knows his belief in himself has to match his ambition as he eyes a rare judo medal in the upcoming Asian Games, which will be hosted in Nagoya, Japan, from September 19 to October 4.
The Philippines has won only one judo medal in Asian Games history courtesy of Kiyomi Watanabe, who bagged the women’s 63kg silver in the 2018 edition in Indonesia.
“My target is to win. I know it will be difficult, but I’m doing everything I can in training and preparation,” said Sy.

Sy also looks to Watanabe, who represented the Philippines in the 2020 Tokyo and 2024 Paris Games, for inspiration, hoping to learn from someone with Olympic experience as they team up in the Asian Games.
“[Kiyomi] has been competing for a long time and I’m looking forward to seeing how an Olympian thinks, how she prepares, and how she approaches every match,” Sy said.
And just as he did in his early years, Sy is determined to live up to the trust placed in him — this time, not only by his family but the entire country.
“I never want to let our country down, myself, or everyone who has put their trust in me,” said Sy. – Rappler.com

articles.title: 'It's like a dog set loose on us' - fear over Kenya's crackdown on foreign traders
articles.summary: The authorities have struggled to contain the fallout, as frightened migrants flee the country.

blocks.text: For Ndaikech Ali, who has been traversing the streets of the Kenyan capital eking out a living as a tuk-tuk driver for the past nine years, Nairobi's traffic - not xenophobia - has been his biggest concern.

During his time in the East African nation, the Burundian says he has always found Kenyans to be friendly and welcoming - that is until last week, when the president ordered a crackdown on foreigners working as traders or operating small-scale businesses.
"Now they have turned against us," he told the BBC at the Burundian embassy in Nairobi where many have been queuing this week for documents to allow them to travel back home.
"The threats are many… even from children," he said, adding: "It's a like a dog has been set loose upon us. We have been bitten."

President William Ruto made his remarks last week when addressing Kenyan traders gathered at state house - in reference to legislation before parliament that seeks to exclude foreign nationals from petty trade and to mandate the local sourcing of certain materials.
During his speech, he said that all foreign nationals operating small businesses had until 7 September to pack up shop, saying such low-level jobs should be reserved for Kenyans.
Ali, like others, panicked, saying it seemed the president's announcement had been interpreted by some Kenyans as a signal that foreign nationals were no longer welcome in the country.

"We face harassment and can't work," he says. "If our work is stopped, we lose the income that enables us to pay rent and buy food. When those jobs are taken away, the only option left is to return home."
Other Burundians and some other foreign nationals have rushed to border crossing points to leave the country, with reports suggesting that a number have ended up stranded there.
Some couples fear they will be forced to separate - and some families have already been divided.
"I have been here from 2019," said a Burundian man, who identified himself only as Prosper and who has a child with a Kenyan woman.
"When I heard the announcement, it was very painful because when I go, I'm forced to leave my family... and I love my family," he told the BBC.
In Nairobi's low-income neighbourhood of Majengo, Kenyan Grace Wamaitha said her Burundian husband had already gone - leaving the day after the president's 3 September directive.
She is distraught as she has been left trying to feed their five children - and has taken on extra work washing clothes.
"Now he's gone, who will help me pay school fees? I don't know what to do. Let them come back," she told the BBC.

In Nairobi and other major towns, migrants from the region can be found working in barber shops and salons, construction, operating motorbike taxis and street vending, as well as selling clothes, food and household goods.

Some have fled conflicts or economic hardship at home, while others have moved to Kenya in search of better opportunities. Within the East African Community (EAC), a regional bloc made up of eight countries, including Burundi and Kenya, the relative free movement of people is allowed - but employment and long-term residence do require permits.
Kenyan law also recognises the right of refugees to work and operate businesses, although they are also required to obtain the appropriate documentation.
Filmon Eyob, a co-ordinator within Nairobi's Eritrean community, agrees with concerns that the crackdown order will be used as pretext to harass foreigners.
He told the BBC that while many Kenyans had been supportive and welcoming, some Eritreans and Ethiopians had closed their businesses and stayed at home over the last week as a precaution.
The president's remarks also sparked a diplomatic row, with the Burundian foreign affairs minister warning that "hate speech against Burundi" could have repercussions for Kenyans abroad.

The authorities in Kenya have struggled to contain the fallout - and as the matter came to a head, Kenyan foreign affairs official Korir Sing'Oei visited and apologised to Burundians at the embassy this week, assuring them of protection from violence.
Critics argue that Ruto's remarks were a populist move that risked stoking xenophobia, although the government has denied this.
Since then, a series of official statements have sought to clarify the directive.

The government has now given a 90-day window for undocumented foreign nationals running small business to register and comply with local laws. During the process, those undergoing registration will be presumed to be living legally in Kenya.
Yet observers and those affected argue that it did not have to be this way.
Academic Hesbon Owilla told the BBC the president's comments were bound to be misinterpreted, especially by people who did not have the right documentation.
He says that while the proposed policy is good for Kenya and in line with global migration protocols, the communication about it ought to have been more diplomatic.
For those not in the audience, Owilla says people interpreted the president words as saying: "We are kicking these guys out."

The president did not stop at small-scale traders. A day later, he ordered India's Tata Chemicals to leave the country, saying the company had not provided sufficient benefits to the local Maasai community in Kajiado county.

Tata has been mining soda ash for years in Lake Magadi, a vast area often covered by a whitish salt crust. The lake's extreme briny environment sustains algae blooms that attract flamboyances of pink flamingos that thrive in the area.

Mining operations began at the lake in 1911 under a British colonial arrangement that is said to have remained largely intact, despite long-running land and resource disputes pitting the company and its predecessors against community and the government.
Economist Odhiambo Ramogi argues that the move to restrict foreign nationals from businesses is too broad - and could do with finessing.
He points out that Kenya hosts hundreds of thousands of refugees as well as other migrants, mostly from the EAC region, as well as other international investors.
Ramogi says that Ruto's intention seemed to go beyond "just protecting jobs for Kenyans".
The president's remarks have prompted a wave of support for foreign nationals, including by civil society groups and ordinary Kenyans who have criticised his approach.
In the wake of the criticism, Ruto, who is up for re-election next year, has sought to counter the backlash.

"Kenya will remain an open, secure and welcoming country, protecting opportunities for its citizens, safeguarding the rights of all persons lawfully within its borders," a statement by his spokesman said.
"Kenya's commitment to the East African Community of the African continent remains firm."
Ramogi says that in the end, it is Kenya that stands to lose when citizens of neighbouring countries are targeted.

He points out that Kenya earned $56m (£41m) in exports to Burundi last year, adding that the country would still benefit by allowing competition, as "locking out aliens simply means you don't want a competitive economy that gets to grow a lot faster".
"Now, if you got $56m out of a country, why are you worried about a hawker who's just trying to make, say, $200 in a month?
"It absolutely makes no sense what the president has done."
For Nairobi resident Lima Kabura, whose husband is Tanzanian, the president's remarks were just too hasty. She says he should have first established those who were in the country illegally.
"When they are forced out, I'm left with no work, no business and no husband," she said.
Additional reporting by Ahmed Bahajj

articles.title: Alberta separatists expect a win, regardless of numbers that say otherwise, poll suggests
articles.summary: A political scientist and pollster say that mismatch of expectations has consequences for what comes next and Albertans shouldn’t expect this issue to be put to rest with this one vote.

image.caption: Pro-unity and pro-independence signs in Airdrie, Alta. A poll of Albertans done during the first week of September suggests that supporters of separation believe their side will prevail in the October referendum. (Mantai Chow/CBC)

blocks.text: Edmonton·Exclusive
A political scientist and pollster say that mismatch of expectations has consequences for what comes next and Albertans shouldn’t expect this issue to be put to rest with this one vote.
Pollster also finds many support Option 2 for reasons other than full independence
Alberta separatists think they’re going to win a referendum that surveys suggest they are poised to lose by a wide margin, according to exclusive new polling.

And that mismatch of expectations has consequences for what comes next — including the likelihood that Albertans shouldn’t expect this issue to be put to rest with this one vote, say the pollster and a political scientist.
Abacus Data CEO David Coletto presented the results of the new poll, done during the first week of September, to CBC’s West of Centre on Friday.
On Oct. 19, Albertans will vote on a question with two choices: Option 1 is to stay in Canada, while Option 2 supports commencing the legal process to hold a binding referendum on Alberta separation.
That ballot question will be in addition to nine others that focus on constitutional and immigration issues.

Coletto’s poll found 64 per cent of respondents would vote to remain a province in Canada and 24 per cent would vote to start the separation process. Nine per cent were undecided and three per cent said they would skip the question.
But the poll also found that Option 2 supporters have surprisingly high expectations, believing that the separatist option will garner a winning 57 per cent of votes.
Coletto chalks it up to the political bubbles people live in and the natural hopefulness that comes with their strong support of the separatist camp.
Lisa Young, a political science professor at the University of Calgary, says that inflated expectation is worth noting — especially in the context of post-referendum ramifications.
"What he found, I think, should be setting off alarm bells in all of our heads," Young told West of Centre.

"If you do walk into this with the expectation that Option [2] is going to get 57 per cent and the actual outcome is 28 per cent ... the first question is going to be, 'Was this a proper result? Can we trust the outcome?'"
Premier Danielle Smith has said the upcoming referendum will be a gut-check of where Albertans stand, and that the province can hold a vote and move on.
But Young and Coletto don't see it that way.

In the event that the winning side supports remaining in Canada, the poll found many Option 2 voters expect the separatist movement to keep growing. Only six per cent of them said they expect the issue will be settled.
"There seems to be this assumption in the UCP premier's office ... that if you let this group let off steam, it will make the issue go away," Young said.
"This does not simply go away afterward. We're going to live with it one way or another for the next months, if not years."
Who is the typical Option 2 voter?
According to the polling, the typical Option 2 voter is a conservative partisan, somewhat more likely to be a man and tends to be slightly older than the provincial average.

They are more likely to live in small cities or in bedroom communities around Calgary and Edmonton. While rural Alberta contributes more than its share, the communities ringing Alberta's main metropolitan centres provide the most voters.
But the group is more distinguishable by its grievances than its demographics, the poll suggests.

It says Option 2 supporters are far more likely to put being an Albertan ahead of being a Canadian, and have a more favourable view of the United States and Donald Trump. That said, the group is split on whether Alberta should become a U.S. state.

The group also shares near-unanimous agreement that Alberta contributes more to Canada than it gets back, the province’s interests are ignored in Ottawa, and the rest of the country does not respect Alberta, the poll suggests.
Young said she wonders if the separatist camp is adequately reflected among people who were polled.
"I did start thinking back to 2016 in the United States," Young said. "People wouldn't tell a pollster that they were going to vote for Trump because it was seen as sort of socially unacceptable."
Coletto said he's confident his poll factored in as many Option 2 voters as possible, but he also acknowledged this is not a typical election.
"Partisan politics can get divisive. But this is being felt much more deeply and much more emotionally on both sides."
"Whatever side you're on, you've still got to live together no matter what happens going forward."
Do they actually want to leave?

What Option 2 voters hope to get out of a favourable result varies significantly. When asked to identify their main motivation for choosing to commence the process for a binding referendum, only 26 per cent said independence.
The rest are voting for leverage, to send a message or on principle, Coletto said.
"For many Albertans who are inclined to look at Option 2, it's not just a black or white, in and out."
That result aligns with recent messaging from the separatist camp.
“Independence isn't actually on the ballot,” Keith Wilson, with independence group Let Alberta Decide, told West of Centre last month.
“Voting Option 2 sends a message that no, we can do better. We want a more respectful and balanced and fair relationship with Ottawa.”
“Others are prepared to vote for Option 2 when they don't even support independence. And that's why I have some optimism we're going to win on Oct. 19.”
Methodology

Abacus Data surveyed 1,000 Alberta adults online from Sept. 4 to 7, 2026, six weeks before the Oct. 19 referendum. Results are weighted by region, age and gender to census data. A probability sample of this size would carry a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 points, 19 times out of 20. For subsets, the margin of error is larger.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Emily is a reporter and producer with CBC's West of Centre podcast. Previously, she covered Edmonton city hall. She can be reached at emily.williams@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Brazil: Flavio Bolsonaro faces corruption probe weeks before election
articles.summary: Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, Lula's top rival in next month's election, is under investigation for alleged corruption linked to financing a biopic about his father, former President Jair…

image.caption: Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro is the son of former President Jair BolsonaroImage: Edmar Barros/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the leading right-wing challenger to President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, is under investigation for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion tied to the financing of a biopic about his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, according to newly unsealed court documents.
What do we know about Bolsonaro's corruption probe?

The probe centers on funds Bolsonaro allegedly sought from Daniel Vorcaro, the disgraced banker behind the collapsed Banco Master, to help produce "Dark Horse," an unreleased film starring Jim Caviezel as the elder Bolsonaro.

Investigators are examining roughly $12 million that flowed from a Vorcaro-linked entity to a fund tied to Eduardo Bolsonaro, the senator's brother and campaign adviser, who lives in Texas. One document alleges Eduardo advised on how the money should be managed once in the United States.
Who is Brazil's Flavio Bolsonaro?

Supreme Court Justice Andre Mendonca, a Bolsonaro appointee, opened the investigation in July at the request of federal police, but the case remained sealed until Chief Justice Luiz Edson Fachin ordered it made public this week, Reuters reported.

Federal police raided the production company behind the film and the office of congressman Mario Frias, its executive producer, on Thursday. Both have been barred from leaving the country and deny wrongdoing.
How did the Bolsonaros respond?
Flavio Bolsonaro has denied any misconduct, telling reporters at a campaign stop, "It is very positive that the documents are unsealed," the Associated Press reported
"I want transparency in everything."

Eduardo Bolsonaro similarly rejected the allegations, telling Reuters the funds were routed through the US to avoid interference from Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who oversaw his father's coup conviction.
"They want to frame this as bribe money, which it isn't," he said.
On social media, he said investigators “are trying to repeat the mechanism that worked against Jair Bolsonaro.”
What did Lula say?

In a Thursday television interview, Lula said Banco Master "was created in the Bolsonaro administration" and shuttered during his own term. He has called for full transparency in the case regardless of political fallout.
The disclosures come three weeks before Brazil's October 4 election, in which polls show Bolsonaro and Lula roughly tied.

Political analysts say the timing leaves Bolsonaro less room to recover than when the scandal first surfaced in May, though the fallout could also cut against Lula given the case's ties to Vorcaro's dealings with multiple political and judicial figures.
A runoff, if needed, is set for October 25.

articles.title: ICC prosecutor opposes bid to refile charges vs. Rodrigo Duterte
articles.summary: The prosecution in the crimes against humanity case of former president Rodrigo Duterte has asked the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III to dismiss the defense's motion to refile…

blocks.text: Published September 12, 2026 5:36pm

The prosecution in the crimes against humanity case of former president Rodrigo Duterte has asked the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III to dismiss the defense's motion to refile the charges against him.

In August, Duterte's legal team argued that his right to be informed of the details of the cases filed against him were violated. The defense asked the chamber to order the Prosecution to refile a document with the charges containing the defined scope.
However, Acting Prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang said the charges against Duterte were already confirmed by the Pre-Trial Chamber and determined that the charges were adequate.

"Questions as to the form of charges are a matter for confirmation proceedings, not trial. The Defence fully participated in the substantive proceedings to confirm the charges, up to and including seeking leave (unsuccessfully) to appeal the Pre-Trial Chamber's confirmation decision on the issue of the form of the charges," Niang wrote in the Prosecution's response dated September 10.
"In any event, the substantive challenges to the confirmed charges are without merit," he added.
Niang also said the notice to the defendant has various means—including the pre-trial filings. Any potential defect, he said, can be cured during the proceedings.
The common legal representative of victims (CLRVs) also objected to the defense team's petition.

In a response dated September 10, the CLRV said the defense has already raised the same arguments during the pre-trial stage. The defense should not be allowed to raise the same concerns again as a matter of "form."

"The charges have been confirmed; Mr Duterte has been committed to trial on the charges as confirmed; and the Defence has already unsuccessfully sought leave to challenge the manner in which the Pre-Trial Chamber delineated their scope," the CLRV wrote.
The CLRV's response was jointly signed by ICC lawyers Gilbert Andres, Joel Butuyan and Paolina Massidda.
The ICC confirmed the charges against Duterte in April. His trial at the ICC is scheduled to begin on November 30. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Sara Duterte highlights local tourism following visit to Palawan's Bato ni Ningning
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte on Saturday shared photos of her visit to Bato ni Ningning, a popular tourist spot in Barangay Sto. Niño, San Vicente, Palawan.

blocks.text: Published September 12, 2026 5:09pm
Vice President Sara Duterte on Saturday shared photos of her visit to Bato ni Ningning, a popular tourist spot in Barangay Sto. Niño, San Vicente, Palawan.

“Labis ang aking kasiyahan na mapuntahan at masilayan, noong mga nakaraang buwan, ang Bato ni Ningning sa Barangay Sto. Niño, na dinarayo ng maraming turista dahil sa preskong hangin at napakagandang tanawin,” Duterte said in a social media post.
(I am overjoyed to have visited and seen Bato ni Ningning in Barangay Sto. Niño in recent months, a place frequented by many tourists for its cool breeze and breathtaking views.)
“Matatanaw mula rito ang nakamamanghang kagandahan ng mga baybayin ng San Vicente, na kabilang sa mga kilalang destinasyon sa buong Palawan,” she added.
(From here, one can admire the breathtaking beauty of San Vicente’s coastlines, which are among the well-known destinations in Palawan.)
Duterte said she takes pride in the Philippines’ natural attractions and that visiting provinces is one way to promote local tourism.
“Lagi kong sinasabi at ipinagmamalaki na sa ating bansang Pilipinas makikita ang ilan sa mga pinakamagagandang lugar at baybayin sa buong mundo,” Duterte wrote.
(I always say and take pride in the fact that the Philippines is home to some of the most beautiful places and coastlines in the world.)
“At ang ating pagbisita sa mga lalawigan ay isa sa mga pamamaraan upang maisulong ang lokal na turismo at makatulong sa lokal na ekonomiya ng isang lugar,” she added.
(Visiting the provinces is one way to promote local tourism and support the local economy.) — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Kilyab’s Karl Ramirez turns Bicol pop into call for good governance
articles.summary: By putting Bicol music at the center of his work, this musician inspires a new generation of artists to celebrate their roots and use their craft to push for change

blocks.text: BICOL POP. Karl Ramirez showcases original Bicol music during a performance at the Pista Nin Teatro 2026, a national theater festival.
By putting Bicol music at the center of his work, this musician inspires a new generation of artists to celebrate their roots and use their craft to push for change

items: Karl Ramirez and his band, Kilyab, are revitalizing Bicol pop music by incorporating local narratives and community struggles, aiming to give voice to regional aspirations for change.
The movement has established Pagsibol, an initiative that trains young musicians in songwriting and music production, encouraging them to create socially relevant music in their native language.

Through partnerships with local government and community support, the movement seeks to empower artists, promote local heritage, and provide opportunities for musicians to reach broader audiences while maintaining their cultural roots.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

ALBAY, Philippines – From the dimly lit corners of local bars and cafes in Naga City, Karl Ramirez and his band, Kilyab, quietly listen to the stories of their community. They transform these local narratives, heritage, and aspirations to reinvent Bicol pop — giving voice to the region’s call for change.
Now, the movement is helping the younger generation of musicians to do the same.

Ramirez, a music industry veteran, returned to Bicol during the pandemic. As a founding member of Musika Publiko, a nationwide network of artists dedicated to advance socially relevant music, he sought to localize the group’s advocacy.

blocks.caption: KILYAB. Karl Ramirez and his band perform at Pista Nin Teatro 2026, introducing the Bicol pop movement to a nationwide audience. Photo courtesy of The Mariners Collegian

blocks.text: Starting without financial backing in an unfamiliar base, Ramirez and his band brought together local musicians from across Camarines Sur to create a platform for original Bicol music. Initially, they had to persuade reluctant bar and cafe owners to grant them a stage to perform. Soon, those same venues were inviting them back, fueling the community’s rapid growth and popularity.

“We were surprised when more and more bars and cafes opened their doors to Bicol pop. It was challenging at first because every venue has its own specific brand, but through their support, our movement grew larger and reached more listeners,” Ramirez said.

By rooting their songs in community struggles, the movement transformed Bicol pop into a platform for local causes. To sustain this momentum, the organization eventually formed Pagsibol, an initiative that trains aspiring musicians, particularly the youth, to write songs about their local experiences in their native language while using music as a driver for social advocacy.
“We decided to form Pagsibol to expand our reach and prepare younger musicians to lead and advance the movement. We realized we needed to grow our ranks,” Ramirez said.

He explained that the organization not only expanded its footprint, but also created a more open environment for continuous growth: “We wanted to encourage the youth to create fresh work that directly serves their communities and generation.”

Pagsibol now functions as a structured platform for training enthusiasts in songwriting and music production. Beyond developing artists, the group focuses on empowering broader communities through local skills training.

blocks.caption: PAGSIBOL. Aspiring young musicians participate in a Pagsibol songwriting workshop aimed at advancing socially relevant original Bicol music. Contributed photo/Verna Abalyan-Velasco

blocks.text: In Naga City, the group has leveraged music to reinforce good governance, placing “active listening” at its core. Partnering with the local government, they have reached more students while advancing advocacy for Musikong Nagueño, a collective pushing for local government support and funding for community musicians and cultural workers.

“We invited Mayor Leni Robredo to a concert held in 2024 at the Jesse M. Robredo Coliseum, where we presented her with a Bicol pop roadmap and policy proposals for the Naga City music industry,” Ramirez recalled.
“Following her election, our movement established a collaborative partnership with the local government, placing active listening at the center of the city’s good governance agenda.”

He noted that if such a partnership can thrive in Naga, there is immense potential for other local government units to provide genuine backing for artists working to preserve and promote their local heritage.

blocks.caption: HERITAGE. The cast of ‘Ibalong Z: A New Bikol Musical’ performs 17 original songs composed by Karl Ramirez in collaboration with the local theater collective Sining Banwa. Reinnard Balonzo/Rappler

blocks.text: In August 2026, Ramirez also served as the lead composer and music producer for Ibalong Z: A New Bikol Musical, writing and producing 17 original songs in just 17 days. The production was funded by the City Government of Legazpi.

“With this play, the original Bicol music we produced, and state support, we proved that local artists and collectives deserve greater investment if we want to advance regional talent and heritage,” Ramirez said. “Ibalong Z stands as a testament that with proper support, local artists can rival mainstream productions.”

Speaking on the shift to mainstream media, Ramirez said that Pagsibol students are fully supported if they choose to pursue mainstream careers. For him, Bicol pop serves as a springboard — helping emerging artists introduce their work to broader audiences and share regional stories with the national music scene.

“We encourage our musicians to seize opportunities to go mainstream and bring Bicol pop to more listeners. Our hope is that wherever their success takes them, they carry the movement with them,” Ramirez said.

blocks.caption: ARTISTIC SUPPORT. In partnership with the City Government of Naga, Bicol pop launched its SongLab initiative for Pagsibol students. Contributed photo/Verna Abalyan-Velasco

blocks.text: Through this hyperlocal music movement, artists gain a solid community to rely on a network that offers support wherever their careers lead. Ultimately, the movement aims to empower budding musicians by giving them greater leverage in their creative expression and stronger control over their career trajectories.

“What we teach the youth goes beyond writing lyrics. We focus on how we, as a community, can support one another in artistic growth and management while advocating for artists’ rights and welfare,” Ramirez shared. “We also guide them as they navigate the music industry and hone their talent.”

For now, Ramirez and Kilyab continue to mentor Pagsibol’s emerging artists by immersing them in local communities. This hands-on approach ensures that every lyric accurately reflects the real issues, places, and people they write and sing about. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Corals as climate archive: Are El Ninos intensifying?
articles.summary: Records from the past few decades show that, during this period, El Nino events have been frequent and often extreme. But is this normal, or is it the result of climate change? Corals can give us a…

image.caption: The coral reefs at the Galápagos Islands are known for their astounding biodiversity, a result of high nutrients and the mixing of cool and warm watersImage: Greg Asner

blocks.text: A storm is gathering. Most likely a very big one. El Nino is a natural climate phenomenon occurring every two to seven years, towards the end of the year, but it comes in various different strengths, depending on the prevailing conditions.

El Ninos are considered strong if the surface temperature of the water off the west coast of South America is more than 1.5 degrees Celsius above average. In July this year, the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) was already observing temperature increases of greater than three degrees Celsius in the eastern and central Pacific.
The German Meteorological Service believes this "could in all likelihood develop into one of the strongest El Nino events since records began."

But a recent article by the Max Planck Institute for Meteorology states that whether or not strong El Nino events will intensify as a result of climate change "remains the subject of ongoing research."
The data gap: What corals can tell us about El Nino

The problem is that the data on ocean surface temperatures is only truly reliable from the 1980s onward, with the start of satellite observation. And this data doesn't tell us how El Nino behaved before industrialization and the burning of fossil fuels.

US researchers say corals can help to close this knowledge gap. Julia Cole, a climate scientist and paleoclimatologist at the University of Michigan, and her team recently published a study on this subject in the journal Science.

"We've known for a long time that the last 40 or 50 years has really strong El Nino events," says Cole. "It's been hard to say whether the recent strong El Nino that we've had is part of a natural cycle, or if it's something a little bit unusual related to being in a warmer than normal world." The coral analysis points firmly in one direction: Unusual. Not normal.
Corals: A repository of 1,000 years of climate history

Cole and her team examined fossilized and living corals around the Galapagos Islands off Ecuador in the eastern Pacific. Corals grow between one and two centimeters per year, and in doing so form a structure similar to growth rings on trees. "We made use of the fact that corals record ocean temperatures as they grow, in the chemical composition of their skeleton," Cole explains.

Corals are living creatures that construct external skeletons through calcification, adding a band of new growth each year with calcium carbonate precipitated from the surrounding water. In this way, over decades and centuries, corals have formed entire reef systems. Other chemical elements are also incorporated into the skeleton during the calcification process — strontium, for example. Sometimes more is deposited, sometimes less, depending on the temperature of the water.

"In colder temperatures, it [the skeleton] absorbs more strontium, in warmer temperatures less," says Cole. The ratio of strontium to calcium in the skeleton provides information about changes in temperature.

Specific isotopes of oxygen in coral skeletons provide clues, as well. "The rare oxygen-18 and the common oxygen-16 are also taken up in a ratio that reflects temperature," says Cole. In colder conditions, more oxygen-18 is absorbed than in warmer temperatures.

In this way, researchers were able to reconstruct the changes in ocean temperatures over the past 1,000 years, according to the age of the corals. Their conclusion was that El Nino events have become markedly stronger compared to the pre-industrial period.

blocks.caption: Scientists Julia Cole and Cameron Tripp collecting samples at the Galápagos IslandsImage: Julia Cole/University of Michigan

blocks.text: Corals give indications, not conclusive answers

Cole's study has confirmed a long-held suspicion. "These developments correspond to the predictions of the best climate models. They predict a quantifiably higher likelihood of extreme eastern Pacific El Nino events in the 2030s," says Jens Zinke, professor of paleobiology at the University of Leicester in England.

However, other scientists are more circumspect in assessing the study's significance. "Coral data does achieve a high temporal resolution — monthly to seasonal — but its accuracy is dependent on local conditions, meaning that direct comparisons with modern measurement data are fraught with uncertainty," says Andreas Fink, professor of meteorology at the Institute for Meteorology and Climate Research in Karlsruhe. According to Fink, the significance of the study is undermined by its regional limitation to the eastern Pacific.

Cole is also aware of her study's limitations. "Our data does fill a gap, but I want to be clear that our record isn't continuous," she says. "We don't have every single year over the last millennium. We have a little bit under half of the years covered."

blocks.caption: An NOAA scientist drilling to collect a coral core at the Galápagos Islands, EcuadorImage: NOAA

blocks.text: Floods, droughts, record heat — the consequences of stronger El Ninos

Although the epicenter of the El Nino phenomenon is the Pacific, it changes the weather across the globe. In countries like Ecuador and Peru it can cause heavy rains and flooding, while Australia and Indonesia may experience a lack of rain, leading to drought and wildfires. El Niño also causes global temperatures to rise for a while.

If the predictions prove right and this El Nino does in fact become a Super El Nino, the coming year, 2027, will probably be another of record heatwaves, according to Thomas Felis. Felis leads the research group on coral paleoclimatology at the MARUM Center for Marine Environmental Sciences at the University of Bremen, and has conducted a similar study to Cole's.
Heat-stressed oceans: El Nino is a threat for corals
A year of record heat "will very probably lead to another global coral bleaching," says Felis. This has happened before, in the years 2023–24 and 2015–16, which were also El Nino years.

Corals get their characteristic colors from certain algae with which they live in symbiosis. Through photosynthesis, the algae provide the energy the corals need to live. If the temperature of the ocean is too high, the algae start to produce toxins, and the corals end the partnership. The coral remains, in its skeleton.

It can survive like that for a few weeks, and if the temperature drops again, the algae return. "But if this state, with abnormally high summer temperatures, goes on for too long, the coral becomes so sick that it eventually dies," Felis explains.
Worldwide coral death would mean not just the end of a unique ecosystem, but the destruction of an archive that preserves the history of the oceans.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: Sherwin Gatchalian pushes localized class suspensions to curb learning loss
articles.summary: Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on Saturday pushed for localized class cancellations instead of blanket, system-wide suspensions, warning that weather-related disruptions could worsen learning…

blocks.text: Published September 12, 2026 4:44pm

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on Saturday pushed for localized class cancellations instead of blanket, system-wide suspensions, warning that weather-related disruptions could worsen learning loss.

“This is concerning. While we know that class suspensions seek to ensure the safety of learners and teachers, widespread disruption to classes can aggravate learning loss,” Gatchalian said in a statement.
He said classes should be allowed to continue in unaffected schools and areas.
Gatchalian said at least 20 weekdays of face-to-face classes had already been disrupted in various parts of the country over the past 30 days due to bad weather.

Citing a study by the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II), he said schools lost an average of 30 to 50 days out of the 180-day academic calendar over the past two years due to class suspensions.
“Bagama’t tinitiyak natin ang kapakanan ng ating mga mag-aaral tuwing may kalamidad, kailangan din nating tiyaking magpapatuloy ang edukasyon sa mga ligtas na lugar,” Gatchalian said.
(While we ensure the welfare of our students during calamities, we must also ensure that education continues in safe areas.)

Under Senate Bill No. 53, or the 21st Century School Boards Act, Gatchalian seeks to empower local school boards to establish and decide on “timely, organized, and localized interventions” to ensure the delivery of basic education during disasters, calamities, and other emergencies. — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Donald Trump lands in Dublin for two-day Ireland visit – live
articles.summary:
US president will hold talks with Ireland’s leftwing president Catherine Connolly, and play golf

Trump landed in Dublin just moments ago, disembarking from Air Force One and being greeted by…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 24m agoTrump begins two-day visit to Ireland

blocks.text: The US president arrived in Dublin on the controversially gifted Boeing aircraft given to him by the Qatari royal family.

blocks.caption: Garda vehicles as US president Donald Trump arrived on Air Force One at Dublin airport. Photograph: Clodagh Kilcoyne/PA

blocks.text: The $400m ‘palace in the sky’ was converted for presidential use, but questions remain over how well equipped it is to protect the president from potential threats. During a trip to Turkey in July, Trump was reportedly moved off the aircraft after a possible Iranian threat, while other senior officials and journalists remained on board.
As the Guardian’s Joseph Gedeon reports, the circumstances surrounding the incident were rather dramatic:

double quotation markIt later emerged that Trump had in fact been spirited away via a catering truck on to a separate, older aircraft after officials learned of a possible Iranian threat in Ankara, leaving the plane he had boarded to fly on as a decoy. Aboard the original, possibly targeted flight were the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio; the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent; several senior aides; and the traveling press pool – the latter, who were definitely not told about the threat, were asked to keep their window shades closed.
Read the full report here:
Trump landed in Dublin just moments ago, disembarking from Air Force One and being greeted by the tánaiste (deputy prime minister), Simon Harris. Here are some pictures from the newswires:

blocks.caption: Workers lay a red carpet before US president Donald Trump disembarks Air Force One at Dublin airport. Photograph: Kylie Cooper/Reuters
Trump disembarks the red, white and blue jet. Photograph: Clodagh Kilcoyne/PA
Donald Trump Jr and wife Bettina disembark Air Force One. Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP
Trump is greeted by tánaiste Simon Harris. Photograph: Clodagh Kilcoyne/PA
Trump stands on the red carpet at Dublin airport. Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

blocks.text: Trump begins two-day visit to Ireland
Donald Trump has touched down in Dublin this morning for a two-day visit to Ireland, where he will hold talks with the Irish president and prime minister, and play golf.
The weekend visit coincides with the Irish Open, a major golf tournament taking place at the beachfront Doonberg golf course owned by the US president.

blocks.caption: US president Donald Trump disembarks Air Force One at Dublin airport. Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

blocks.text: He will meet with president Catherine Connolly, who has previously been highly critical of Trump, not least because he mistakenly referred to her as a man. As the Guardian’s Irish correspondent, Rory Carroll, reports, the meeting has prompted headlines asking: “What could possibly go wrong?”

double quotation markMany in Ireland are rooting for Connolly to let rip at Trump for his policies and rhetoric on immigrants and the Middle East. Others hope she will stifle any criticisms to avoid provoking a visitor who could upend Ireland’s economy.”

Trump is then scheduled to meet the taoiseach Micheál Martin, with whom he has a more cordial relationship, before heading to the US ambassador’s official residence at Deerfield to speak with American and Irish business leaders. Then it’s off to his golf resort at Doonbeg for the night, before another day of golf on Sunday and his return to Washington.

The visit has left some Dubliners distinctly unimpressed. “He’s causing mayhem in this city because he wants to go down to Doonbeg and play golf,” taxi driver Christopher Fox told the Associated Press. “The world’s in turmoil and this fella’s down playing golf.”
We’ll be following the action throughout the day and bringing you all the latest from the fairway, the political stage and everywhere in between.

articles.title: Grammy-winning US rapper Lil Durk acquitted in murder-for-hire trial
articles.summary: The Chicago rapper was arrested in 2024 and accused of involvement in a shooting that killed the cousin of rival rapper Quando Rondo.

blocks.text: Grammy-winning rapper Lil Durk was acquitted on Friday of all charges in a federal murder-for-hire case accusing him of orchestrating the revenge killing of a man shot dead in a daytime ambush in Los Angeles four years ago.
The Chicago rapper was arrested in 2024 and accused of involvement in a shooting that killed the cousin of rival rapper Quando Rondo.
Defence lawyer Drew Findling said the recording artist, whose real name is Durk Devontay Banks, was "thankful" following the verdict.
Lil Durk has had seven albums in the US Billboard chart's top five since 2019 and has also collaborated with stars including Drake and J Cole on hit singles.
Supporters cheered outside a Los Angeles courthouse after the verdict, which came following three days of jury deliberations.
The 33-year-old faced five felony counts, including murder for hire resulting in death and conspiracy. If convicted, he could have faced a life sentence.
Although Banks was found not guilty of the charges in the case, he remains in custody and faces a separate trial on 5 October, where he will face racketeering murder and firearms charges.

"While we are disappointed with the jury's decision regarding Durk Banks, a.k.a. 'Lil Durk,' we look forward to presenting our evidence at his second trial", First Assistant US Attorney Bill Essayli said in a statement.

In the three-week trial, two co-defendants were tried alongside Banks. Deandre "OTF Dede" Wilson and David "Browneyez" Lindsey were convicted of stalking and conspiracy to commit stalking, but acquitted of murder-for-hire charges, the BBC's US partner CBS News reports, external.
The trial relied on three co-operating witnesses, Kavon "OTF Vonnie" Grant, Keith "Flacka" Jones and Kacey "OTF Jam" Hester, who reached plea deals and testified against Banks, Wilson and Lindsey.

It stemmed from a fatal shooting in August 2022 at a petrol station in Los Angeles, where a car carrying Rondo, whose real name is Tyquian Bowman, was shot at. Bowman was unharmed, but his cousin Saviay'a Robinson, who was also in the car, was killed.

Federal prosecutors accused Banks of plotting to kill Bowman, in retaliation for the earlier murder of Chicago OTF rapper King Von, who was signed to OTF. Von was killed in 2020 during an early-morning exchange of gunfire in Atlanta.
A friend of Bowman was charged with King Von's murder, but the charges were later dropped. Bowman was not arrested or charged.
Authorities said Banks made it known that he would "pay a bounty" to anyone who killed Bowman. Prosecutors argued that Banks felt pressure on social media to avenge Von's death.
Banks founded OTF in 2010. He won the 2024 Grammy Award for Best Melodic Rap Performance for his single "All My Life" featuring J Cole. He has also been nominated for a Grammy three other times.

articles.title: What the settlement left out: Meta can still collect data from kids
articles.summary: Meta's $17.1 billion settlement over youth addiction claims falls short, leaving data collection and targeted ads intact, raising concerns about the effectiveness of consumer protection measures
articles.byline: The Conversation, Randolph A. Robinson II

blocks.text: ZUCKERBERG. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg attends the annual Allen and Co. Sun Valley Media and Technology Conference at the Sun Valley Resort in Sun Valley, Idaho, U.S., July 9, 2026
Meta's $17.1 billion settlement over youth addiction claims falls short, leaving data collection and targeted ads intact, raising concerns about the effectiveness of consumer protection measures

items: In August 2026, Meta agreed to a $17.1 billion settlement over claims that its platforms are addictive and harmful to youth mental health, but the settlement does not restrict data collection from young users.
Meta's business model relies on advertising and data collection, incentivizing the company to keep users engaged on its platforms to maximize ad revenue.

Despite previous settlements with the government, Meta continues to violate terms and maintain its data collection practices, raising concerns about the effectiveness of the latest settlement in protecting young users.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

In August 2026, Meta agreed to one of the largest consumer protection settlements in American history. The settlement resolves claims from 47 states alleging that Meta intentionally designed its Facebook and Instagram platforms to be addictive to young users and harmful to youth mental health.

As part of the settlement, Meta agreed to pay up to US$17.1 billion — approximately 20% of Meta’s 2025 pretax profits — in penalties over the next 10 years. Meta also agreed to implement changes to its platforms for young users, including daily time limits, access restrictions during school hours and late nights, and “productivity breaks” that interrupt scrolling every 60 minutes.

The $17.1 billion penalty and promised changes to the platforms have grabbed the headlines. But, as a law professor who studies social media regulation, I believe that what the settlement does not include will prove more important to youth safety in the long run. The settlement does not restrict Meta from continuing to collect data from young users, from using that data to sell its targeted ads, or from serving those targeted ads to young users.
In short, while Meta agreed to some limited changes to safeguard young users, it also succeeded in protecting its surveillance-based business model.

Meta’s core business is advertising. It is the world’s second-largest digital advertising company by revenue and will soon overtake Google to claim first place. Last year, Meta generated over $200 billion in revenue, up 22% over the prior year.

Meta’s growing revenue comes from delivering more ads to platform users and charging advertisers more for those ads. For Meta, maximizing the amount of time that users spend on its platforms is critical to revenue growth. The more time users spend on Meta’s platforms, the more ads Meta can serve to those users and, consequently, the more money Meta makes.

Meta’s ad business operates on a surveillance model that gives advertisers the ability to serve personalized ads to the users who are most likely to purchase the advertiser’s goods or services. Meta does this by collecting a large amount of data about platform users. This data includes users’ friends, followers and other connections; the websites they visit, the apps they use, the games they play and the purchases they make; their demographics, including education level; the ads they see and how they interact with them; and how they use third parties’ products and services, online or in person.

The more time a user spends on Meta’s platforms, the more Meta learns about that user and the more effective its targeted ads become. This means Meta has a strong incentive to keep users scrolling on its platforms and to collect as much data as possible from those users. The recent settlement does not change that incentive structure.

This is not the first time that Meta has settled with the government and agreed to change its platforms to improve user safety. In 2012, Meta, then Facebook, Inc., settled with the Federal Trade Commission to resolve claims that it deceptively designed its privacy settings and collected data from users without their knowledge.

Then, in 2019, the FTC again sued Facebook, alleging that it violated the terms of the 2012 agreement by continuing to collect user data without consent. Again, the company settled, agreeing to pay a $5 billion penalty and again promising to stop its deceptive data collection practices.

Based on Meta’s prior conduct violating the terms of its settlements, many observers questioned whether the $5 billion penalty would deter Meta from continuing its data collection practices. It did not take long to get an answer.

In 2023, the FTC brought yet another action against Meta, alleging that it had violated the terms of the 2019 settlement. As a result of this violation, the FTC sought to restrict Meta from collecting and monetizing the data of young users.
Meta responded by challenging the FTC’s authority to impose those restrictions. Litigation in that case is ongoing.

In 2026, Meta has again settled with the government, again paid a penalty and again promised changes. And again, those promises do not restrict it from collecting data and monetizing young users, nor does the settlement restrict Meta from continuing to serve young users targeted ads.

Youth safety advocates and legislators have long fought to stop social media platforms from collecting data from young users and targeting ads to them. They have argued that doing so would remove social media companies’ incentive to design platforms that addict young people. By not including data collection and targeting restrictions in the settlement, I believe that the states missed an opportunity to change this incentive structure.

Repeatedly violating the terms of its settlements with the government seems to be an effective strategy for Meta. The company has learned that penalties for doing so are small in comparison with the profits gained through its conduct. This recent settlement looks like more of the same. With this pattern in mind, it is fair to ask whether the settlement will provide meaningful protection for young social media users or just allow Meta to continue with business as usual.

As former FTC Commissioner Rohit Chopra stated when dissenting from the FTC’s 2019 settlement, “When companies can violate the law, pay big penalties and still turn a profit while keeping their business model intact, enforcement agencies cannot claim victory.”
I believe this most recent settlement repeats the patterns of the past and continues to leave young users vulnerable on Meta’s platforms. – Rappler.com
This article originally appeared on The Conversation.
Randolph A Robinson II, Associate Professor of Law, University of Illinois Chicago

articles.title: Time for a digital divorce? Trade war puts spotlight on Canada's relationship with U.S. big tech
articles.summary: Tensions between Canada and the United States have raised concerns about Canada's digital sovereignty, but what does that term mean, and how can Canada promote it? Experts say it's about making sure…

image.caption: Experts say promoting Canada's digital sovereignty means having alternatives when it comes to tech platforms, but Canada's reliance on American companies could make that difficult. (Jenny Kane/AP)

blocks.text: LISTEN | Canada's data in foreign hands: why digital sovereignty matters:
Just Asking1:06:22Canada’s data in foreign hands: why digital sovereignty matters
Trade and political tensions between Canada and the United States have raised concerns about Canada's digital sovereignty, but what does that term mean, and how can Canada promote it?
While it may sound like jargon, experts say digital sovereignty can be defined simply.
It's about regulation, Vass Bednar, managing director of independent public policy think-tank the Canadian Shield Institute, told CBC Radio's Just Asking.

"Fundamentally, our digital sovereignty is our ability to regulate digital environments using the tools that we have," she said, including regulation of algorithms that influence what information we see online.
It's also about choice and the law, according to Michael Geist, Canada Research Chair in internet and e-commerce law at the University of Ottawa.

"It's fundamentally about both the ability to make Canadian choices … so we have alternatives to some of the larger — predominately U.S. — players, and also ensuring that Canadian law applies," he told CBC Manitoba's Information Radio last week.

items: Google updates maps to show Lake America in the U.S. — but Canadians are now seeing it, too
'Lake America' change highlights Canada's reliance on U.S. tech

blocks.text: The federal government also has a definition.

"Digital sovereignty means Canada stays in control of its own digital future — including its data, technology and essential online services — instead of relying on foreign companies, foreign systems or foreign laws," a government webpage reads.
"Think of it like this: Just as we want our homes, money and identities protected in Canada, we want the same protection for our digital information and services."

A mid-August X post from the U.S. Trade Representative account said a potential trade deal between Canada and the U.S. would include "digital trade alignment," which prompted expert concerns and speculation about digital sovereignty. Only days later, talks between the two countries fell apart at the last minute, reportedly over American insistence that U.S. streaming companies be exempt from Canadian content rules.

After talks broke down, President Donald Trump signed an executive order that Lake Ontario be renamed Lake America. Google and Apple Maps quickly implemented the change for American users, but some Canadians reported seeing it on their maps.
So, how American is our tech?
Right now, Canada doesn't have many alternatives to American technology companies and digital platforms.

"We are heavily dependent on the American big tech companies when it comes to our Canadian businesses and the public sector," said Shion Guha, assistant professor in information and computer science at the University of Toronto, on Just Asking.

The federal government also uses the Microsoft Office and Microsoft 365 platforms. In January, Shared Services Canada, which is responsible for providing IT services to the government, renewed its agreement with Microsoft in a deal worth $940 million over seven years.
Guha was part of a study on the federal government's AI Register which found that Microsoft was the single biggest supplier of systems, accounting for 42 of 409.

"An American big tech company is very heavily intertwined, not just with things like email or OneDrive … or Microsoft Office, but also in the types of predictive analytics and other types of AI products that the federal government has currently acquired," Guha said.
"This type of dependence on one big tech company is generally not a good thing for any kind of sovereignty."
There is precedent for switching, Bednar said, noting, "France has been a little bit ahead of the curve here."

items: Canada ready to further distance itself from U.S. on military procurement
Why isn't Canada blocking the Welland Canal? Other trade war questions answered

blocks.text: France's Interministerial Directorate for Digital Affairs announced in April that it will remove Microsoft's Windows operating system from government computers. Open-source software Linux will replace it.

The French government also developed Tchap, an instant messaging application, and mandated its use for public sector employees, citing security and privacy concerns. The French government says over 600,000 public sector employees use the app.
What can Canadians do?

But if getting the Canadian government to switch platforms could be difficult, getting Canadians to change everything from their credit cards to their cloud storage to their social media and instant messaging platforms and more could be even harder.

Gander Social launched in July, marketing itself as a nicer, Canadian alternative to U.S. social media platforms. The company posted on Facebook last week, saying it's approaching 50,000 users, though Bednar pointed out that Prime Minister Mark Carney isn't among them.
Homegrown app Gander wants to make social media more Canadian
But having Canadian options doesn't mean Canadians will want them, Guha said.
"There is a certain amount of inertia in getting Canadians to switch to things, because convenience usually rules over most things," he said.

"Just because we can, or do, have Canadian alternatives — and they may provide better features, they may be good for us — doesn't mean that we can overcome the social inertia to get people to switch."
But it is one way ordinary Canadians can promote digital sovereignty, Bednar said. Though she also acknowledged it's going to require more "institutional imagination in Canada" to move forward.
Staying sovereign in the AI age

The Canadian government released its National AI Strategy in June. In it, the government pledges to develop a home-grown supercomputer, as well as "sovereign cloud, AI, cyber and quantum initiatives."
Geist said the government should take an approach that balances building Canadian AI programs with access to foreign ones.

"If a single government gets to determine whether or not you have access to those frontier models, they're really determining whether or not you've got the very best tools to counter things like cybersecurity threats," he said.

items: Canada wants sovereign AI data centres. What does that actually mean?
Want to build a data centre in Canada? These are the federal government's new expectations

blocks.text: Guha said the federal government has also started referring to the data centres that help power AI and other services as "critical infrastructure."

The federal government's five principles for data centre construction, released earlier this month, require projects to "strengthen Canada's long-term digital resilience, security and compute capacity." They also say that the facilities must follow Canadian laws on cybersecurity and data protection.

"If we don't make the rules here, we will have to follow someone else's,” AI Minister Evan Solomon said at a news conference announcing the principles, which arrive amid concerns about the U.S. government using its laws to access Canadian data.
Bednar said Canada's current effort to assert its sovereignty against the U.S. is different from those of the past because of how much more of our lives exist digitally.
"Digital ... is the infrastructure of our economy," she said.
"It is just as, if not arguably more, important than manufacturing, automobiles, aluminum, steel — take your pick."

articles.title: Your guide to the U.S. midterms, and why they're crucial for Donald Trump
articles.summary: Here's everything you need to know about the upcoming U.S. midterm elections and why they're potentially crucial to how U.S. President Donald Trump wields power in his final two years in the White…

image.caption: Attendees hold signs promoting U.S. President Donald Trump's Make America Great Again movement at a campaign rally for South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham in Myrtle Beach, S.C., on Aug. 21. (Jacquelyn Martin/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·CBC Explains

Here's everything you need to know about the upcoming U.S. midterm elections and why they're potentially crucial to how U.S. President Donald Trump wields power in his final two years in the White House.
Republican control of House, Senate at stake in nationwide elections on Nov. 3

The upcoming U.S. midterm elections will determine whether Republican President Donald Trump will be free to pursue his agenda during his final two years in office or whether he'll face constraints from a Congress where the Democrats hold new power.
Here's what you need to know about the midterms.
Why do U.S. midterms matter?
The midterms are a contest for control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, which together make up the U.S. Congress.

The party that controls the Senate holds sway over presidential appointments to cabinet, the courts and senior posts in federal agencies. The party that controls the House can launch impeachment proceedings and has the power to initiate budget bills .
If one party controls both, it has broad influence over legislation as well as the potential to thwart some presidential actions.
How is the race shaping up?
The Democrats are generally excited about their prospects in the midterms and the Republicans a little worried.

History gives the Republicans plenty of reason to fret. The incumbent president's party has suffered a net loss of seats in Congress in all but two midterms since the 1930s. The only exceptions were Bill Clinton (1998) and George W. Bush (2002), when each had sky-high approval ratings.
Trump's approval rating is anything but sky-high.
What's at stake?
With slim majorities in each chamber, the Republicans have little wiggle room to lose seats and still maintain their hold on Congress.

The Democrats need to flip just four districts to take control of the House (if they hold on to all their current seats). The Democrats also need to take just four Republican-held states to win control of the Senate. But that's a tougher task than flipping the House because there are far fewer Senate seats up for election and winning each requires a statewide victory.
All 435 seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are up for grabs, as members of the House are elected to two-year terms.
Only 35 of the 100 seats in the Senate are up for election this fall. U.S. senators are elected to six-year terms.
When does voting happen?
Midterms, like the word implies, come at the two-year mark of a president's four-year term. This year, midterm election day is Nov. 3.
Many U.S. voters will choose to vote before then, either in advance polls or by mail-in ballots, a method the Trump administration is trying to restrict.

items: Supreme Court rejects challenge to Trump order on mail-in ballots, but more legal battles are expected

blocks.text: You may also have heard that people across the U.S. have been voting at various times since the spring in primaries, which are the contests to select each party's candidates. In most states, only people who are registered Republicans or Democrats can vote in the party's primaries.
How does Trump factor in?
Trump is not on the ballot in the midterms, but his influence on the campaign will be unavoidable.

Only one president since 1950 has headed into a midterm with an approval rating below 40 per cent: George W. Bush in 2006 (at 37 per cent), when his Republicans lost 30 seats in the House and six in the Senate.

Despite his low polling numbers, Trump is vowing to give "a lot of speeches" in states and districts where the races are tight to help Republican candidates. Some of those candidates are quietly asking the White House to keep him away, according to reporting by Politico.

items: Trump looms over U.S. midterms. Will he help or hurt Republicans?

blocks.text: What are the key issues in the midterms?
While U.S. polls differ slightly on the precise numbers, there's a strong thread of consistency suggesting the top issue of concern among voters right now is the cost of living.
Whether it's gas prices pushed up as a result of the war against Iran or the prices of consumer goods rising because of Trump's tariffs, pocketbook issues predominate the midterm polling.

Trump, as the dominant figure in U.S. politics for the past decade, will undoubtedly be an issue, particularly for moderate Republican or swing voters who backed him in the 2024 presidential election but have soured on him since then, according to polling.

Turnout in midterms is always lower than during presidential election years, so each party will be striving for ways to motivate their base. For the Democrats, weakening Trump's power could be that driving force. For the Republicans, stoking fear about what a Democratic-controlled Congress would do to the economy is a key advertising message.

items: Trump attacks U.S. election integrity, as Republicans face risk of midterm defeat

blocks.text: Where are the key Senate races?
Of the 35 Senate seats up for election this time, fewer than 10 are considered by campaign analysts to be at risk of changing hands.

The Republicans are considered most vulnerable in North Carolina and Maine, but polling suggests they also are in tough to hang on to their Senate seats in Ohio, Alaska, Iowa and even Texas, where no Democrat has won a statewide election since 1988.
The Democrats' biggest challenges to hold appear to be in the Senate races in Michigan and New Hampshire.

items: A Michigan Democrat wants to put Canada on the ballot during the midterms. Are voters listening?
With U.S. midterm elections looming, Democrats are clashing over how to win

blocks.text: Where are the key House races?

More than 80 per cent of House seats are considered safe for either the Republicans or the Democrats, according to the University of Virginia Center for Politics newsletter Crystal Ball, which has forecast and analyzed every election for U.S. president, House, Senate and state governors since 2002.
That political inertia leaves only a few dozen districts across the country truly "in play," as campaign strategists describe races where the outcome is in doubt.

Crystal Ball has labelled 17 Republican-held districts as toss-ups, including three in Pennsylvania and two in Michigan. All will be races to watch because they're prime targets for the Democrats as they try to win back control of the House.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Mike Crawley is a correspondent for CBC News, based in Washington. He began his career as a newspaper reporter in B.C., spent six years as a freelance journalist in various parts of Africa, then joined the CBC in 2005. Mike reported on Ontario politics for 15 years. He was born and raised in Saint John, N.B.
