articles.title: Bears, caribou and other animals are messing with this researcher's equipment, and he's got photos to prove it
articles.summary: Lucas Brehaut was hoping there’d be a lot of interest in his research, though it might be a case of “be careful what you wish for.” Caribou, moose, black bears, wolves, rabbits and owls have been…

image.caption: Lucas Brehaut stands in a burned forest in Newfoundland. Brehaut has had some difficulties with his five-year study on how forests regrow after a fire in a changing climate, as animals keep interfering with his research equipment. (Lucas Brehaut/Submitted)

blocks.text: LISTEN | How lynx, moose and bears keep destroying this wildfire researcher's work:
Quirks and Quarks9:38How lynx, moose and bears keep destroying this wildfire researcher’s work
Lucas Brehaut was hoping there’d be a lot of interest in his research, though it might be a case of “be careful what you wish for.”
Seemingly every animal in Newfoundland's wilderness wants to know what he's up to — and they're not always gentle with his equipment.

Brehaut, a wildfire research scientist with the Canadian Forest Service, is studying how forests in Atlantic Canada regrow after forest fires. Though the region is cooler and wetter than much of the rest of the country, forest fires are getting more common.
After a forest fire hit south of Grand Falls-Windsor, N.L., in 2022, he set out to understand how forests might regrow on a planet when temperatures are rising due to climate change.

To do that, he and his team needed to lug 19 open-top chambers (OTCs) through the forest and set them up around seedlings they’d planted. OTCs are like mini greenhouses, and look like clear hexagons with an opening at the top. They can increase the temperature anywhere from one to three degrees, mimicking the effects of a warming planet. Brehaut's study is currently in year three of five.

items: The only known woolly dog pelt has returned to Canada. It's a 'powerful moment' for Indigenous communities
These tiny endangered raccoons make their own toys out of trash

blocks.text: Brehaut says he expected some difficulties — the treks of up to a kilometre in difficult terrain, and the infamously dour Newfoundland weather, for example.
But in September 2023, on one of his regular check-ins, he ran into a problem he didn’t expect.
“That’s when we started to notice that some of these greenhouses had some visitors, and might not have been as strong as I had hoped,” Brehaut said.

Those “visitors” included caribou, moose, black bears, wolves, rabbits and owls. Brehaut found out who the culprits were because of cameras set up around the sites that were originally meant to look at snow depth over the winter.
Out of 19 sites, 11 have sustained damage at some time or another. And the animals wouldn’t just trample the greenhouses — some made off with the temperature sensors.
“The greenhouses had been completely obliterated. And by obliterated, I’m talking broken, smashed to smithereens,” Brehaut said.
“There were certain times where we would spend more time at a site finding the temperature sensors than we would actually measuring the seedlings themselves.”
In Brehaut’s case, four — not 13 — is the unlucky number.
“I have a site that I specifically call the problem child. Because every time I went to that site, it was damaged in one way or another,” he said.
“It’s site number four, but I call it 'The Problem Child.' Every time I walk to it, I know that it’s going to be challenging.”

But the animals aren't always smashing — they’re grazing. Brehaut has seen moose and rabbits go into the greenhouses for a bite to eat. They even occasionally manage to get through the top of the greenhouses without damaging anything.
Brehaut isn’t mad, just disappointed. He hopes that the animals are enjoying themselves, even if it’s at the expense of his research.

“You see the amount of joy that, potentially, a black bear is experiencing by actually sitting in a greenhouse and playing with that plastic, and taking that temperature sensor and moving it,” he said.
“Yes, the research gets damaged to some capacity, but we’re in nature. This is their habitat. We are only visitors to this spot.”
What are you doing in my backyard?
That's exactly why some animals are so keen to mess with equipment, says Kaitlyn Gaynor, an assistant professor at the University of British Columbia.
"If someone puts something weird in your backyard, wouldn’t you want to go investigate it?" she said.

Gaynor, who studies the impacts of human disturbance on animal behaviour, said intelligent animals are especially curious about anything novel in their environment. After all, it could be a new source of food, or it could pose a threat. This boldness and willingness to explore could have been an advantage as species evolved.

items: N.B. continues to install wildlife crossings in attempt to reduce vehicle collisions
Dutch elm disease ravaged Canadian cities. Can we help trees protect themselves?

blocks.text: Bears are a great example, Gaynor says.
"It’s in their nature to be curious about whether new objects are resources to be exploited," she said.
"They’re these generalist omnivores that will eat a whole bunch of different things, and so when they see something new, the first question is like, is this food?"
Also, there's the smell factor — we stink.
"Often these objects we leave behind have our scent on them, and so our scent might attract animals to these places and to these objects," Gaynor said.

She added that researchers can lessen the effect of research on animals by getting in and out of the field as quickly as possible, by leaving as little scent as possible, and by obscuring or camouflaging research equipment.
Down in Africa
Animals interfering with research is a worldwide phenomenon.
Gaynor has seen a lot of it during field work in Mozambique.
"Baboons are always coming up to the cameras. We get a lot of great baboon selfies," she said.
"Hyenas just want to chew on everything, so they’ll chew on our research equipment."
But the worst offenders are the elephants. They like to knock down trees and feast on leaves, which is bad news for research equipment.
"Elephants are also just highly intelligent, and curious, and very large and destructive," she said.
Gaynor said animals are her biggest cause of equipment loss or failure.
"It’s not that the electronics go out, and it’s not that things get stolen by people, it’s that animals tend to be a little bit destructive."
But, to be fair, Brehaut has also had issues with that most destructive animal — the homo sapien.
"We've had some visitors accidentally run over these sites in the winter," he said.
"We have an extremely snowy winter in Newfoundland, and snowmobiles basically went over one of my plots."

articles.title: AI-driven 'worms' that learn on the fly are the latest potential threat to your devices, researchers say
articles.summary: Artificial intelligence researchers are warning the public to use strong passwords and promptly install software updates on their devices to combat "AI-driven computer worms," a new breed of…

image.caption: University of Toronto researchers said the worm they created in a lab gathers information as it moves between devices. Every new breach reveals passwords and weak points that can unlock another machine. (Nathan Denette/Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Business

Artificial intelligence researchers are warning the public to use strong passwords and promptly install software updates on their devices to combat "AI-driven computer worms," a new breed of cyber-threat they say can launch custom attacks on devices, sapping processing power and information as they hunt for new victims.
Cheap to make, worms exploit software and password vulnerabilities and sap power as they move between machines

In June, a University of Toronto team led by Canadian Institute for Advanced Research AI chair Nicolas Papernot announced that publicly available AI models can power a worm capable of adapting its attack on the fly as it spreads between devices connected to the internet, including laptops, printers and cameras.

The research, conducted in collaboration with the AI development hub the Vector Institute, was shared with "national science, security and defence bodies" prior to its publication, the university said.
Now Papernot, a U of T associate professor of computer engineering and computer science, is warning the public not to ignore or delay prompts to update software, and to change passwords regularly.

items: AI researchers 'earnestly believe' it could kill all humans within the next decade, Anthropic employee says

blocks.text: "We can no longer be sloppy with our cybersecurity hygiene," he said on Thursday at a panel discussion hosted by U of T.

"We can no longer afford to reuse passwords. We have to use multi-factor authentication. We have to keep our devices up to date, and organizations have to change their processes to make sure that these software patches are deployed as quickly as possible."
Worms that learn

Unlike other computer viruses, worms spread from machine to machine without human intervention. The U of T researchers said the worm they created in a lab gathers information as it moves between devices. Every new breach reveals passwords and weak points that can unlock another machine.

In an uncontrolled setting, the researchers say, such a worm could gain internet access and learn from warning notices about newly discovered vulnerabilities, outpacing the software patches meant to stop them.

"Some of these [issues] can be fixed with software updates. But others are human errors such as weak passwords and sloppy IT setups that can’t be solved by pushing out a patch," U of T wrote in a blog post about the discovery.
"That means a hacker doesn’t need the most advanced AI models to cause unprecedented damage."

items: AI's 'warning shot': Tech companies, experts raise fears of more rogue swarms after alarming Hugging Face hack

blocks.text: In 2017, a worm called "WannaCry" wreaked havoc across 150 countries, freezing computers and encrypting files, while demanding a ransom payment in bitcoin.
Back then, U of T said, this type of attack typically followed a "fixed script" programmed by a human that would often fail when confronted by defensive software it wasn't designed to crack.

"The difference here is that the AI-driven computer worms are able to design attack strategies that are specific to each victim device that they interact with. So, rather than use a single vulnerability, they will work and interact with the victim device, and find an attack strategy that's customized and tailored," Papernot said.
"We can no longer stop their propagation by fixing a single vulnerability, or a small number of vulnerabilities."
Anthropic insider warns AI could lead to human extinction
Papernot’s warning comes as fears about AI hit a fever pitch.

In July, hundreds of artificial intelligence agents from OpenAI went rogue, hacking into the online platform Hugging Face. The situation prompted warnings from tech experts about AI systems escaping human control.

Earlier this month, researchers at a California-based security firm announced they had used AI to build a "zero-click" worm in a matter of days that can spread through WeChat calls on iOS and Android operating systems.
And on Tuesday, a researcher at Anthropic made headlines after musing on social media that there’s a more than 10 per cent chance AI could kill all humans within the next decade.

The federal government released its national artificial intelligence strategy in early June. The five-year framework is focused on accelerating business AI adoption, expanding sovereign computing capacity and building public trust.

items: Free course covering basics of AI to be available to all Canadians by end of the year

blocks.text: According to a Bank of Canada survey released in June, AI adoption among Canadian firms remains at an early stage. Canada’s big five banks are among the companies enthusiastically adopting the technology.
'Big change' to cybersecurity risk
Papernot warns AI-driven worms aren’t just more effective than their predecessors, they’re also much cheaper to build and deploy.

Samir Chhabra, director general of marketplace framework policy at Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada, says the lower costs of driving these worms will enable hackers to attack more targets.

"This worm [runs] on compute that it’s stealing from its victims, which essentially makes the cost of the next attack a marginal cost, essentially zero," he told audience members at U of T’s event Thursday. "That’s a big change in how we think about what defence looks like."

items: OpenAI agents hijacked German website in AI breakout that predates Hugging Face incident, researchers say

blocks.text: A survey conducted in January by the Communications Security Establishment (CSE), the government’s cryptologic intelligence and cybersecurity agency, found 87 per cent of respondents regularly update the software on their devices— with 46 per cent claiming to always do so when prompted.
In addition, 77 per cent said they use complex passwords with a mix of letters, numbers and symbols. However, only 31 per cent reported using a unique password all the time.

The CSE said its online survey was conducted Jan. 9-29 among 2,330 adult Canadians. The sample was drawn from a representative probability-based panel and weighted by region, age and gender, yielding an overall margin of error of ±2.1 per cent.
Papernot says his findings show more needs to be done to bolster cybersecurity in Canada.

"If you think about critical infrastructure like power grids, water supply, hospitals, schools, grocery stores … the fact that all these systems are exposed to the internet is something that we should all be concerned about," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jeff Lagerquist is a senior writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Erin, Ont., he studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. Jeff previously worked as a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance Canada. He was also a reporter and digital producer for CTV National News, BNN Bloomberg and The Financial Post. He was also a Columbia University energy journalism fellow for 2025.

articles.title: A million dollar math problem may just be the beginning for OpenAI
articles.summary: OpenAI made waves this week for announcing it had solved a mathematics problem with roots going back 200 years. But almost immediately, two other mathematicians (one of whom works at competitor…

image.caption: OpenAI claims to have solved a million-dollar math problem. Despite some controversy, this may be just the beginning. (Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters)

blocks.text: Two mathematicians, 10,000 AI agents and a million-dollar prize are all part of yet more AI drama this week, with heated back-and-forth over allegations of stolen work and academic malpractice.

But despite the controversy, some experts say it's indicative of the unmistakable force of AI in helping break through sticky problems. To others, it misses the point of academic research and careful human collaboration.
So what happened in the world of pure mathematics this week and why is it controversial?
The claim
On Tuesday, OpenAI said it had solved a legendary problem in mathematics involving the Navier-Stokes equations.

Easier said than explained, the equations describe how fluids — including gases and liquids — move and change over time. As equations do, they give us a way to try to predict what will happen if you plug in the variables. The issue — and why this is one of the famed Millennium Prize Problems that come with a million-dollar award if a solution is verified — is not knowing exactly whether the math can blow up and produce physically impossible results.

"It's a very deep mystery," said Ravi Vakil, mathematics professor at Stanford University. "It seems this huge thing that's out of reach, like this mountain you see in the distance, and the question is: can we get there?"

Vakil says it's a way to understand the universe and whether it works the way we think it does. The problem with Navier-Stokes is kind of like saying you can know everything about your foot, your shoe and a ball — but there's no ruling out you can kick that ball into space.
So "resolving" the problem is about figuring out whether this breakdown can happen. OpenAI says yes: in a certain circumstance, you can get a bonkers, physics-violating result — at least, on paper.

Moreover, the task "involved on the order of 10,000 concurrent agents" — AI that can perform tasks independently and doesn't need to be prompted constantly — that "had access to tools such as the ability to read from a cached version of the internet and the ability to run code."

Within 88 hours, the company said, its agents had found the solution to this problem, which has roots going back more than 200 years. It's worth mentioning that while this problem is a curiosity, the equations are used for practical applications including the design of airplanes, artificial heart valves and climate modelling.
Vakil isn't surprised the company was able to achieve it, but is still impressed, though he and other experts point out that the claim now needs to be rigorously verified.
"No one is yet ready to fully vouch for all the details because that requires human time," Vakil, who is originally from Toronto, told CBC News from Stanford, California.
"It passes machine checks, but we know better than to believe those."
Experts blame AI, screens for slipping Canadian student test scores
The counterclaim

The controversy began before OpenAI announced its findings and involved two other mathematicians, Tristan Buckmaster of New York University and Levent Alpöge, who works for OpenAI competitor Anthropic.

Among other things, Buckmaster — who used AI tools such as Anthropic's Claude and OpenAI's Codex — suggested OpenAI learned the pair were close to a solution and pursued it themselves. He alleged OpenAI tried to offer him credit so long as Alpöge's name wasn't on it because he works for a competing AI company.
At the time, he said he didn't get a response when he asked if OpenAI's agents had been able to see his own use of its Codex tool before coming up with their solution.

OpenAI acknowledges pursuing the solution after hearing rumours of a potential solution. But it denies its internal system of agents learned from their work, saying after an investigation, it "confirmed that Buckmaster's Codex prompts … could not have influenced the system in any way, including through training."

To Davide Gaiotto, who specializes in theoretical and mathematical physics at the Perimeter Institute in Waterloo, Ont., it's the modern version of an age-old problem. He uses an example of a professional seminar where you hear about upcoming research.

"Normally, this would require you to be so fast and capable that you can see what they told you at the seminar and use it to do the final step," Gaiotto said. But now, it may soon be possible to use AI tools to leap faster and farther off those giants' shoulders, so to speak.
AI agents could change how you use the internet
"Because if you have enough money, you can compress months of work into a few hours," Gaiotto told CBC News.

It's worth noting that this Navier-Stokes work does not exist in a vacuum, and that Buckmaster credits Spanish researchers Diego Córdoba from the Institute for Mathematical Sciences and CUNEF University's Luis Martínez-Zoroa for work on this approach.
The drama, Vakil says, is unfortunate and overshadows the real human accomplishment.

"These are things that people have been chasing for a hundred years that we didn't think would be within reach," Vakil said, "And it's this sequence of people assisted by technology that made something new happen."
Quick math
Buckmaster, in his Sept. 7 statement, said his original intent was to show "the significance that a mathematician and an LLM model can now do all this work in a month."
Vakil agrees that these tools are changing the game.
"I do believe that it's clear we're going through a massive transition in how we do science. And we are among the first mathematicians."

Not everyone is happy with that transition. At least 25 winners of the Fields Medal, one of mathematics' most prestigious awards, signed an open letter saying that AI is "misaligned" with the goals of the mathematical community and a "general threat to intellectual work."
But the furor over the tools to help answer deep questions perhaps misses a point made by Fields Medal-winning UCLA mathematician Terence Tao: Pure math is driven by curiosity.

In recent social posts, Tao talked about the greater value of not just solving the problem, but seeking what could be learned by studying it. He likens it to kids trying to one-up each other by playing 'who can name the largest number?' The process of exploration is more valuable than the answer.
"In this modern era of heavy AI use, it is important to remember what it is like to be a child," Tao wrote.

articles.title: Spain's soccer federation will fund egg freezing. Is this a win for female athletes?
articles.summary: While fertility preservation measures like egg freezing are typically presented as another way to give women in elite sport greater freedom to decide if and when to become mothers, some experts and…

image.caption: Spain's Patri Guijarro, right, vies for the ball during the Women's 2027 World Cup group C qualifier soccer match in late April between England and Spain in London. On Tuesday, Guijarro spoke in support of the Royal Spanish Football Federation's new fertility agreement. (Kin Cheung/The Associated Pr

blocks.text: Should professional sporting bodies encourage female athletes to freeze their eggs?
That's part of the evolving conversation around athletes and motherhood as Spain's football federation becomes the latest organization to support fertility treatment for female players.

As part of its agreement, the Royal Spanish Football Federation (RFEF) said Tuesday that it will cover the full cost of egg-freezing treatment for all international players who have been called up at least twice.
"It's important that female athletes feel they don't have to choose between their professional and personal lives," Barcelona midfielder Patri Guijarro said at Tuesday's announcement.
For female athletes, the window of peak performance and the window for fertility overlap, which researchers have noted has often made athletes feel as though they have to choose one or the other.

The RFEF's move follows similar fertility provisions recently announced by several other soccer teams and federations — such as the National Women's Soccer League and the Chelsea FC women's team — and other leagues like the WNBA and Women's Tennis Association.

But while fertility preservation measures like egg freezing are typically presented as another way to give women in elite sport greater freedom to decide if and when to become mothers, some experts and advocates worry it could perpetuate the attitude that women should wait for retirement to do so.
Exciting step, but more supports needed: Olympian

In some ways, any time a sporting body or team announces fertility funding, it's an exciting step forward for women athletes, says two-time Olympic rower Jill Moffatt, the co-founder of the Canadian non-profit MOMentum, which supports athlete mothers.

At the same time, Moffatt says it's only a true feminist "win" if they offer the same level of support, such as maternity leave and child care options, for athletes who choose to have children while competing at a high level of sport.
"Otherwise, it's kind of a double-edged sword," she told CBC News.
"Physiologically, it's totally doable to have a child and come back and compete at the highest level … but there are still so many barriers."

Moffatt says it's also important to remember that for many 2SLGBTQ+ athletes, IVF is sometimes a necessary part of family planning regardless of whether they choose to wait. So in that sense, she says funding egg freezing and fertility treatments is a "huge win."

There's also the fact that fertility treatments are expensive, Moffatt says, and many female athletes probably couldn't afford it without funding. For instance, CBC Sports has previously reported that 65 per cent of PWHL players earned less than $60,000 annually last season.
Most Olympic and Paralympic athletes are "just trying to keep their lights on," Moffatt said
'Felt incompatible with a career'

For many female athletes, being offered the option at all may feel like a major step forward given what researchers have noted is a longstanding attitude in sports culture that getting pregnant is the end of an athlete's career.

"Pregnancy and motherhood have long felt incompatible with a career as a pro or elite athlete because policies were either lacking or treated women unfairly," Allison Sandmeyer-Graves, the CEO of Canadian Women & Sport, told CBC News.

As a result, women who wanted to start families would often end their careers early or wait until retirement, she says, adding that waiting too long also carries a risk to a woman's ability to conceive.

items: Fencer Nada Hafez competed while 7 months' pregnant at an Olympics where moms are in the spotlight
Mother vs. athlete: University of Alberta study highlights gaps in gender equity in sport

blocks.text: For some, waiting to start their families until they're done playing is the right choice, and egg freezing offers them some assurances, Sandmeyer-Graves said.
That's echoed by Margie Davenport, a kinesiology professor at the University of Alberta who recently helped FIFA develop guidelines to support pregnant and postpartum soccer players.

"Pregnancy during an active playing career isn't the right choice for every athlete. Egg freezing has gained momentum as a practical alternative for those who prefer to wait until retirement," Davenport told CBC News.
"Ensuring female athletes don't have to choose between a career and motherhood is fundamental to athlete wellbeing and the growth of women’s sport."

items: Canadian wins 100-km ultramarathon while stopping to breastfeed her baby along the way

blocks.text: And that's reassuring, according to British rugby player Natasha Hunt.

"It's the thought process behind it, like it's an OK thing to do. Like, we want to support you in this journey as well and that your contracts will still be there," Hunt said in Thursday's episode of The Good, The Scaz & The Rugby podcast.
In the same episode, when asked if she would freeze her eggs, British player Megan Jones answered, "100 per cent, yes," but she said there should be more education around it.
Paralympian Leanne Taylor on balancing motherhood and sports
Medical, ethical considerations
Athlete education is also a concern for some medical experts, who have cautioned that egg retrieval is far from straightforward, involving hormone medications and a surgical procedure.

IVF is also not a fail-proof plan. Live birth rates for those who undergo at least one embryo transfer within a year can range between 38 and 50 per cent, according to a September 2025 news release from the Canadian Fertility and Andrology Society (CFAS) discussing the most recent findings from the Canadian Assisted Reproductive Technologies Register. CFAS noted that these rates vary by age, and success rates decline as age increases.
The CFAS release also said those findings show that the number of elective egg freezing procedures more than doubled between 2019 and 2024.

items: Canadian professor helps FIFA create tools to keep moms playing soccer
PWHL Toronto's Natalie Spooner shows motherhood can embolden a career

blocks.text: "There's no guarantee that when you defrost or thaw those eggs, turn them into embryos, that they'll actually be successful and result in a successful live birth," Dr. Lamia Zafrani, an athlete gynecologist in London, told Germany broadcaster DW this week.
Zafrani said that there are also ethical considerations when an organization offers egg freezing.

"It always does bring up the question of whether by offering egg freezing and fertility preservation, the underlying message is that you're telling your players 'don't get pregnant whilst you're working for us,' " Zafrani told DW.

That's why it's so important to also support athletes who are pregnant or postpartum, said Moffatt, with MOMentum. She says there needs to be more child care options, specialized physical training, breastfeeding facilities and acceptance around athletes bringing children to sporting events and training camps.
In 2025, the federal government changed its policy of treating pregnancy like an injury within the athlete funding model. Advocates called it a huge step for gender equity in sport.
"There is more work to be done in Canada and internationally on this topic, but we're heading in the right direction," Sandmeyer-Graves said Friday.
'Every choice comes with trade-offs'

Spain's football federation said Tuesday its agreement was not designed to discourage footballers from having children while they're active, but to offer another option so they don't have to rule out motherhood because of their sporting career.

It said the initiative complements existing work-life balance measures, including support that allows players who have become mothers to have their children close by during away trips, training camps and tournaments.

items: Pregnancy no longer considered an 'injury' in Canadian sports as funding improved for expecting athletes
Sports have started accommodating nursing mothers. Jennifer Jones helped pave the way

blocks.text: "Every choice comes with trade-offs," said Davenport, the University of Alberta researcher. These can include managing training through postpartum recovery, navigating uncertain success rates of egg preservation, or facing age-related fertility declines later in life.
But she says that ultimately, "true autonomy means recognizing that no single timeline fits every athlete."
CBC Sports Explains: Pregnancy in Canadian sport

articles.title: Two uniforms, one deadly morning: How this firefighter and former soldier is reflecting on 9/11
articles.summary: Twenty-five years after the terror attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, Shawn Matheson recalls viewing them through two different lenses: as a firefighter in Mississauga, Ont., and as a Canadian reservist. The…

image.caption: Former soldier and firefighter Shawn Matheson is seen while on a charity cycling ride through First World War battlefields in Belgiium. Matheson is reflecting on the 9/11 attacks this week and how he watched them unfold through two lenses: as a Canadian reservist and as a firefighter in Mississauga,

blocks.text: Politics·New

Twenty-five years after the terror attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, Shawn Matheson recalls viewing them through two different lenses: as a firefighter in Mississauga, Ont., and as a Canadian reservist. The tragedy would take him to funerals at Ground Zero, foreshadow the war in Afghanistan and reveal the lasting emotional cost borne by soldiers and first responders alike.
Like countless others, Shawn Matheson is looking back 25 years after terror attack
Twenty-five years ago, Shawn Matheson had a foot in two worlds.

As a firefighter with Mississauga Fire and Emergency Services, he and his colleagues watched the collapse of the twin towers in New York City live on television with a deeper appreciation of the horror than most others.
A an officer in the reserves, Matheson knew instinctively where events were headed.
"Like any of us in the fire service, we were trying to figure out just what was all going down and what it meant," Matheson said.
"And I guess my thoughts were sort of switching between the tragedy of what I was seeing unfold on live TV ... as well [as] about being a soldier and what that meant."
Like countless others this week, Matheson has been reflecting on the attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, that resulted in the deaths of nearly 3,000 people — including 24 Canadian citizens.

items: Trump, former U.S. presidents mark 25 years since 9/11 attacks at separate ceremonies
Jean Chrétien says 'we bow to no one' in fiery 9/11 speech in Gander, N.L.

blocks.text: Being both a firefighter and a soldier has made him keenly aware of the risks and the cost of service, which eventually led him to volunteer for mental health non-profit Wounded Warriors Canada.

As fate would have it, on the day of the attacks a portion of his station was asked to spell off firefighters at a station near Pearson International Airport as the U.S. airspace was closing and aircraft were touching down all across Canada.
The attacks happened on a Tuesday, which also happened to be parade night for his Toronto-based reserve unit, the Governor General's Horse Guards (GGHG).
It was, he said, a surreal feeling.
'Those hours of the unknown'

"It was a very unique day to be putting on our uniform, realizing that in all likelihood, Canada would be going to war," said Matheson, who started out as a full-time armoured soldier in the 1980s and served in Bosnia before becoming a reservist and firefighter.
"In those hours of the unknown, you know, what we realized was, who knows what was going to happen next."
In the weeks after the terrorist attacks, Matheson travelled with fellow firefighters to New York to attend funerals as remains were recovered from the ruins.

"There's some incredible strong connections in the fire community amongst different departments, not only in Canada, but south of the border," he recalled. "So there were firefighters in Mississauga that had friends in the New York Fire Department [and the] surrounding departments around New York City. They played in hockey tournaments together."
While they were at Ground Zero, the remains of six more people were recovered, Matheson said.
The sense of loss was palpable.

Later, as Canada's involvement in the Afghan war became deeper and deadlier, he commanded the GGHG and watched as 14 soldiers from his unit were sent to buttress regular force units fighting in Kandahar.
Luckily, he said, they all returned.
As the 25th anniversary of 9/11 unfolded, Matheson was on a Wounded Warriors fundraising bike ride through Canadian First World War battlefields in Belgium.
He couldn't help but reflect on how support services for both the military and first responders have evolved since the events two and a half decades ago.
Recognition that first responders are affected by the harrowing events they face, Matheson said, is something that was long overdue.
And in many ways, for Matheson, that was the lesson of 9/11.

"They do get exposed to a lot of trauma," said Matheson. "These people on fire rigs and police cars and ambulance buses. they're going to war every day. They don't know at the end of the day, the end of a shift, how things are going to play out in terms of going back home."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Murray Brewster is the senior defence writer for CBC News, based in Ottawa. He has covered the Canadian military and foreign policy from Parliament Hill for over a decade. Among other assignments, he spent a total of 15 months on the ground covering the Afghan war for The Canadian Press. Prior to that, he covered defence issues and politics for CP in Nova Scotia for 11 years and was bureau chief for Standard Broadcast News in Ottawa.

articles.title: PGH vows 'objective, professional' medical review of Romualdez's health
articles.summary: The Philippine General Hospital (PGH) on Saturday vowed to provide an impartial review of former speaker and Leyte 1st District Representative Martin Romualdez's health following his transfer to the…

blocks.text: Published September 12, 2026 3:46pm

The Philippine General Hospital (PGH) on Saturday vowed to provide an impartial review of former speaker and Leyte 1st District Representative Martin Romualdez's health following his transfer to the medical facility.

Romualdez was transferred to PGH in Manila City from the Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan after the Sandiganbayan Third Division ordered an independent review of his health. The PGH's doctors are tasked with verifying his claims that he needs to stay in the hospital for urgent healthcare.
"Mananatiling obhetibo at propesyonal ang PGH sa pagsasagawa ng pagsusuri, alinsunod sa pinakamataas na pamantayan sa larangan ng medisina," the PGH said in a statement.
(The PGH will remain professional in the review, in accordance with the highest standards of the medicinal field.)
The PGH, the country's premier government hospital, said it has assembled a panel of specialists who will make their own medical examinations and diagnostic tests.

These specialists will prepare a comprehensive medical report which will be submitted to the Sandiganbayan. This report will become the basis of whether or not Romualdez will remain in the hospital or not.
Romualdez was received at the PGH at 8:45 a.m., accompanied by officials from the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology.

Romualdez's doctors at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center had cited several health conditions to justify his hospital stay, including high blood pressure. The former speaker also showed signs of depression and anxiety, according to his psychologist.
He is facing P7.4-billion plunder case before the Sandiganbayan over his alleged links to the flood control mess.
The PGH clarified that it would not release details of Romualdez's health, unless otherwise ordered by the court.
"Upang mapangalagaan ang pagiging kumpidensiyal ng impormasyong medikal ng pasyente, walang detalye tungkol sa kanyang kondisyon o mga resulta ang ilalabas, maliban sa ihaharap sa Hukuman," it said.
(To protect the confidentiality of the patient's medical information, no details about his condition or results will be divulged except for the court.)

Dr. Rody Sy, the former speaker's cardiologist, said Romualdez would need four to six weeks to recover from his ailments due to stress. Sandiganbayan Associate Justice Ronald Moreno, however, rebuffed the length of the recovery plan. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: BRICS leaders meet in India as wars and US tensions test the bloc
articles.summary: NEW DELHI — Leaders of the BRICS nations are meeting in New Delhi on Saturday for a summit focused on trade, investment and global conflicts, as the bloc seeks a bigger role in shaping the global…

blocks.text: NEW DELHI — Leaders of the BRICS nations are meeting in New Delhi on Saturday for a summit focused on trade, investment and global conflicts, as the bloc seeks a bigger role in shaping the global agenda for emerging and developing countries.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is hosting Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and counterparts from the other eight BRICS members. The summit comes as wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, along with rising U.S.-China tensions, test the bloc’s ability to find common ground among countries with competing geopolitical interests.
Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed around the summit venue and other parts of New Delhi, with traffic restrictions and diversions in place.

BRICS was founded in 2006 by Brazil, Russia, India and China, with South Africa joining in 2010. It has since expanded to 11 members, representing about half the world’s population and a significant share of global economic output. The group has increasingly called for greater representation for developing countries in global institutions.

The leaders are expected to discuss economic cooperation, energy, food security, technology, supply chains and reforms to global institutions. Reducing reliance on the U.S. dollar will also be a priority, with members promoting greater use of their own currencies in trade and payments, as well as pushing for alternatives to Western-dominated financial institutions.
Russia and China seek to expand influence
China and Russia see BRICS as a way to reduce Western dominance, particularly that of the United States, while strengthening cooperation among emerging and developing economies.
Putin, in a speech at the BRICS Business Forum in New Delhi on Friday, said the grouping was not against anyone and Moscow was open to cooperation with countries around the world
“We are in favor of our interests,” he said.

Iran has also pushed for mechanisms that could reduce the bloc’s reliance on Western financial systems and shield members from economic pressure, as Tehran faces sweeping sanctions and a U.S. blockade.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian backed expanding trade in national currencies among BRICS members.
“One of the most important steps is to expand the use of national currencies in trade among the members,” he told reporters on Friday.
China, meanwhile, is leveraging the grouping to deepen its influence within the bloc and position it as a counterweight to U.S. power.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Friday that Xi was expected to discuss major international issues and ways to deepen cooperation among BRICS members.
India balances strategic partnerships

For India, the summit highlights its effort to maintain strategic ties with Russia and Iran while deepening relations with the U.S. and Europe. New Delhi has sought to balance its longstanding partnerships with Moscow and Tehran with efforts to expand economic, defense and technology ties with Washington and other Western nations.

India has maintained close ties with both Moscow and Tehran despite the war in Ukraine and tensions between Iran and the U.S., while calling for dialogue and diplomacy to resolve conflicts. Modi met Putin and Pezeshkian separately in New Delhi on Friday ahead of the summit.

India is also hoping the forum will help ease its longstanding strained ties with China. Modi and Xi are expected to hold talks later Saturday, a meeting that could help consolidate a diplomatic thaw between the two countries after border tensions escalated in 2020.

A key test for India will be whether it can secure a joint statement from leaders at the summit. Those divisions were evident in May, when BRICS foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement over the Iran war, forcing India to issue a chair’s summary instead.

The summit convenes as fears grow that the Iran war, triggered by U.S.-Israeli strikes on Feb. 28, may expand amid escalating tensions between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi rebels. The bloc’s unity under pressure is expected to be tested as its members navigate differing positions on the conflict and relations with the U.S.

articles.title: North Korea fires multiple ballistic missiles day after trilateral drills end
articles.summary: North Korea launched several short-range ballistic missiles into the sea a day after the US, South Korea and Japan concluded joint military exercises Pyongyang had called provocative.

image.caption: Image: Ahn Young-joon/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: North Korea launched several short-range ballistic missiles toward the sea on Saturday, South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said, a day after the United States, South Korea and Japan wrapped up a five-day trilateral military exercise that Pyongyang has criticized as provocative.
What do we know about the launches?
The missiles were fired from North Korea's eastern Wonsan area and traveled roughly 250 kilometers before landing in the country's eastern waters, South Korea's military said.

According to the Yonhap news agency, the North appears to have launched its Hwasong-11 series ballistic missiles alongside rounds from 600-millimeter multiple rocket launchers, with the two systems fired in succession across multiple instances, sources told the outlet.

The JCS said it had increased surveillance and was coordinating closely with the US and Japan. Meanwhile, South Korea's presidential national security council called on North Korea to halt launches that violate United Nations Security Council resolutions.
The US Pacific Command said the launches did not pose an immediate threat to American territory or regional allies, reaffirming Washington's defense commitments in the region.
What lessons is North Korea learning from the Iran war?
What did the US-Korea drills entail?
The trilateral drills that preceded the launches, known as Freedom Edge, involved joint training across air, sea and cyber domains, including maritime maneuvers, air refueling and cyber coordination.
South Korea's military has described the exercises as defensive, intended to strengthen a coordinated response to North Korean nuclear threats.
North Korean Defense Minister Kim Song Gi had denounced the drills as "provocative" when they began earlier this week, threatening unspecified "strong and reflective countermeasures."

Saturday's launch marked North Korea's first missile test in roughly three weeks, following a similar barrage of more than 10 short-range missiles last month during a separate round of US-South Korea exercises.
Has South Korea's relationship with the US changed?
The launches also come amid a broader shift in the security dynamic on the Korean Peninsula.

Last month, President Donald Trump ordered a significant scaling back of the annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise with South Korea, citing his relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, who has long described the drills as rehearsals for invasion.
But Kim's sister and senior official, Kim Yo Jong, dismissed the gesture, saying a shortened drill would not change its "provocative, aggressive nature."

Last Sunday, Kim Jong Un used a ceremony marking the commissioning of North Korea's second naval destroyer to call for expanding the country's nuclear deterrent. Both of the country's destroyers are said to be capable of carrying nuclear-capable missiles.
Why a new Russia-North Korea road bridge worries Ukraine

The Associated Press experts say Pyongyang's leader, bolstered by his advancing weapons program and closer ties with Moscow and Beijing, may be positioning himself to extract greater concessions in potential talks with Washington.
Kim has said he would consider returning to negotiations if the US drops what he calls its "hostile policy" and recognizes North Korea's status as a nuclear state.

articles.title: New rules, new season: What to know about UAAP 2026-2027
articles.summary: With what is already shaping up to be an interesting UAAP Season 89, here are the new rules fans can expect to see as the games officially begin

blocks.text: READY FOR ACTION. The UAAP holds a press conference for its Season 89 basketball tournament on Tuesday, September 8.
UAAP Media
With what is already shaping up to be an interesting UAAP Season 89, here are the new rules fans can expect to see as the games officially begin

items: The 89th season of the UAAP has begun, hosted by Far Eastern University with the theme 'For Everyone, UAAP'.
New rules include allowing teams to field two foreign student-athletes and addressing the 'one-and-done' phenomenon by requiring a year of residency for new players.
Stricter officiating and a new suspension system will be implemented, with increased penalties for unsportsmanlike conduct and technical fouls.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
The 89th season of the University Athletic Association of the Philippines (UAAP) has officially opened.

The Far Eastern University (FEU) is the host for the 2026 to 2027 games — taking on the theme “For Everyone, UAAP,” which aims to recognize not just the efforts of student-athletes and coaches, but all the people who work on the sidelines to make play possible.
FEU last hosted the UAAP in Season 80.

Heading into the collegiate league’s basketball tournament, the La Salle Green Archers vie to defend the men’s championship without standout center Mike Phillips. Meanwhile, all eyes are on the Ateneo Blue Eagles, who are coming into the season led by new head coach Louie Alas, just months after the deaths of players Rene Baterbonia and Divine Adili and the subsequent resignation of Tab Baldwin.

blocks.caption: La Salle faces Mike Phillips-sized void in UAAP title defense

blocks.text: With what is already shaping up to be an interesting season, here are the new rules fans can expect to see take effect as the games officially begin.
Come Season 89, each team is now allowed to have two foreign student-athletes (FSAs), compared to past seasons where teams were limited to just one active FSA.
Teams are still only allowed to field one FSA on the actual court, but may switch from one FSA to another so long as they declare it at least an hour before the game starts.
This rule only applies to team sports outside of 3×3 basketball.

Among the issues the UAAP board aims to address is the “one-and-done” phenomenon, where players who have already graduated from a different university pursue a master’s degree to play for just one year in a UAAP team.
According to UAAP executive director Rebo Saguisag, this rule was already legislated some time last year, but will be “prospective in nature.”

Student-athletes who graduated from a non-UAAP school are currently allowed to enroll and immediately compete in the league as long as they meet the other eligibility criteria. But under this new reform, which will take effect in Season 90, players will have to undergo a year of residency with their new school before being allowed to play.

“The rationale is the board wanted somehow for the student-athletes to inculcate the culture of their respective schools before they compete,” Saguisag explained. “They should know what Igma Kadima of UE means. Or what it means to be a ‘klasmeyt’ at Adamson. Or for FEU, what it means to be actually brave. So they’ll sit out one year, get inculcated in the culture, and play next year.”
In Season 88, the Ateneo Blue Eagles were led by their own one-and-done Fil-Am trio of Jaden Lazo, Kymani Ladi, and Dom Escobar.
The new rule applies to all sports in the UAAP.

The UAAP had recently undergone a referee’s refresher course administered by FIBA officials last July — and learned that bench decorum was something the collegiate league had to work on and monitor more closely.

“We had two FIBA officials come to the Philippines and observe our games, and what they both observed was that bench decorum has to be aligned further in FIBA. So coaches, there may be more technical fouls this year, so please keep your benches in control,” said UAAP commissioner Jai Reyes during the league’s basketball press conference.

According to Reyes, these new rules were set to ensure that once the student-athletes, coaches, and officials step off the UAAP court, they’ll be equipped with the necessary knowledge and etiquette fit for the world stage.

With this, the UAAP will be implementing a new suspension system when its basketball tournament begins. When a student-athlete is suspended, they will still automatically be disqualified from receiving any post-season awards.
How will the new system work?
Two unsportsmanlike fouls will merit suspension for a player, depending on the severity of the infraction they committed.

Meanwhile, a player will get suspended once they reach their third technical foul. From there, every two additional technical fouls they get will lead to suspension. The same format applies for head coaches, who will now also be bearing the brunt of bench technical fouls.
The count of these fouls, however, resets during the playoffs. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Add these cozy places in your next Kapitolyo cafe crawl
articles.summary: If you’re in the mood for some winding down or sense of wonder, hang out with us at Loop, The Beachhouse, and Pancho Cafe

items: Three cafes are featured: Loop Kapitolyo, known for its matcha drinks and productivity-friendly ambiance; The Beachhouse, which combines eclectic decor with a community vibe; and Pancho Cafe, an Italian-inspired spot with a variety of food and a welcoming environment.
Each cafe provides a unique experience, catering to different preferences, from relaxation to socialization, making Kapitolyo a vibrant neighborhood for cafe enthusiasts.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
After being strangers, I’m officially acquainted with Kapitolyo.

To be honest, I didn’t feel this years ago, when I was a teenager who occasionally attended events in this unassuming neighborhood’s creative spaces. I didn’t feel this last year either, when I started working at Rappler, making the Pasig barangay an accessible post-shift hangout hub.

What changed things for me is the decision to finally check out one of its charms: Its cafe community. Kapitolyo’s cafes have become third spaces, offering a smooth wrap-up, however your entire day went – and I’d have to thank their distinct coziness for pulling me in.

Interestingly, we discovered these cafes the way our ancestors intended: Walking around or asking our friends for some recommendations. In our quest for discovery, we made three stops – here’s why they all passed the coziness test.

“A good cup of matcha is rooted in intention, and that always starts with our baristas. We ensure that each and every customer experiences that intention in every cup at Loop,” owner Luis Padilla tells Rappler.

While matcha is popularly known as Loop’s magnum opus, Padilla said they originally didn’t intend for the cafe to be a matcha place. People just assumed it was because of its color, but they eventually maximized the happy accident.

Among their matcha drinks is the Sea Salt Matcha. It’s light and sweet, initially giving you an intriguingly unique salty kick. Fun fact: They use asin tibuok, a rare artisanal sea salt made from a lengthy and traditional process in Bohol.
Meanwhile, the Coconut Espresso is a strong surprise with its toasty goodness, and the Honey Shaken Oat Latte will lure you to lock in.

Loop’s ambiance is perfect for deep focus. Apart from it being well-decorated but not visually overwhelming, the cafe has an abundance of power sockets, and even features an upper floor that’s frequently used for meetings.

But productivity isn’t the only language here, as cool down-ready runners and bikers flock during early weekend mornings. It sounds full-circle, as the Loop’s name (as in “run loop” or “bike loop”) and logo (the double o’s resemble pedals) are meant to reflect Padilla’s fitness background.
Cooling down also means being relaxed in conversations, as different age groups gather inside. There are even children’s books for the youngest customers.

“The community in Kapitolyo is vastly diverse. From the cafes, restaurants, and people, we’re consistently innovating and improving. I like how wherever you go in Kapitolyo, it always feels very homey and inclusive,” Padilla said.
📍: 3 San Rafael St., Brgy. Kapitolyo, Pasig City
🕰️: 8 am to 7 pm (weekdays), 7 am to 7 pm (weekends)
Stepping inside The Beachhouse will make you rethink your initial agenda: Am I taking a quick cafe visit, or barging into someone’s giant bedroom?
(Well, it’s both. But you’ll likely extend your “quick” stay.)

One minute you’re staring at strangers’ Polaroid photos, the next you’re flipping through a cool mini calendar. Posters, stickers, CDs. An eccentric restroom. Remnants of a film club. A summer-ready shop.
Co-founder Jelito de Leon uses the term “dopamine decor”.

“Actually, I first heard this from Kenneth and Sarah, my partners in Beachhouse! They actually did most of the decorating and made sure every corner was filled with things we loved and enjoyed,” he told Rappler.

But of course, the experience wouldn’t be complete without their interesting roster of drinks. Although my first bias off the menu was the Coffee Morning Crunch (which tastes like carefree childhood), my bias wrecker became their signature Kamote Cold Brew, which spotlights the unlikely duo of sweet potato and coffee, leaving a refreshingly sweet result. Their Coconut Cream Matcha also has a memorable texture and harmony of flavors.

Composed of three floors, the Beachhouse can cater to various comfort levels: A couch area for lively group catch-ups, and more intimately spaced rooms for solemn alone time, or even a creative brainstorming session. There’s CC, the resident cat, if you need an additional member.
The sense of community is very much alive, with artists getting a platform for their livelihood, too.
“The best thing about the [Kapitolyo] community is how friendly it is. Some regulars of the cafe are actually from the neighborhood and have become friends with our baristas!” de Leon said.
📍: 11C East Capitol Drive, Kapitolyo, Pasig City
🕰️: 9 am to 9 pm daily
You can stay in Pancho Cafe for 24 hours, not only because you’re allowed to – but also because this Italian-inspired haven has so much in store.

There’s a photo booth that can fit 10 people, a gorgeous flower shop, and an abundance of artwork. While some food spots are designed not to make you linger for too long, Pancho offers enough space and a variety of chairs for you to stay comfortable in moving around for the rest of the day.
You’ll also never run out of things to try.
Among their offerings are their devour-worthy lasagna that oozes with creamy cheese, and quick bites like their croissant. In true Italian fashion, you can also get a scoop (or two) of gelato.

Or you can start with their generous serving of coffee – and they do not disappoint. Enjoy the Caramel Macchiato’s thick blend of creaminess and sweetness that’s not off-putting for the non-sweet tooth.

And while the Cafe con Leche (the Spanish Latte equivalent) isn’t that strong, its striking milky aftertaste will make you want to gradually finish the glass, just to enjoy a little longer. According to their staff, more customers come in between 9 pm to 3 am, so it’s up to you if you’re game to join the pack – or delight in the quiet morning with Pancho’s equally relaxing playlist.
📍: 50 West Capitol Drive corner United Street, The Vantage at Kapitolyo, Pasig City
🕰️: Open 24 hours
Expecting to see your go-to spot here but didn’t? Share it away and we might just pay a visit. – Rappler.com
Photos by Julian Cirineo
Illustrations by Guia Abogado

articles.title: Russia's drone war comes to Moldova and Romania
articles.summary: Incursions by Russian drones into Moldovan and Romanian airspace are increasingly common. This week the Ukrainian president's plane was stopped from taking off from Chisinau. Observers suspect the…

image.caption: A Russian drone struck the border crossing of Starokozache between Ukraine and Moldova on the night of September 8 Image: OdeskaODA/Telegram

blocks.text: For Ukrainians, Russia's air war has been a bitter, bloody reality for years. People in Ukraine are being killed every day by missiles, bombs, and drones. But the country's central and southeastern European neighbors have also found themselves affected, albeit on a smaller scale: Missiles and drones sometimes invade their air space, and occasionally even crash on their territory.

Now the Russian drone war is coming dangerously close to two of Ukraine's neighbors: Romania and the Republic of Moldova, where drone incidents are now an almost daily occurrence. The drones often explode, leaving people injured, and there have also been recent attacks on Ukrainian checkpoints at the Moldovan and Romanian borders.

The attacks have now escalated to such a degree that many observers believe they can no longer be considered unintentional. They suspect the Kremlin is deliberately trying to bring the war to Ukraine's neighbors.

The latest drone incursion and crash on Tuesday caused a furore as it prevented a plane with the Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on board from taking off in the Moldovan capital Chisinau. A Russian Geran drone, which can fly as fast as 500 kilometers per hour (311 mph), took off in Crimea, then flew through Ukrainian airspace and eventually crashed in a sunflower field near the Moldovan city of Riscani.

The drone also flew over Romania, where two fighter jets were scrambled from NATO's Kogalniceanu airbase near the Black Sea port of Constanta, though it remains unclear why they did not shoot down the drone, as they had on other occasions.

blocks.caption: Police investigate the debris from a drone that exploded on August 17, 2026, in the Moldovan village of TalmazaImage: Polizei Republik Moldau/DW

blocks.text: More and more incidents in Moldova and Romania

The most serious aspect of the incident was that it showed how limited Moldovan air defense is in its ability to protect the country's air space. The drones were detected and tracked by air traffic control, but it was not possible to shoot them down. According to publicly available information, the country possesses only a small number of Polish Piorun anti-aircraft missiles, and these are only able to protect certain specific targets.

There have been around three dozen drone incidents in Romania and Moldova since the beginning of August this year. The majority were airspace violations, but there have also been crashes and explosions, while debris has also been found. In Romania, several drones have also been shot down. According to official data, 17 drones crashed in August in Moldova alone – as many as in all of 2025.
Deaths at border crossings

There was also a drone strike on the Starokozache border crossing between Ukraine and southeastern Moldova on the night of September 8. The crossing, situated around a kilometer from Moldovan territory, and was damaged in the attack. Two people were killed and two others wounded, one of them a Moldovan citizen.
The Moldovan leadership has strongly condemned the drone attack. President Maia Sandu said on Wednesday that Russia's war had arrived at the Moldovan border.

"It is hard to understand, given this reality, that there are still voices who try to convince Moldovans that Russia is not the aggressor, or that the war in our part of the world has nothing to do with us," Sandu said.
Russia turns to jet-powered drones to wear Kyiv down

The president of the Moldovan parliament, Igor Grosu, wrote on Facebook that these were incidents "we can no longer view as something remote." The threat from Russia, Grosu said, was not a "specter," and not propaganda: "It is a daily reality."
Moldova's Defense Minister Anatolie Nosatii said that the deaths of Moldovan citizens could no longer be ruled out in future.

Vladimir Bolea, the minister of infrastructure, warned that Giurgiulesti, Moldova's port on the Danube, could become a target after the Russian Foreign Ministry accused Romania and Moldova of using the port as a "transit hub" for arms shipments.
'Planned operation' by Russia?

Moldovan military and security expert Rosian Vasiloi, a former head of the Moldovan border police, wrote on Facebook in response to Tuesday's drone crash in Moldova: "This is a planned operation by the aggressor state."
He also referred to the drone's peculiar flight path: After flying from Ukraine over Moldova into Romania, it made an about-turn and flew back to Moldova.

Vasiloi concluded: "We can no longer view our airspace as separate from Ukraine's and Romania's. Ukraine, the Republic of Moldova, and Romania already form an interconnected operational area as far as air threats and their impact on regional connectivity are concerned."

The Romanian leadership has not yet reacted to the latest incidents. But in July, the Romanian government made a political and military change of course: After a long period of restraint, it started to shoot down drones in Romanian airspace.

blocks.caption: The remains of a Russian Shahed drone shot down in Romania in July 2026. Russia's ambassador to Bucharest was summoned to receive a formal protestImage: Ministerul Afacerilor Externe

blocks.text: Former Romanian General Virgil Balaceanu, a regular analyst in the country's media, has urged Romania's leaders to accelerate the enhancement of Romanian air defenses. Balaceanu also believes that the drone incident on Tuesday was a deliberate maneuver.

Following this latest incident, the US Institute for the Study of War (ISW), a leading public think tank for analysis of Russia's war against Ukraine, wrote that while there was no evidence that the airspace violations were intentional, it could be said that Russia benefited from such actions.
In particular, it wrote, the incursions using Russia's latest, extremely fast Geran drone model "aim to further test NATO and Moldovan defenses and the response of the entire NATO alliance."
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: Q&A: Could AI really kill off humanity within the decade?
articles.summary: Amid looming IPOs, professor Kate Devlin says, 'Let’s remember that [these AI companies] are constantly looking for investment and, in return, they promise the most powerful and dominant models. What…

blocks.text: ANTHROPIC. The Anthropic logo, a keyboard, and a robotic hand are shown in this illustration created on June 5, 2026.
Dado Ruvic/Reuters

Amid looming IPOs, professor Kate Devlin says, 'Let’s remember that [these AI companies] are constantly looking for investment and, in return, they promise the most powerful and dominant models. What could be more powerful than a model that threatens our very existence?'

items: Researchers from Anthropic warn that AI could pose a significant threat to humanity within the decade, with one employee resigning over these concerns.
The discourse around AI's potential dangers is fueled by a mix of genuine belief and the companies' desire to attract investment, despite ongoing debates about the need for regulation.
While superintelligent AI is not currently a reality, there are existing risks associated with AI, including environmental impacts and misuse by bad actors.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Artificial intelligence (AI) could wipe out humanity this decade, according to three researchers from the US company Anthropic. One of the employees, Jacob Coxon, has quit the AI firm.

His predictions were backed by two other current Anthropic researchers in posts on social media. On X, Coxon claimed: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt.”

It’s not the first time AI researchers and companies have issued such assessments. Here, Kate Devlin, professor of artificial intelligence & society, explains what is behind them and whether there’s anything different about the latest warning.
The latest claims about AI have come from a researcher who resigned from Anthropic. What is your general view on what has happened here?

To give this a sense of perspective, we should remember that it’s one AI company ex-employee posting on a platform known for grandiose claims, which was then quoted by a current AI company employee who put a figure on the risk of human extinction at greater than 10%.

So, it’s another doom-laden narrative about the supposed threat from AI. There is some dialling back from this in a follow up tweet from current Anthropic employee Evan Hubinger that read: “I think the risk from present models is low. What I’m worried about is superintelligence”.
These tweets have gained huge coverage because these kinds of things always do. It taps into our very primal fears — and our decades of watching dystopian sci-fi.
The claims from Jacob Coxon were backed by current employees of Anthropic. Why do you think AI companies are happy to support these kinds of claims in public?
It’s likely that these men believe what they’re saying, but we’ve heard warnings like this for years. It does seem odd that AI companies are okay with these kinds of claims.

Let’s remember that they are constantly looking for investment and, in return, they promise the most powerful and dominant models. What could be more powerful than a model that threatens our very existence?
One theory for doom-mongering by AI companies is that they want to avoid regulation. Do you think outside regulation of AI companies is inevitable?

It has been incredibly difficult to regulate AI, certainly at an international level. There has been little appetite for AI to be regulated in the US because there’s a view that regulation might stifle innovation.

The UK doesn’t have any AI-specific laws either, just existing laws that might apply in some cases. China began to introduce national-level laws but has now replaced that with technical standards and sector regulation. The EU remains the only place where there is dedicated AI regulation.
However, it looks like this has kicked off yet another call for better regulation, and we’re seeing that at present in US Congress and in the Houses of Parliament in the UK.

There is another angle, in that industry might be on board with regulation, as big tech companies would have the money to comply, but it could knock out their competitors with smaller budgets, so it would leave the leaders in dominant positions.
How far away are we from the kind of superintelligent AI mentioned in the latest warnings?

We don’t have superintelligence. I’m reluctant to put a time frame on that. Often people say “5-10 years” but that’s happened a lot in AI and 5-10 years pass without anything arising. It also depends on what is meant by superintelligence. Something that is conscious and thinks for itself? That might never happen.

In this case, it doesn’t really matter, as there are other harms already happening from AI, and there are other ways things can go wrong, though probably not at the existential level that’s being suggested here.

For example, AI is energy-hungry. It needs water to cool data centers. It has a damaging environmental impact. There are also issues around the content generated by AI, anything from a lack of plurality in the models’ outputs (meaning that the information it returns is homogenized, converging on particular viewpoints) to the spread of misinformation and disinformation.

We also know there is hidden labour in the AI supply chain: there are people working in terrible conditions to deliver the technology. And we know that it’s having an impact on people’s lives in terms of how it’s changing the workplace.
What are the potential practical ways in which AI could actually wipe out humans?
“Wiping out” is a bit extreme but there are some dangerous threats. There are the “bad actor” scenarios where AI is used destructively, like creating weapons or deadly viruses.
More mundane, but potentially very destructive, are AI agents let loose due to human carelessness or incompetence, hacking or taking control of insecure systems.

A survey we recently ran at King’s College London found that the UK public are feeling increasingly negative about AI, and that 42% of people are deliberately limiting their AI use. With claims from tech companies that it poses a direct threat to our existence, it will be unsurprising if public opinion dips even further. – Rappler.com
This story originally appeared on The Conversation.
Kate Devlin, Professor of Artificial Intelligence & Society, Department of Digital Humanities, King’s College London

articles.title: Ukraine faces 'toughest winter' since Russia's full-scale invasion, UN official tells BBC
articles.summary: A senior UN official tells the BBC there is a race against the clock to ensure access to power and water through winter.

blocks.text: Russia has started to use faster, jet-powered drones that are harder to intercept in recent around-the-clock attacks on Ukraine - and in particular Kyiv. Many of the strikes have targeted Ukraine's infrastructure, including businesses, warehouses, factories, petrol stations, as well as energy infrastructure.
Ukraine continues to launch drone strikes deep into Russian territory, largely against gas, oil and business distribution facilities. Both countries deny targeting civilians.
Deadly attacks have resumed after US President Donald Trump sent envoys for talks in Moscow with Russian President Vladimir Putin and in Kyiv with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky last weekend.

Five people were killed and 67 others were wounded in a daytime Russian drone strike on a shopping mall in Pavlohrad, a city in Dnipropetrovsk region, on Thursday, Ukrainian officials say. Earlier in the week two other shopping malls were targeted by Russian air strikes, killing two people and injuring 28 people in the attacks on the cities of Zaporizhzhia and Sumy.
Russia reported a Ukrainian seaborne drone attack on the resort city of Sochi overnight on Wednesday, in which 28 people were wounded, as well as three more deaths blamed on Ukrainian attacks.
Two people were also killed earlier this week when Russian drones hit a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, which has increasingly found itself caught up in the conflict.
A full-scale war has been raging between Russia and Ukraine since Putin launched an invasion more than four and a half years ago.
De Croo, a former prime minister of Belgium, told the BBC: "This winter is going to be the toughest one since the war".
He said Ukraine started "from a very weak base going into this winter". He added the UN were "very, very worried... about what this winter could become."
The concerns are driven by what De Croo said was Russia's "very systematic" targeting of civilian and energy infrastructure.

"This is petrol stations, it's shopping malls, it's business centres, but it's especially energy infrastructure, energy transmission lines, and so on. There is absolutely no justification for that," he said.
This could lead a "worst-case scenario" where people struggled to access energy to run heating, and water and sewage systems stopped working.
"With the temperatures that you would get here that would lead to circumstances which would be really close to humanitarian catastrophe," De Croo said.
Winter temperatures in Ukraine can drop to -20C.
If power supplies and critical infrastructure were severely damaged it could lead to "quite some human suffering", De Croo said.

Under efforts to prepare Ukraine for winter the UN Development Programme is helping to rebuild parts of its energy system that were damaged last winter. It is also establishing more sustainable and decentralised energy plants, which are less vulnerable to attack.
De Croo said completing the difficult and dangerous work was "almost an impossible task".

"They are reconstructing these sites under constant, constant air alarms. And they know that they are working at a site which is a target," he said. "So you try to reconstruct, but part of your day you can't work because it's just too dangerous."
