articles.title: NBI flags foreigners getting PH birth certificates through late registration
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) Director Melvin Matibag on Friday flagged the acquisition of Filipino birth certificates by thousands of foreign nationals through late…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) Director Melvin Matibag on Friday flagged the acquisition of Filipino birth certificates by thousands of foreign nationals through late registration, mostly Chinese, during a Senate hearing.

Matibag raised the issue following recent raids on Chinese-owned steel plants over alleged irregularities, Philippine Sanjia Steel Corporation in Misamis Oriental, linked to Tony Yang—brother of former presidential economic adviser Michael Yang—and the Chinese-owned steel plant in Pampanga that supposedly manufactured substandard steel products.

During the Senate committee on economic affairs hearing, Matibag cited Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) records showing that over 50,000 individuals had obtained birth certificates through late registration.

“Yung PSA po nag-audit sila, noon na-audit nila, there were about like two or seven million who availed of late registration,” Matibag said, noting that the registration mostly took place in two municipalities in Mindanao.
(The PSA conducted an audit; when they audited, there were about two or seven million who availed of late registration.)
“When that audit was done, there were about 5,000 foreign nationals, and the majority of them are Chinese who availed of that registration na naging Pilipino na,” he added.
(When that audit was done, there were about 5,000 foreign nationals, and the majority of them are Chinese who availed of that registration that has become Filipino.)
With this, the NBI Director appealed to the Senate and House of Representatives to look into the Late Registration Law, which he called already “obsolete.”
“Kasi ang nangyayari po rito, nakakalat-kalat siya eh, kahit saan civil registry ka, nagkakapag-rehistro ka. So wala pong enough guards para ma-check po ito,” said Matibag.
(Because what’s happening here is that it’s scattered everywhere, no matter where you go to the civil registry, you’re registering. So there aren’t enough guards to check it.)
Sen. Risa Hontiveros, chair of the economic affairs committee, in response, affirmed that lawmakers would revisit the law, which was passed in 1930. /dp

articles.title: India's BRICS strategy tested with Xi, Putin set to visit
articles.summary: New Delhi's "America Plus" approach sees India deepening its ties with China and Russia, while also trying to keep BRICS from turning into an anti-Western platform.

image.caption: Modi will be hosting the leaders of Russia and China for a two-day BRICS summit in New Delhi (file photo)Image: Suo Takekuma/REUTERS

blocks.text: India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi will host the 18th BRICS summit this weekend in New Delhi, welcoming Chinese President Xi Jinping to India for the first time since 2019.

The summit comes at an important moment for India. As New Delhi's year-long BRICS presidency draws to a close, India is stepping up engagement with China and Russia, and its relationship with Washington remains difficult.

Modi met both Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on August 31 and September 1. Just two weeks later, Modi is set to see them again in New Delhi for the BRICS summit.
India's difficult BRICS chairship
But with BRICS both growing in size and increasingly troubled by internal divisions, the forum might limit Modi's diplomatic gains.
New Delhi and Beijing locked in 'armed coexistence' and competition
Indian diplomats are trying to protect their room for maneuver in a changing international order.
Ashok Kantha, a former Indian ambassador to China, said India's engagement with BRICS and the SCO is part of New Delhi's longstanding strategy of strategic autonomy.
"These groupings give India a seat at the table and allow it to pursue its own interests while maintaining relationships with different major powers," Kantha told DW.
However, as Modi prepares to host Xi in New Delhi, ties between India and China are less than ideal.

blocks.caption: India's geopolitical strategy is heavily impacted by its relationships with both the West and fellow BRICS powersImage: Manish Swarup/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Both countries reached a border patrol agreement in 2024, ending a four-year military standoff along their disputed frontier.

International flights have resumed, the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage has reopened and some visa restrictions have eased. But major problems remain between Beijing and New Delhi — India is reporting a trade deficit of over $112 billion (€96.5 billion) with China, and the two countries argue over market access.
The Modi-Xi meeting will therefore be watched for signs of a major diplomatic thaw, particularly on trade and investment.
Kantha said the visit could bring some stabilization but should not be mistaken for a reset.

"The border remains heavily militarized and major differences over trade, investment and security remain. India needs a stable and predictable relationship with China, but without lowering its guard," said Kantha.

"It is a relationship of armed coexistence and managed competition. We should not reduce it to a simple 'elephant and dragon' story," he said, referring to traditional symbols of the world's two most populous nations.
BRICS gets bigger, divisions grow
India's presidency has already exposed the difficulty of reaching agreement within BRICS, which has grown from its original five members to 11.

With nations such as Brazil, South Africa, Indonesia and Egypt all part of BRICS, its leaders struggle to reconcile its very different relationships with the US and different interests in conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine. The group now also includes Iran and the UAE, countries that have found themselves on opposing sides of the war in Iran.
Earlier this year, BRICS foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement on the Middle East crisis, forcing India to issue a unilateral chair's statement instead.
With Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian expected at the Delhi summit, this diplomatic divide is likely to take center stage.

"Differences between members such as Iran and the UAE show how difficult it can be to find common ground," says Harsh Pant, vice president for Studies and Foreign Policy at the Observer Research Foundation.
"BRICS can still work on areas where members share interests, such as reforming global economic governance. But such disagreements are likely to become more common," he added.
Fears of Chinese dominance
The future of BRICS will also be impacted by the rivalry between India and China.
Tracking the tense relationship between India and China

India wants BRICS to give greater weight to the concerns of developing countries and to support reform of other global institutions such as the United Nations, IMF and World Bank. At the same time, New Delhi does not want the grouping to become a China-led challenge to the West.

India has been pushing for easier cross-border payments between BRICS countries and greater use of national currencies in international trade. At the same time, the Modi government has also been careful not to present this as an attempt to replace the US dollar or create a common BRICS currency.
What is BRICS Pay?
"Local-currency transactions are likely to become an important area of cooperation," Pant said, but stressed that India and other BRICS countries are not necessarily seeking 'de-dollarization.'"
"Instead, they are looking for greater resilience and alternatives to dollar-based financial arrangements."
India's 'America Plus' strategy

Despite its disagreements with the Trump administration, New Delhi still wants stronger economic and strategic ties with the US, while also maintaining its longstanding relationship with Russia and improving relations with China.
EU-India trade agreement: consequences for the economy
India's diplomatic course is not a pure "multi-alignment" approach but an "America Plus" strategy, strategic affairs analyst C Raja Mohan told DW.

"India remains dependent on the West for capital, technology, markets and security, while deepening ties with Russia and China for strategic reasons," said Mohan, a professor of American studies at Jindal Global University.
But this balancing act will become harder as great-power rivalry intensifies, Mohan warns.
"A US-China accommodation could leave India exposed, while Russia's growing dependence on China is changing the Eurasian balance," he said.
In this calculation, a more anti-Western BRICS could put pressure on India over its continuing dependence on the West.

The upcoming Delhi summit is likely to show the extent of India's power — especially as it wraps up its BRICS presidency. For Narendra Modi, the test is whether India can advance its priorities for BRICS and give itself more room to maneuver internationally, without allowing the grouping to become dominated by China or reduced to an anti-Western platform.

articles.title: Grab, NCMF Region XI partner for easier, more credible halal food discovery
articles.summary: Grab Philippines has partnered with the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF) Region XI, to make halal food discovery easier and more accurate for consumers when ordering food online.…

blocks.text: Grab Philippines has partnered with the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF) Region XI, to make halal food discovery easier and more accurate for consumers when ordering food online.

blocks.caption: Grab Philippines and National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF) Region XI formally sign a Memorandum of Understanding at Bajada Suites in Davao City, marking a collaboration to improve the discoverability of halal-certified and Muslim-owned restaurants on GrabFood.

blocks.text: Piloted in Davao city, this collaborative initiative equips the Grab app with enhanced search and filtering features, allowing consumers to confidently identify halal-certified and Muslim-owned restaurants that align with their dietary needs.

The partnership was formalized through a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) signing on September 9 at Bajada Suites in Davao City, bringing together key stakeholders from the Consulate Office of Malaysia, the City Government of Davao, NCMF Region XI, and Grab Philippines.

blocks.caption: The collaborative initiative between Grab and NCMF paves the way for a more inclusive, worry-free ordering experience for Muslim consumers and travelers in Davao City.

blocks.text: “Our vision is to build an inclusive platform that empowers consumers to make food choices with absolute confidence,” said RJ Cabaluna, Grab Philippines Vice President for Cities. “That means going beyond basic food delivery and equipping our app with the right filters and verification systems needed by the Muslim community. We are proud to partner with NCMF Region XI in taking this practical step toward strengthening the local halal food ecosystem and ensuring Grab remains a trusted partner for diverse dietary needs.”

With transparency and credibility as guiding principles, NCMF endorsement is required before Davao City-based halal merchants can be appropriately tagged on GrabFood, ensuring consumers are guided to food choices that align with their needs. This guarantees that when users search for the word “halal,” the results exclusively display merchants that have been vetted by halal certification bodies. The universal “Philippine Halal” logo will also be placed on the merchant’s icon as an additional identifier.
Following NCMF endorsement, Muslim-owned merchants also have the option to display a “Muslim-owned” tag, enhancing their visibility and classification in relevant search results.
Furthermore, Grab is undertaking a clean-up of inaccurate or unsupported uses of the word “halal” in restaurant names, reinforcing the integrity of the platform.
Building an inclusive food ecosystem

While the immediate focus remains on platform enhancements, Grab and NCMF Region XI are exploring future opportunities to strengthen the local halal ecosystem. Potential collaborations under the MOU include halal merchant education, consumer-awareness campaigns, and capacity-building sessions.

“This partnership goes beyond just an app feature—it is about respecting traditions and building a community where Muslim Filipinos and travelers can order food without worry or hesitation,” said Arch. Sherrila Porza-Sawah, Regional Director of NCMF Region XI. “By working directly with a platform like Grab, we are reducing the barriers to discovering certified halal food and ensuring that our Muslim merchants and consumers are supported.”

With NCMF guiding the community’s interests and Grab adapting its technology to meet those needs, both organizations are laying the groundwork for a more inclusive and credible halal ecosystem in Davao City.

articles.title: Uber leaves two key African markets — and their drivers in despair
articles.summary: Uber's departure from Nigeria and Uganda has left countless customers high and dry. But what about drivers? With fuel prices, maintenance and other operating costs rising, many say they're struggling…

image.caption: Uber has become part of daily life for many people across Africa - but financial shrotcomings have forced the ride-hailing app to minimize its footprint on the continentImage: Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: A week ago, Uber unexpectly announced its departure from the Nigerian market after spending over a decade building up its presence in Africa's most populous country. The ride-hailing platform also announced that it would be winding up its operations in Uganda — also with immediate effect.
With the exit from both Nigeria and Uganda, Uber now remains operational only in a handful of African countries — namely Egypt, Ghana, Kenya, and South Africa.

"This decision is limited strictly to these two markets and does not impact our operations across the rest of the continent," Uber said in a statement, adding that their "immediate priority is supporting drivers, riders, and local team members throughout this transition."
In the last year, the company also closed shop in Ivory Coast and Tanzania while also cutting its global workforce by 10%.

blocks.caption: Ride-hailing apps have gained in popularity across Africa over the past decade, but not all seem to be profitableImage: Afolabi Sotunde/REUTERS

blocks.text: A difficult market to crack
Uber has not managed to grow across much of the African market despite its massive global scale.
The profit-driven ride-hailing app faces stiff competition from rival platforms, including Bolt, inDrive and SafeBoda, which operate in the Nigerian and Ugandan markets and beyond.
However, it's not only Uber that is dealing with frustration over the current situation.
Many of its drivers across Africa have been raising complaints about shrinking profit margins amid rising fuel costs, inflation and currency volatility in markets like Nigeria.
In their view, Uber's business model of pocketing around 20 — 25% of any trip fare in commissions is no longer tenable.
Discontent, discombobulated and disregarded drivers
Abbas Olamide, an Uber driver in the Nigerian capital Abuja, said the company's overall service was "good" while stressing that the high commissions were adding to his existing woes.
He told DW that a ride of 30,000 Naira (€ 20) "to the airport means the ride-hailing app would deduct 6,000 Naira as commission," still leaving him to "then pay a gate fee at the airport."
"Probably because you do not want to go back to town empty handed, we also pay to park at the airport [to pick another client]," he explained.
"At the end of the day, what's left is no longer enough."
Uber makes UK drivers workers
Samuel Olatunji, an Uber-driver in Lagos, also shared his concerns with DW following the abrupt announcement of Uber's exit, saying he will now have to recalibrate his own business more.
The 43-year-old driver says he'll have to join hundreds of other driver who "have to depend on other [ride-hailing] apps now" to ensure any steady stream of income.
"But the amount I take home won't add up like before again."

In recent years, drivers like Olamide and Olatunji have staged protests and strikes over soaring operating costs, low fares, and working conditions as well as Nigeria's fuel hikes, which this year have been worsened by the surge in prices at the pump following the war in Iran.
Their please and concerns, however, remain unheard as they prepare for a bumpy ride ahead.
Dollars versus naira

Uber meanwhile did not provide a detailed explanation for its decision, however, it comes amid a backdrop of double-digit inflation in many places across Africa, which has eroded purchasing power while pushing millions of people deeper into poverty and the making them less likely to use the transport company.

Ikemesit Effiong, partner at SBM Intelligence, a consulting firm based in Lagos, explained that "[r]ising costs for such things as fuel, vehicle maintenance, insurance, coupled with a currency that is less valuable now than in 2014 means fares were climbing faster than the average Lagos or Abuja rider's willingness or ability to pay for the convenience."

blocks.caption: Rising fuel costs due to the war in Iran coupled with Nigeria's abolition of the state fuel subsidy have led petrol prices to skyrocketImage: Sunday Alamba/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Effiong added that when Uber's cost base is dollar-linked but the drivers' revenue base is the shrinking naira, the maths stop working, forcing Uber to operate under unsustainably thin profit margins — despite the fact that Nigeria's ride hailing market alone is estimated to be worth around $450 million per year.

"These platforms are trying to hold fares low enough to retain price-sensitive riders, while the driver take-home shrinks in real terms. This pushes drivers toward multi-apping, off-platform negotiation, or exit altogether," he noted.

Effiong further highlighted that one of Uber's local competitors, InDrive, does operate under a negotiated-fare approach, resulting in "less reliance on the capital-heavy, standardized-fare template that works in wealthier markets."
The complex economics of ride-hailing
There are some striking similarities between the Nigerian and Ugandan markets: Both countries have huge populations and a growing demand for more transport solution.
But both across both Kampala and Lagos, Uber's exit creates a loss of a service many users had considered safe and reliable option — more so than some of the other options.
Mary-Esther Anele, a Lagos resident, told DW that she knows that she is "going to start looking for alternatives.
"But most importantly, I'm going to travel less anyway now because transportation costs are going to increase," she added.
Spain restricts ride-hailing services

There also are questions about any knock-on effects beyond the current decision by Uber: Will the California-based multinational leave its remaining African markets? Will its pricing change to bring in more money from the continent? And how will competitors respond?

In some other African countries like South Africa, ride-hailing apps like Uber have also long been a thorn in the side of taxi companies and minibuses, whose operators say they don't want to compete against those drivers, at times resorting to violence as part of local taxi wars.
Will Uber's shrinking footprint in Africa impact these kinds of developments in other markets?
As countless drivers prepare for an unknown future, the end of their partnership with Uber might — for many — spell their journey's end.

blocks.caption: In some markets, the competition between ride-hailing apps and traditional taxi services can have brutal consequencesImage: Daniel Irungu/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Frank Yiga from Kampala contributed to this report.

articles.title: Iran’s Houthi allies capture strategic island on vital oil shipping route
articles.summary: Rampant Yemeni rebels take control of island in narrow point of Bab al-Mandab strait, which Saudi is relying on for oil exports

blocks.text: Yemen’s rampant Houthi forces have captured a strategic island in the Bab al-Mandab strait, expanding their control of the narrow waterway, one of the ​world’s vital shipping routes.

The Iran-aligned Houthis took control of the volcanic island after forces allied to the UN-backed, Aden-based government left in the latest of a dramatic series of reverses along Yemen’s west coast in recent days, including the loss of the port city of Mocha on Thursday.
Saudi Arabia, which supports and bankrolls the official Yemen government, mounted air raids on Houthi positions in Mocha on Friday.

The Bab al-Mandab links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez canal. Perim island, also known as Mayun, divides the waterway in two, close to its narrowest point. The United Arab Emirates, a former Saudi ally in the anti-Houthi coalition, had been building an airbase on the island before ending its active involvement in the conflict in January.

Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab to export its crude since Iran has been targeting vessels in the strait of Hormuz. About 12% of the world’s goods are typically shipped through the strait.

blocks.caption: Fighters loyal to the Houthi authorities march during a rally to recruit more fighters, in Sana’a on Thursday. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Full Houthi control of shipping in the strait, alongside Iranian control of the strait of Hormuz, would strengthen the chokeholds of anti-western forces over global energy shipments. Oil prices have risen to more than $100 a barrel as the fighting in Yemen has escalated.

Iran hailed the Houthi advances in an official statement on Friday, its first extended comment on the renewed fighting inside Yemen. Iran and the Houthis have been allied ever since the Houthis rose to power inside Yemen in 2014.

British diplomatic sources said they did not at present expect Donald Trump to sanction any US bombing of Houthi positions in Yemen, despite requests to do so from Saudi Arabia. The pace of the Houthi advance, and political divisions in the Yemen governorates not controlled by the Houthis, have left western capitals fearful that even the Yemen government capital, Aden, could fall to the Houthis. The UK effectively treated Yemen as a British protectorate until 1967.

The surge in fighting in the past week has sent over 46,000 people fleeing, and “overnight, large numbers of people were reportedly seen leaving Mocha with their belongings”, the UN migration agency said on Friday.

blocks.caption: Perim island seen in a 2021 satellite photograph. Photograph: Planet Labs Inc./AP

blocks.text: The Houthi progress down the Red Sea coast from the port of Hodeidah also strengthens Iran’s hand in trying to reach an agreement with other Gulf states on future control of the strait of Hormuz, the central dispute between the US and Iran. Iran has reached an agreement on temporary approved routes with Oman, the country sharing the southern coast of the Hormuz strait. The proposed deal is supposed to be discussed at a meeting of Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) foreign ministers in the Omani coastal city of Salalah on Monday.

The deal, including a temporary approved route for shipping largely under Iranian control, would – if agreed by the GCC – put pressure on the US to lift its highly effective blockade of Iranian oil ports, a blockade that is severely damaging the Iranian economy.

The US struck a surprise ceasefire deal with the Houthis in May 2025 after the cost of a bombing campaign escalated, and Houthis gave private assurances that they would not attack US shipping in the Red Sea. The Houthi leadership this week continued to give similar assurances to all shipping except Saudi Arabian oil tankers.

On 14 August Saudi Arabia assembled a 14-country international maritime naval coalition to protect freedom of navigation in the Bab al-Mandab strait and the Gulf of Aden. The coalition, including Bahrain, Pakistan, Somalia, Djibouti, Turkey and Egypt, has so far been invisible, though Riyadh would argue that such a coalition of the willing takes time to assemble.

Recriminations are under way over the fall of Mocha, with the role of Maj Gen Tareq Saleh, leader of the National Resistance forces that retreated from the city, under scrutiny. He said the retreat was necessary to regroup his forces.

On her Facebook page, the Yemeni 2011 Nobel prize winner Tawakkol Karman called on Yemen’s president, Rashad al-Alimi, to dismiss Saleh and to refer him for investigation and trial of charges of conspiracy and high treason.
Saudi Arabia is now facing a familiar dilemma: whether to reach a negotiated settlement with the Houthis on the future of Yemen or to try to push the highly stretched Houthi forces back.

Although the Houthis operate independently of Tehran’s instructions, it is hugely to Iran’s advantage for them to be fighting Saudi Arabia as the Saudis are more likely in turn to put pressure on Washington to relent over Iran.

There is also concern in western capitals about the use of western weaponry by the Saudis in Yemen, and whether their activity complies with international humanitarian law, including whether the Saudi strikes can truly be seen as acts of self-defence.

articles.title: Iran war: Saudi-Houthi escalation intensifies Yemen conflict
articles.summary: The Houthi takeovers of Mokha, Dhubab and Perim in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait threaten to push Yemen deeper into the Middle East war. The Iran-backed group has made advances against Yemen's government…

image.caption: Yemen's Houthi rebels are seizing strategic towns near the key waterway Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Will Yemen be pulled into the wider US-Iran war?Image: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Fighting between the Houthi militia and Yemen's internationally recognized government escalated further this week as the Iran-backed group seized territory and exchanged missile and drone attacks with Saudi Arabia.

On Thursday, the Houthis seized the port city of Mokha and by Friday had taken control of the town of Dhubab and the island of Perim, Yemeni government sources told the news agency Reuters. Mokha, Dhubab and Perim had been held by forces aligned with Yemen's government. All three are strategically located near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

With Iran having blockaded the nearby Strait of Hormuz, the narrow Bab el-Mandeb Strait has become increasingly important as an alternative route for Saudi oil exports. As the Houthis are aligned with Iran, control of and potential attacks on shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait gives Iran additional leverage in its war with the United States.
The government-aligned National Resistance Forces announced on Thursday that troops were reorganizing and consolidating their defenses in Mokha in coordination with other anti-Houthi forces.

The conflict has also spilled into Saudi Arabia, a close US ally and regional rival of Iran's. This week, the Houthis launched dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at four cities in Saudi Arabia. The Houthis said Saudi Arabia responded with dozens of airstrikes across four Yemeni provinces.

"This is actually a full-scale war," Farea Al-Muslimi, a Yemen researcher at the London-based think tank Chatham House, told DW. "It hasn't been given that name yet but we are marching there full time," Al-Muslimi said.
Houthis 'much stronger'

The latest escalation, which started in July, ended a period of relative calm after years of war. A Saudi-led coalition intervened to support Yemen's government in 2015 following the 2014 Houthi insurgency. The war between the Houthis — which the United States redesignated as a foreign terrorist organization in March 2025 — and the Saudi-backed government ended in 2022 with a UN-brokered truce. However, the country remains de facto split.

The Houthis control Yemen's capital, Sanaa, and most of the country's north, as well as parts of the center, and now also much of the western coastal stretch, including Mokha, Dhubab and Perim. The internationally recognized government, represented by the Presidential Leadership Council, is based in Aden. Many senior officials operate from Saudi Arabia. Government-aligned forces control parts of the south and east, while tribal groups retain significant influence in parts of the east.

The political landscape was further fragmented in December, when secessionists backed by the Southern Transitional Council (STC), backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE), seized areas in the south and east. The fallout between Saudi Arabia, which aims to keep Yemen united, and the UAE-backed secessionists ended with the termination of Yemen's joint defense pact with the UAE and the withdrawal of Emirati forces from the country. The STC was dissolved in January.

Elham Manea, the director of the Middle Eastern and Gulf Studies Research Competence Area at the Institute of Political Science at the University of Zurich, told DW that the current situation is very different from that of 2015. "The Houthi movement is militarily and institutionally much stronger," Manea said, "while the camp opposing it, that is, the internationally recognized government, remains more fragmented."

blocks.caption: The Houthis targeted infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and said Riyadh retaliated across four provinces in YemenImage: Al Masirah/REUTERS

blocks.text: What's Pakistan's role?

Manea said Saudi Arabia had changed its approach. In 2015, Riyadh joined the war in support of Yemen's ousted government. "Now, it is providing greater military, technical and logistical support to the internationally recognized government and forces aligned with it," Manea said.

The key question is whether Saudi Arabia is preparing for a war aimed at defeating the Houthi group or seeking to change the military balance, restore deterrence and eventually negotiate from a stronger position.
"At present, I consider the second scenario more likely," Manea said.
Al-Muslimi offered a similar view: "The Saudis would like to avoid war at any cost."

The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, recently signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, has not yet been invoked. Reuters reported on Thursday that Pakistani officials said no military response under the agreement was currently being discussed, but the government would act when the time came.

Alice Gower, director of geopolitics and security at the London-based political consultancy Azure Strategy, told DW that she doubts Pakistan would join the conflict directly. "But the escalation in Yemen will increasingly test its ability to stay out," Gower said. "Islamabad does not want to antagonize neighboring Iran," she added, "and will try to preserve its role as a mediator, while meeting its growing security commitments to Saudi Arabia through intelligence, advice and other forms of military support short of direct participation."

blocks.caption: Thousands of civilians fled their homes this week, while nearly 200 were killed in the fighting, according to international bodiesImage: AFP

blocks.text: Humanitarian toll rises
Hans Grundberg, the UN envoy to Yemen, said the country was facing the "harsh reality" of a return to war.

The UN Development Programme estimated that 377,000 people had died as a result of Yemen's conflict between 2014 and late 2021. Of these, approximately 154,000 deaths were directly caused by combat and violence.

The current conflict has already killed nearly 200 people, according to the World Health Organization. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) also warnedthat around 18,500 people have been displaced. "Families are arriving with nothing: no shelter, no food, no way to know if it's safe to go back," Abdusattor Esoev, IOM Yemen's chief of mission, said in a statement. "Many of these are people who have already been displaced once, twice, even four times before," he said. "Every time fighting flares up, they lose whatever little they had managed to rebuild."

This view is echoed by Niku Jafarnia, a Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch. "When you have a country in which nearly two-thirds of people are in need of aid, any additional precarity and displacement will have a real civilian cost," she said.

"Thousands of civilians were killed in the fighting between the Saudi-led coalition and the Houthis between 2014 and 2022, and warring parties repeatedly demonstrated extreme disregard for civilian life," she said. "The renewed fighting now threatens to repeat the devastating civilian casualty events of the earlier years of the war," she added.
Iran war: Analyzing the Houthi blockade against Saudi Arabia

articles.title: India looks to steer BRICS away from anti-Western turn
articles.summary: The BRICS summit 2026 takes place in Delhi this weekend. Unlike last year, Putin and Xi are expected to attend. Can India keep the expanded bloc united?

image.caption: This year's BRICS host India has to balance welcoming new members like Iran without appearing to snub the USImage: Qamar Sibtain/IANS

blocks.text: In preparation for hosting the 18th BRICS summit in Delhi this weekend, India came up with a slogan which tried to keep the group's brand intact without alienating its many new members.

"Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability" matches the acronym for the body's five original members — Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa — whilst also denoting goals which the new members — Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates — can get behind.

"It's an elegant way to reinterpret BRICS so that the acronym represents a joint mission rather than country names," Mihaela Papa, director of the BRICS Lab at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, told DW.
For Sushant Singh, lecturer in South Asian Studies at Yale University, the vague slogan reflects India's desire as hosts to keep BRICS as low-key and neutral as possible.
"India doesn't want to offend Russia or China, but the fact is that Indians are looking more towards the United States these days. The desire to build up BRICS is not there."
Why India's role at the BRICS summit matters
Yet host India's status as a rising global geopolitical power has added clout to this year's gathering when compared with last year's summit in Brazil.

At the Rio de Janeiro gathering, six of the bloc's 11 heads of state skipped the event, including major players like Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Putin is expected to attend, while Xi is widely expected but not yet formally confirmed by Beijing.
"The participation of China's top leadership is crucial," says Papa.
She also thinks it would be a significant sign of the BRICS' strength as a "stabilizing force" if the leaders of regional rivals Iran and the UAE were shown to be able to work together.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will attend but UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan is expected to send representatives. Saudi Arabia, another Iranian foe, is also expected to. The country's BRICS status remains somewhat ambiguous, although current official BRICS materials generally list it as a member.

blocks.caption: Several heads of state skipped the 2025 gatheringImage: Fabio Teixeira/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: For India, the summit is as significant for the bilateral meetings it brings as much as for the BRICS gathering itself. Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi are due to meet on Friday while the summit will also present an opportunity for Xi and Modi to speak face-to-face amid continued strain in the China-India relationship.
However, that does not mean much of substance will emerge from the weekend.
"In terms of concrete outcomes and what is achievable, I think it's going to be very, very limited," says Singh.

Modi has spoken of BRICS as an important forum for the 'Global South' to present a common front on various issues. He has also spoken about "a people-centric approach" and the spirit of "humanity first".
However, Singh says BRICS is simply not a priority for India and that in general, Delhi has not appreciated what many have interpreted as the "anti-western" turn the group has taken in recent times.
"With India as chair, India won't be comfortable with any kind of anti-western line," he says, pointing to the focus it places on defense ties with the US and trade ties with the West as a whole.

blocks.caption: The leaders of Russia, China and India will all be present this yearImage: REUTERS/ANI

blocks.text: "India's idea of BRICS is more to look at improving trade ties, etc. In other words, can we do things which are beneficial to us without in any way being confrontational or critical of the West?"
Yet ironically, India's non-aligned status means it may actually be able to keep the bloc aligned.

"India adds clout because it has significant geopolitical weight and relationships across competing camps, making it an important bridge-builder," says Papa. "Its approach is likely to keep BRICS focused on practical cooperation and global governance reform rather than overt bloc politics."
What is BRICS for anyway?
BRICS is soon approaching its 18th birthday, so in a sense it should be coming of age. Yet the bloc has struggled for coherence in recent years amid doubt over its purpose.
The scale of what it could represent is not in doubt. It boasts nearly half the world's population among its members and around 40% of its GDP.

Last year, its joint declaration called for reforms of global governance, specifying representation on multilateral bodies such as the IMF and the World Bank. It also condemned tariffs and decried what it called the "polarization" of the international order.
"Ideologically, BRICS remains where it was during the last summit in Brazil, focused on practical, functional cooperation while seeking to avoid geopolitical tensions," says Papa.

blocks.caption: BRICS foreign ministers have already met ahead of the summitImage: ANI

blocks.text: She says that the expansion of the group from five to 11 members — if we include Saudi Arabia — has made it harder to reach consensus on various issues.

There are also now more autocracies among its members than democracies, while many members have tense bilateral relations. "These internal contradictions will always be hard to reconcile," says Singh.
What could the BRICS summit achieve?

Nonetheless, Papa says she expects progress this year in three areas: trade, monetary cooperation, and agriculture. Discussions are likely to focus on improving trade between the members, alternative financial architecture for exchanging currencies and on issues around food security.

While talk of reforming global governance will still be central, she thinks BRICS' best hope to focus on the institutions which it agrees most on. For example, India is reluctant to press for UN reform but is keen for a co-ordinated approach from BRICS to trade and the WTO.
"India's WTO ambitions are shared by more members," she says, which makes movement in that area "more likely."
Yet many still share Singh's view that the group will "continue to underwhelm."
He says issues ranging from China's growing global dominance to the Trump administration's stance on tariffs have made the bloc's limited goals even harder to achieve.
"With the kind of world that we are in and the lack of coherence and internal contradictions that BRICS has, it's very unlikely that it will achieve anything major," he says.

articles.title: Turks in Germany anxious after AfD wins in Saxony-Anhalt
articles.summary: The Alternative for Germany party's win in Saxony-Anhalt has alarmed people of Turkish origin in eastern states. Will workers and business owners abandon the increasingly AfD-friendly region for the…

image.caption: Ahead of Sunday's election, people of migration background went on a symbolic daylong strike in the eastern state of Saxony-AnhaltImage: Monika Stefanek/DW

blocks.text: The nationalist Alternative for Germany (AfD) party's 43.8% share of the vote in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt has prompted nationwide alarm. People of Turkish origin are especially worried.

Gökay Sofuoglu, the co-chair of the Turkish Community in Germany (TGD), told DW that business owners he has spoken with in Saxony-Anhalt have been especially alarmed. "After the AfD's success, some were thinking of shutting up shop and leaving, first Saxony-Anhalt, then Germany," Sofuoglu said.

He said that initial response was emotional. "We've had a chance to speak to some of them again since," Sofuoglu said. "They're going to wait and see: They're waiting for the formation of a government."
'Problem for Germany'

Sofuoglu said people of Turkish descent in Saxony-Anhalt regard the rise of the AfD "as a problem for Germany as a whole." He said the party's election win was a threat to the stability of democracy in Germany.

blocks.caption: Anti-AfD protests were held across Germany after Sunday's electionImage: Fabian Sommer/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Although the AfD campaigns heavily against migration, Sofuoglu said he believed that the party's true target is Germany's constitution. He said many people of Turkish origin were inclined to see the party's election win as an immediate threat to their communities rather than look at the AfD's wider aims.
"Much as the rise of the AfD affects us, this is a generally anti-democratic development, and we, along with all democratic forces, must act to counter it," he said.

The AfD's victory has also raised concerns about an increase in nationalist violence within Germany. "There's a fear that the coming days could see more attacks like the ones carried out by the National Socialist Underground, and that there will be no clarification of what's behind them," Sofuoglu said, referring a yearslong neo-Nazi terror spree in Germany.
Grasping the root

A feared increase in nationalist violence is only one part of the discussion. "I don't think that just being concerned achieves anything," Alaz Sümer, a lawyer who works with a nongovernmental organization in Berlin, told DW. "You have to think about the causes. I don't think the established parties have sufficiently addressed the problems that allowed the AfD to become so strong."

blocks.caption: According to current polls, 29% of German voters support the AfDImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Sümer came to Germany nine years ago to study. He's currently working on a PhD about extreme-right political parties, and advises people from migrant communities on how to get their international qualifications recognized in Germany.
"Saying 'the AfD is bad, the AfD is dangerous' is the easy way," Sümer said. "We already know that."
Win no surprise
Irmak, who asked that her real name not be used, moved to the eastern city of Leipzig to study 12 years ago. She said the AfD's victory was worrying, but not a surprise.

"It was to be predicted that the far right would do well, and would emerge from the election as the strongest party," Irmak said. "But the ground for this result was also prepared by government policies not addressing citizens' needs."

Irmak said the rise of the AfD would not address Germany's structural problems. "Even with a change of government, it won't alter the need for workers and young people," she said, "especially not in a state with an elderly population, like Saxony-Anhalt."
An AfD ban?

Sümer said German authorities would need to be cautious in dealing with the AfD, which he called an extremist party that is now "a reality in Germany." He said banning the AfD, as many have called for, would only make the party stronger.

blocks.caption: Sümer said politicians must try to address the concerns of AfD votersImage: Privat

blocks.text: If the AfD were banned, Sümer said, a new party would be founded, and more extremist members might fall in with less-visible organizations. That would make Germany "even more uninhabitable" for migrants, he said.

Sümer said Germany's other parties should engage with AfD voters to understand their motives. He said the problem of racism in Germany was bigger than just the AfD, and that the issues that migrants face withing the country were not created by to the party.

According to the Federal Statistical Office, Saxony-Anhalt had a population of about 2.1 million people in 2025. Approximately 249,000, or just over 10%, had a migration background; 6,120 were people of Turkish origin. There are roughly 3 million people of Turkish origin in Germany.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: The 'end of an era' as Goethe-Institut in Russia closes
articles.summary: The Goethe-Institut was one of the last German institutions still operating in Russia. However, following Moscow’s decision to close its offices, all employees will have to stop working by September…

image.caption: The Goethe-Institut will close its doors in Russia on September 13Image: Igor Ivanko/AFP

blocks.text: In recent years, Moscow has declared numerous foreign foundations and organizations "undesirable" and banned them from operating in the country. However, despite the significantly deteriorated relations between Russia and the West as a result of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine, the Goethe-Institut, which opened in Russia in 1992, had been able to continue operating.
But that's no longer the case. Employees of the Goethe-Institut must stop working on September 13 — and staff members sent from Germany must leave the country by that date.

According to Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, the closure of the Goethe-Institut's three locations in Moscow, St. Petersburg and Novosibirsk comes as a response to the announced closure of the Russian House in Berlin, the minister said. Germany intends to terminate its contract with the cultural and events venue as a punitive measure. The German government holds Russia responsible for the attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport.

"The announcement by the Russian foreign minister marks the end of an era in German-Russian cultural relations," wrote Gesche Joost, president of the Goethe-Institut, in a press release. She said it was bad news for people in Russia and that the Goethe-Institut had connected the two countries through culture and language.

blocks.caption: Gesche Joost has been President of the Goethe-Institut since 2024Image: Goethe-Institut / Loredana La Rocca

blocks.text: As early as 2023, the Russian Foreign Ministry had demanded the Goethe-Institut's staff be significantly cut. Cultural exchanges with German artists were limited extent and kept to digital formats. Nevertheless, interest in German-language courses remained high, with around 10,000 students taking part. "Our work in Russia was and remains important," Joost said, referring to learning the German language, the many encounters and mutual understanding between people.
A fresh start after World War II
For the past 75 years, the Goethe-Institut has represented Germany abroad, promoting the German language and sharing German culture with people around the world.

It was founded in 1951, at a time when Germany was seeking to rebuild international trust in the aftermath of World War II and the crimes of the Nazi regime. Originally established as the "Goethe Association for the Further Training of Foreign Teachers of German," the organization initially focused on inviting foreign teachers to Germany for language training.
Its mission soon expanded, however, to promoting the German language abroad.
The first Goethe-Institut opened its doors in Athens in 1952, and just a decade later, the organization had already established 54 branches around the world.

blocks.caption: Language students from Ghana stroll through Murnau with their host family in 1969Image: Goethe-Institut / Michael Friedel

blocks.text: Today, the Goethe-Institut operates a global network of 154 institutions in 100 countries, employing nearly 4,500 people.
Around one million people take an official German exam at a Goethe-Institut or one of its partner organizations each year.

In a speech honoring the institute's 75th anniversary, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier emphasized the significance of promoting German culture abroad, stating, "For countries like ours, which are not great powers, our foreign policy will continue to have to rest on four pillars: yes, military strength, so that we are taken seriously, but also smart diplomacy to devise solutions and forge alliances; wherever possible, an international legal order to provide a framework and direction in addition; and, fourthly, culture and science as soft power, as something we offer to the wider world."

blocks.caption: German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier speaking at an event marking the Goethe-Institut's 75th anniversary in June 2026Image: Bernd von Jutrczenka/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: From classical music to jazz

One element that proved crucial to the institute's success from its founding onward is its credibility as an independent association. Although two-thirds of its funding stems from the German Foreign Office, the organization itself determines its programs — and over the decades, these programs have regularly been adapted to be in step with the prevailing political and social climate.

The institute promptly made its ambitions clear to expand its scope beyond mere language instruction by striving to provide a more comprehensive picture of Germany through a range of cultural and informational programs. "And it was also very clear that this was not about exporting so-called German culture to the world," explained Gesche Joost, president of the Goethe-Institut since 2024. "On the contrary — the aim was to reflect on how we could have a fresh start and how we want to shape society and the future together."

In its early years, the institute's cultural programs deliberately drew on Germany's rich heritage in the areas of classical music and literature. Figures such as Schiller, Bach and Beethoven had lost none of their international appeal despite the Nazi era.
Then, in the 1960s, German jazz was a hit among the institute's cultural exports — with musician and composer Klaus Doldinger and his band touring the globe.

blocks.caption: Klaus Doldinger (right) also played jazz in Lahore, Pakistan thanks to the Goethe-InstitutImage: Goethe-Institut / Michael Friedel

blocks.text: Over the decades, Nobel Prize-winning authors Günter Grass, Heinrich Böll and Herta Müller also traveled internationally on behalf of the Goethe-Institut.

With the spirit of change ushered in by the generation of 1968, with flower power and student protests, the institute's profile changed once again, and it increasingly incorporated critical viewpoints on social issues into its programs, including efforts to critically examine Germany's Nazi past.
A space for dialogue

In this period, West Germany was redefining itself under Social Democratic Chancellor Willy Brandt. In 1970, sociologist Ralf Dahrendorf, then parliamentary state secretary at the foreign office, announced a new set of guiding principles. Cultural policy was to become the "third pillar of foreign policy."

But Dahrendorf didn't simply wish to give culture a higher profile — he advocated for a new way of thinking. "What we give is worth only as much as our willingness to receive," he said. "Openness toward others is thus a principle of our foreign cultural policy." As a result, the Goethe-Institut moved away from the idea of simply exporting culture and toward dialogue, cooperation and reciprocal learning. That approach continues to guide the organization's work today.

blocks.caption: The late Pope Francis also studied German at a Goethe-Institut: In 1985, he took a course in Boppard, Rhineland-PalatinateImage: Vatican Media/picture alliance

blocks.text: While Germany was divided, East and West also competed to forge political alliances abroad through their foreign cultural policies, especially during the Cold War. In the 1970s, the East German press even spread rumors that Goethe-Instituts were being used to conduct espionage.

After the Iron Curtain fell in 1989, the Goethe-Institut opened numerous new locations in Eastern Europe and the former Eastern Bloc, including in Moscow in 1992. Despite turbulent times, its doors had remained open there until now.

For its part, the Kyiv branch, in Ukraine, has also remained open throughout the war. The institute offers a flexible hybrid scheme for its German courses there: When an air raid alert sounds, in-person classes are moved to a shelter. A range of digital and hybrid options are also available if necessary.
The 'turning point' has already come

"I have the impression that working under crisis conditions has become the norm in many regions," Gesche Joost explained. "Either because democracy is being pushed back, because colleagues are working under censorship or because they are being threatened by armed conflicts." In many Goethe-Instituts, she said, the much-discussed Zeitenwende — or "turning point" — has long been reality.

This term entered public discourse after a famous speech by former German Chancellor Olaf Scholz after the war in Ukraine broke out in 2022 and refers to the dawn of an era marked by geopolitical turmoil in Europe.

"We've recognized that we're important partners for civil society in crisis regions. At the same time, we have to make sure that we act sensitively and diplomatically so that we don't get expelled," added Joost.

In times where freedom of cultural expression, freedom of speech as well as science and education are increasingly coming under pressure, the Goethe-Institut plans to continue providing spaces for dialogue where open debate, critical reflection and cultural exchange remain possible.

Meanwhile, Germany's position on the Middle East conflict is currently making the organization's work more challenging in many countries. Some partners in the Arab world have suspended their cooperation as a result, while Goethe-Institut events have seen boycotts elsewhere.

"Our task then is to explain the German position and the history behind it, but also to show the debates taking place on the issue within Germany," Joost said. "At the same time, we also convey the criticism coming from many countries back to Germany."
The Goethe-Institut's work has also been made more difficult in recent years due to deep cuts in federal funding, forcing it to restructure and even shut down some locations.

At the same time, integrating Germany's growing number of foreign skilled workers presents new challenges; Joost feels her institute plays a crucial role here. "We see that many foreign skilled workers see a future for themselves in Germany. But settling into life in Germany is not always easy," she said. "To support them, we have our welcome coaches who are available to answer questions about living and working in Germany and provide guidance, especially in the early stages. That is an important contribution the Goethe-Institut can make in Germany."
This article was originally published in German on June 22 and updated on September 10, 2026, ahead of the closure of the Goethe-Institut in Russia.

articles.title: Magyar vs. Moscow: Hungary toughens stance toward Russia
articles.summary: Prime Minister Peter Magyar has abruptly ended the era of his predecessor's warm relations with Russia: Hungary has expelled 10 Russian diplomats. The Kremlin is considering halting gas supplies in…

image.caption: The close and friendly ties between Hungary and Russia ended when Peter Magyar became prime minister earlier this yearImage: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP

blocks.text: While Viktor Orban was in power, no other EU member state was as pro-Russia as Hungary. Indeed, the prime minister's apparent eagerness to be of service to the Russian president earned him the nickname "Putin's pinscher" or "Kremlin agent."
For years, Hungary was seen as a security risk both in the EU and NATO. Russian spies were able to operate in the country largely unhindered for a long time.
In February, it came to light that Peter Szijjarto, Orban's foreign minister from 2014 to 2026, had passed on confidential information from EU meetings to his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov.
All this came to an end in May, when the government headed by Peter Magyar took office.
An unambiguous signal to Russia
In a clear departure from the government line under Orban, Hungary's new prime minister has already heavily criticized Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine several times.
The government also recently declared Russia a threat to Hungary's national security.

This week, it took its biggest step yet against the Kremlin, expelling 10 Russian diplomats for engaging in activities "that are unacceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention," as announced by Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orban (no relation to the former prime minister).

blocks.caption: Foreign Minister Orban announced this week that Hungary was expelling 10 Russian embassy staff for activities "that are unacceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention"Image: Daniel Vogl/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Although Orban did not provide any more details, the phrase is generally understood to mean that the diplomats in question were spies.

Orban said the decision "protects Hungary's security and sovereignty." She added: "It does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia. Hungary intends to continue the necessary dialogue, based on mutual respect and adherence to the rules."
Restoring old alliances

The minister's brief announcement immediately generated a huge number of headlines and comments — hardly surprising given that this was not only evidence of a 180-degree turn on the government's policy toward Russia but also one of the toughest diplomatic sanctions targeting Moscow since the collapse of communism in 1989/1990.

Speaking to Hungarian news website Index, secret service expert Peter Tarjani said this was "not a diplomatic conflict, but a serious secret service matter" and that with this decision, Hungary was simultaneously returning "to the mainstream of its allies' security policy."

Political scientist and leading Hungarian Russia expert Andras Racz told the Hungarian national news agency MTI that Hungary was the only EU and NATO member not to have made such an expulsion in recent years.
Racz said such a step "should really have been taken four and ahalf years ago." He added: "Hungary is now settling its old debt with its allies."
Reliance on Russian gas?
Under Viktor Orban, Hungary was the only EU country never to unreservedly condemn Russia's all-out war against Ukraine.
Indeed, during the final two years of his rule, Orban even blamed Ukraine and the West for Russia's aggression.

blocks.caption: The Russian Embassy in BudapestImage: Aled Betts/cc-by/Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text: But long before that — even after he came to power back in 2010 — Viktor Orban took a markedly pro-Russian line, which he justified, among other things, with the claim that Hungary was more dependent on Russian energy supplies than almost any other country in the region.

His government's repeated assertion that Russian gas was cheaper has long been disproved. What's more, the expansion of the Paks nuclear power plant with Russian support will cost Hungary dearly for decades to come.
In the light of all this, Orban's close ties to Russia remain a mystery.
Absurd situations

For Hungary, this closeness to Russia often led to absurd situations in which the country's national security was put at risk. At the same time, Orban repeatedly told his critics that it was they who were a threat to Hungary's sovereignty.
For example, Russian secret service agents for years took part in military-style training exercises in the far-right scene right up until 2016.

Starting in 2012, Russian secret service operatives for years stole huge amounts of data from the Hungarian Foreign Ministry and other Hungarian authorities without the government ever publicly condemning it.

In 2019, Russia got permission to move the headquarters of the International Investment Bank (IIB) to Budapest. The IIB was known as the "spy bank" because its leadership was made up of individuals linked to or associated with Russia's FSB intelligence service. It was only after the US imposed sanctions on the bank in 2023 that it left Hungary again.

Investigative journalist Szabolcs Panyi has warned multiple times in recent years that Hungary had become a "logistical center and deployment zone for Russian secret services," thereby putting the whole region at risk.
Rejection of Orban's pro-Russian course
Orban's strictly pro-Russian course was laterally rejected by many Hungarians.

blocks.caption: Former Prime Minister Viktor Orban (left, pictured here with Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2025) maintained close ties with Russia while he was in powerImage: Alexander Nemenov/Pool/AFP

blocks.text: The decidedly pro-European and pro-Western orientation of Peter Magyar and his Tisza party had a considerable role to play in their election victory earlier this year. The EU flag was often seen and spontaneous cries of "Russians, go home" often heard at election rallies last spring.

Unlike Viktor Orban, Magyar and leading politicians in his Tisza party are convinced that Hungary's place is exclusively in Europe and that the country should only maintain pragmatic, low-level relations with Russia.
Nevertheless, many observers and experts are surprised at how radically the Magyar government has turned away from Russia.

Andras Telkes, the former deputy head of Hungary's foreign intelligence service (IH), wrote in the newspaper Nepszava that the expulsion of diplomats shows that the presence of Russian secret services in Hungary obviously runs "very deep" and that the country has a serious problem.
Telkes says that the expulsion of 10 diplomats will help rebuild trust in Hungary in the eyes of the secret services of its NATO allies.
At the same time, he emphasizes the scale of the move: "Expelling two or three people would have been a sign. Expelling 10 people already means war."
Telkes went on to say that the move creates a serious security problem for Hungary.
Will Moscow turn off the taps?

The spokeswoman for the Russian Foreign Ministry condemned the expulsion of Russian diplomats in unusually strong terms: She spoke of a "Russophobe lobby in Budapest" and announced a "hard and painful" response.
Russian lawmaker Andrey Kolesnik, a member of the State Duma's Defense Committee, said that halting gas supplies to Hungary would have to be considered.

Hungary's Foreign Minister Anita Orban knows more about such Russian threats than anyone else in the new Hungarian government: She wrote her doctoral thesis in 2007 on Russia's energy policy in Central Europe. A year later, she published a book entitled "Power, Energy, and the New Russian Imperialism."
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Jean Chrétien says ‘we bow to no one’ in stirring 9/11 speech in Gander, N.L.

image.caption: Former Prime Minister Jean Chrétien received multiple standing ovations during his speech in Gander. (CBC)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador

Former Canadian prime minister Jean Chrétien drew thunderous applause on Friday during a fiery and patriotic speech in Gander, N.L, where many had gathered at a sports arena to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks
'Never mistake our kindness for softness,' former PM says
'Never mistake our generosity for weakness,' Chrétien says at 9/11 memorial

Former Canadian prime minister Jean Chrétien drew thunderous applause on Friday during a fiery and patriotic speech in Gander, N.L., where many had gathered at a sports arena to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, and the legendary humanitarian response as thousands of stranded air travellers had their flights diverted to more than a dozen Canadian airports.

Chrétien was the final speaker during a lengthy and nationally televised event. He began his speech by describing Sept. 11, 2001 "like a nightmare … one that can never be erased." And then recounted how Canadians stepped up, fought side-by-side with U.S. troops in Afghanistan — which drew loud applause.
But then, Chrétien's became the first person to speak on a subject no one else who stepped to the microphone would: the fractured political relationship between Canada and the United States.
"We bow to no one," Chrétien said to an audience that included Pete Hoesktra, the U.S. ambassador to Canada.
"And the more we are insulted or threatened and abused, the more we will stand up for ourselves and stand united."

items: We can make a difference in a 'sometimes broken world,' says Gander mayor at 9/11 ceremony
One woman survived 9/11. Another helped out in Gander. Now they’re as close as sisters

blocks.text: It was a powerful moment in an two-hour event filled with stories of remembrance, honour and sacrifice.
Trade war ongoing

U.S. President Donald Trump initiated a trade war with Canada, and has hurled insults at Prime Minister Mark Carney. Trump has also threatened Canada’s sovereignty by expressing his desire to make Canada’s the 51st U.S. state.
Hoesktra has amplified the rhetoric through his own public comments and by sharing Trump’s social media posts.

Hoesktra avoided the issue of trade and tariffs during his visit to Gander, and praised the longstanding partnership between the two countries. He offered thanks for the kindness and compassion shown to thousands of stranded American travellers in the wake of the terrorist attacks.

"This is to say one more time, thank you," he said, when asked about his visit to the central Newfoundland town. "We’ll get back to the economic issues from, at least our standpoint, when we get past 9/11."
Chrétien, 92, described the U.S. as a "neighbour and our closest friend," and said a massive rally in Ottawa in the days after the 9/11 attacks was "one of the most emotional moments of my life."

Chrétien’s government initiated the process in 2001 to invoke the so-called Article 5, which stipulates that an attack on one member of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) is an attack on all members.
Chrétien also ordered Canadian troops into battle in Afghanistan, fighting alongside U.S. allies, and 158 of those soldiers were killed, including 13 from Newfoundland and Labrador.
"Our friends were hurt, and we were hurting with them," Chrétien said. "I was proud of how we stepped up."
He described the response to 9/11 as "the Canadian way."
But 25 years later, the world has changed, and Canada’s relationship with its powerful southern neighbour has also grown more distant.
So Chrétien concluded his speech — which received no less than three standing ovations — with a strong message "to our American friends."
He said Canada is an open, generous country, and the response to 9/11 in communities such as Gander is an example of this. But he said Canada’s generosity should not be mistaken for weakness.
"Never mistake our tolerance for lack of determination. And never mistake our kindness for softness. We know who we are and we are proud of it," he said.
Chrétien said building a country like Canada, welcoming people from around the globe, and caring for the weakest, "is a sign of strength."
Chrétien said his "honest" message was "from one friend to another," and he called on the U.S. to "respect the friendship" and "be a good neighbour."
He concluded with the following words in French: "Long live the United States and long live Canada."

articles.title: Dutch tour bus overturns in Switzerland, several people dead, police say
articles.summary: GENEVA — A Dutch tour bus overturned in eastern Switzerland in a serious accident that left several people dead and others injured, police said. The bus overturned Thursday afternoon between the…

blocks.text: GENEVA — A Dutch tour bus overturned in eastern Switzerland in a serious accident that left several people dead and others injured, police said.

The bus overturned Thursday afternoon between the villages of Susch and Zernez in the Alpine canton of Graubuenden, and rescue teams were responding to the scene, authorities said. The police did not specify the number of dead and injured.
According to Swiss media, 48 people were on the bus. A spokeswoman for ANVR, a Dutch travel industry association, told the Blick newspaper that the passengers were Dutch.
A police spokesman said the coach collided with the crash barrier and then overturned. No other vehicles were believed to be involved.

Oad, a travel agency behind the trip, said in a statement in Dutch that it was “deeply shocked and devastated by the tragic bus accident” and its thoughts were with those involved and their loved ones.

The Dutch Foreign Ministry said it was too early to know the number of victims. Swiss President Guy Parmelin, writing on X, vowed that Swiss authorities would ensure a “comprehensive and thorough investigation” of the case.
Several ambulances and five helicopters were deployed to the location, according to Swiss media./dp

articles.title: ‘Magnitude slowly hit’: 9/11 remembered 25 years on
articles.summary: CANBERRA, Australia – A political reporter has recounted being in Washington with an ex-prime minister a quarter of a century ago when terrorist attacks on the US changed the world. What should have…

blocks.text: CANBERRA, Australia – A political reporter has recounted being in Washington with an ex-prime minister a quarter of a century ago when terrorist attacks on the US changed the world.
What should have been a routine international trip with the prime minister quickly devolved into chaos and the start of a new era of global paranoia.

James Grubel was AAP’s chief political reporter covering then-prime minister John Howard’s first meeting with then-US president George W Bush in Washington DC for the 50th anniversary of the ANZUS treaty.
Day one of the visit had gone smoothly.
Day two was to start with a press conference before the prime minister was to deliver a speech later in the day.
News of two planes striking the World Trade Centre in New York had reached the press pack in Washington moments before Mr Howard spoke to the media.
“It had become a little bit more obvious that this was a serious event,” Grubel told AAP.
“The prime minister gave his condolences. And still, at that stage, we were thinking the day was going to go ahead as as normal.”
But as the curtains were opened in the Willard Hotel at the close of the press conference, smoke was billowing from across the Potomac River.
A third plane had struck the Pentagon just 5km away.
The gathered journalists were forced to evacuate, walking one mile down the road to the Australian embassy as thousands of people scrambled to get out of the city.
“The whole of Washington was in gridlock,” Grubel said.
“There were armed police and soldiers on the corners … I think every building in Washington and everybody was evacuating.
“It was a totally different city to the one that we’d been wandering around in for the past couple days.”
The mood in the Australian embassy was sombre according to Mr Grubel as journalists continued writing for the media back home.

“The magnitude of this awful event slowly, slowly hit, and you had to occasionally stop yourself and just focus on what you were doing and try and put it out of your mind so you could write about it clearly.
“Otherwise, you’d kind of get a bit caught up in it.It was very unclear whether there were going to also be attacks on on London, on Paris and Sydney, on Canberra.”
Ten Australians were among the almost 3000 people who died when al-Qaeda militants hijacked four planes on September 11, 2001.
The hijackers flew two planes into the twin towers at the World Trade Centre in New York and one into the Pentagon just outside of Washington.
The fourth plane crashed into a field in rural Pennsylvania.
John Howard decided to invoke the ANZUS treaty three days later on the advice of his foreign minister. If the United States was under attack, Australia had an obligation to send troops.
It’s a poignant end to an event which Mr Grubel says has rippled out to the present day.
“Now with AUKUS, we’re still going through these issues and these debates about our national security,” he said.
The shift in political rhetoric to security and defence bolstered support for the Liberal government heading into the 2001 federal election which it ultimately won.
A quarter of a century on, Mr Howard said the lesson to be learnt was in being vigilant to the world around us.
“We must be alive to the threats that face us but not live in constant fear,” Mr Howard said in a statement.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who was a Labor backbencher at the time of the attack, said it remained a harrowing anniversary a quarter of a century on.
“Alongside the many Americans who lost their lives, were people from nations across the world, 10 Australians among them,” Mr Albanese told the parliament on Thursday.
“America was shaken to its core, but it did not yield. It did not break.”/dp
