The negotiations started in 2020, when Kikon wrote to the museum after reading “an article in the Guardian that they were doing an ethical review” of the collection. “They replied within 24 hours,” said Kikon.
That was just the beginning of a lengthy process that soon expanded into a wider community-led campaign.

The Forum for Naga Reconciliation, a community peace group, assembled a team known as Recover, Restore and Decolonise, bringing together Naga volunteers from across the region to work on the repatriation effort.

blocks.caption: Members of the Naga delegation view the relics on display at the Pitt Rivers Museum. Photograph: Pitt Rivers Museum

blocks.text: “They travelled to villages and organised meetings to inform people about the remains,” said Arkotong Longkumer, a Naga anthropologist who worked closely with Kikon to lead the initiative, which he described as “open and transparent”.
“It was an intergenerational journey that brought together students, civil society, tribal leaders and the church,” said Longkumer, who teaches at Edinburgh University.
A Naga delegation, including tribal leaders, visited Oxford in 2025 to officially register a claim to the remains.
“I had never known our ancestral human remains had been taken away like that,” said Wangsa. “I felt angry when I saw them.”

Laura Van Broekhoven, director of the Pitt Rivers Museum and a professor of museum studies and ethics at Oxford University, said the museum was completing paperwork to enable the return of the remains.
“We will then start working towards the ceremonial aspects so we can have everything ready,” she said. “In our experience, handover ceremonies can be very emotional.”

articles.title: Remulla to bring Co home during France trip: We know where he is
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said on Thursday that the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) knows where former lawmaker Elizaldy Co lives and that the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said on Thursday that the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) knows where former lawmaker Elizaldy Co lives and that the intention behind his upcoming trip to France is to bring Co back to the Philippines.
After the Senate budget hearing of the DILG, Remulla was asked by the media about his trip to France.
“Zaldy Co is the agenda. We know where he is. We know the address. We know his house. [The trip] is to get him back here,” he replied.
Co, believed to be seeking asylum in France, was charged in November 2025 and subsequently issued an arrest warrant in connection with a flood control project in Oriental Mindoro.
Remulla previously said his flight to France was to follow up with the International Criminal Police Organization on the Philippine request for a red notice against the at-large congressman.
Similarly, his brother, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla, announced that he would also fly to France to find Co. /mcm

articles.title: Japan’s empty temples seek new ways to survive
articles.summary: The 370-year-old structure has all the attributes of a classically designed Japanese temple, from the curved roof to the timber-frame walls, spacious tatami-mat prayer hall and elaborately decorated…

blocks.text: The 370-year-old structure has all the attributes of a classically designed Japanese temple, from the curved roof to the timber-frame walls, spacious tatami-mat prayer hall and elaborately decorated altar.

Set in manicured gardens on the Chita Peninsula in central Japan, the 350-square-meter (3,767-square-foot) property is on the market for 482 million yen (€2.66 million, US3.01 million). The estate agent’s pitch says the price includes dismantling by “expert heritage craftsmen” and delivery to anywhere in Japan, where it would be fully restored into a “stunning” two- or three-bedroom home.
The sale and removal of the temple marks the end of its role in the local community in the hills above the Nagasawacho district, but it is a better fate than many places of worship across Japan.

There are around 77,000 temples across the country, but as many as 17,000 no longer have a full-time resident priest as congregations have shrunk — particularly in rural districts experiencing rapid depopulation — and financial pressures have taken their toll.
That means many temples are being sold off or simply shuttered and left to deteriorate quietly.
A temple brought back to life
Tomomi Iwayama took on the abandoned Ganshu-ji temple in Odawara, a coastal town about 80 kilometers (50 miles) southwest of Tokyo, a decade ago. Today, he is the abbot of a growing congregation.
“The temple had no abbot for 70 years before I arrived because it was just so difficult to operate, and it has taken me until now to get it financially back on track,” he told DW.
“Even in a relatively large urban area such as Odawara, which has around 200,000 residents, it has been very hard,” he said. “In the countryside, it is much more difficult.”

Iwayama’s biggest problem is the country’s shrinking population: fewer worshippers and falling demand for funerals and other traditional rites make it harder to finance the temple’s upkeep. He has worked hard to reach out to the local community and has had success in selling plots in the temple graveyard.
One innovation that has attracted attention is the temple’s “smart graveyard,” where families scan a card, and a robotic system recovers a relative’s ashes from the columbarium.
Temples in rural areas of Japan face far greater challenges, he said.

“Young people in villages usually leave to go to university, and then they find a job in one of the big cities, so they rarely go back,” he said. “Maybe they will go back once a year to pay their respects to their ancestors at the village temple, but that is not enough for the temple to get by on.”

Equally, when the head priest of a rural temple retires, his children are unlikely to want to take the role on because of these challenges. All too often, Iwayama said, the result is the temple closing.
But he denies the suggestion that religion in Japan is following the same path as in the West, where Christian congregation numbers have plummeted over the decades.
Demand for Buddhism remains
“I sense there is still a lot of demand in Japan for Buddhism,” he said, contrasting the fast-paced, technology-focused lives that people typically lead with the serenity that they are often seeking.

“Buddhism is a style of living, of an enlightened person,” he said. “A lot of people are looking for that. And while the traditional rituals of funerals and anniversaries are declining and that revenue is shrinking, we are finding that more people want to take part in traditional temple cuisine cooking classes, meditation and other things that we can offer.”
Temples that are not able to shift to offer experiences more in tune with modern Japan are at risk of closing, said Joey Stockermans, one of the founders of the Mokomoko online real estate service.
“We have had a temple on our site in the past, and we were approached by a foreign potential buyer, so there is certainly interest when these properties become available,” he said.

Other foreigners who are long-term residents are doing their best to protect Japan’s religious heritage for future generations. American journalist and author Jake Adelstein is currently a Zen priest at Zenshoin Temple in Tokyo’s Toshima Ward and is training to become an abbot.

“I do not think that Japanese are becoming less religious; I believe they are becoming fewer because of population decline, and they are becoming less wealthy because of the economic situation,” he said.

“Families want to keep the grave plot that they have had for generations, but for many of them it is just too expensive to maintain, and they often live a long way away, so they are unable to regularly visit to pay their respects,” he said.
The annual fee for a grave can be up to 100,000 yen, while memorials and other rites can be an additional financial burden, Adelstein explained.
Young people shun religious careers

“Young people are not interested in a career as a priest because temples earn so little money, so there are positions that cannot be filled, and that is especially a problem in the countryside,” he said.
Some temples have amalgamated their operations and share a priest, but that will become more difficult in the future, Adelstein said.
As elsewhere, Zenshoin Temple has started vegetarian cooking classes and Zen meditation sessions to appeal to the local community, and Adelstein hopes that will be enough to keep the temple open.
“The training to become an abbot is very tough, and the economics of a temple today often just do not add up, but I see it as a critical part of this society and this nation,” he said. /dl

articles.title: Trafficked into fraud: An African crisis in Cambodia
articles.summary: Southeast Asia has long emerged as a major hub of highly organized online fraud operations, targeting people all around the world. According to the United Nations, these operations generate tens of…

blocks.text: Southeast Asia has long emerged as a major hub of highly organized online fraud operations, targeting people all around the world.

According to the United Nations, these operations generate tens of billions of dollars annually, having long surpassed the illegal drug trade as the most profitable activity for criminal networks, as reported by the United States Institute of Peace.

However, those who fall prey to scams and other fraudulent activities aren’t the only victims of these criminal rings; alone in Southeast Asia, the scam industry is powered by at least 300,000 trafficked workers from 66 countries. They are routinely subjected to torture, sexual abuse and forced labor, according to a recent UN Human Rights report.

African nationals now form the largest group of those trafficked to and stranded in countries like Myanmar and Cambodia, without any viable pathway to go back home, says the NGO Freedom Collaborative.
In Cambodia, one of the main obstacles to helping stranded Africans return home is that many countries on the continent, such as Uganda, Liberia, Ghana and Nigeria, lack consular representation.
But there are other reasons.
“Some countries have zero interest,” says Montse Ferrer, co-regional director of Amnesty International, who also blames the home countries for their inaction.
“They’re not even picking up the phone, let alone providing the paperwork or the money for them to go back.”
Cambodia’s reluctant crackdown on scam operators

Ferrer believes that the Cambodian government also has an interest in keeping scam trafficking victims in the country. This is because many of the victims now have overstay fines for their visas against their names in Cambodia, reaching thousands of dollars in many instances.
“They don’t allow NGOs to provide the support these people need, and instead they have resorted to arresting and threatening them,” Ferrer told DW.

Following great pressure from the international community — including threats of financial sanctions by the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada and the European Union — Cambodia did eventually agree to launch a crackdown on the scamming industry earlier this year.
According to the Cambodian Ministry of Information, the initiative resulted in many arrests and triggered a mass exodus of dubious operatives from scamming industry.

But the crackdown also created a secondary crisis: Thousands of trafficked foreign workers remain stranded in the country without documentation nor legal status; now, they also lack shelter and money in many instances, NGOs say.
Many who have sought help in Cambodia have reportedly been placed in immigration detention, while others have to sleep rough and beg for food.
Instead of being given protection, trafficking victims often face stigmatization and abuse on the street of the capital Phnom Penh and elsewhere.
Lured to Cambodia under false pretenses
Emmanuel David is one of those stuck in Cambodia. The 28-year-old Liberian national arrived there in 2025 after a treacherous irregular journey originating in Vietnam.
“My friend told me there was work in Cambodia, but he did not explain that it was scamming work,” David explained.
The scamming company had offered him a lucrative deal of making around $800 (€700) per month, which is more than double the average wage for qualified individuals in Liberia.
The reality hit quite differently: Once there, David was forced to work 14 hours a day to deceive women on various dating apps to part with their money.
But David was initially unable — and later unwilling — to meet the set target quota of scams per day.
In response, the criminal group he worked for started billing him for food and accommodation through his wages and later even confiscated his belongings, including his passport.
David says he also faced substantial physical violence, including beatings, for four months.
Eventually, he left “with no documents and no money,” and is now hoping to find a way back to Liberia.
His story is far from unique.
‘Hundreds’ of Africans trafficked to criminal compounds
Another survivor, who asked to remain anonymous for fear of retaliation, also recounted how he was “beaten and [subjected to] electric shocks.”
The abuse resulted in him having to be hospitalized for three weeks, and he is now unable to pay his medical bills.
Pia Oberoi, chief of the Right to Development Section at UN Human Rights, told DW that “despite the promise of a good salary, most come out in debt.”

She also confirmed that a growing number of trafficking victims in Southeast Asia come from African countries, “because there is clearly a recruitment industry that’s built around Africa, targeting African nationals.”
Other victims have corroborated this development, describing hundreds of Africans packed into heavily fortified compounds.
“Once you’re inside there’s no way out,” an informant, who also chose to remain anonymous, told DW.
He said the compounds have their own laws, and that sexual abuse and psychological violence are an integral part of how they operate.
The police, he says, just turn a blind eye.
No government assistance from any direction
Amnesty International speaks of an unfolding humanitarian crisis, warning that escapees are widely being treated as criminals rather than as trafficking victims, a sentiment the UN shares.
“They shouldn’t be punished for crimes they were forced to commit,” the UN’s Oberoi highlights.
Several of the victims contacted by DW meanwhile said their governments were notably “slow” to help with their repatriation.
DW also attempted to contact several African foreign ministries for comment but has yet to receive a response.

A statement issued by the Cambodian government meanwhile said that more than 700 compounds run chiefly by Chinese nationals had been raided, with 58,266 foreign nationals deported and nearly 30,000 suspects arrested over the past year.
However, the Cambodian government did not reply to DW’s direct request for further information.

The UN’s International Organization for Migration (IOM) explained it’s trying its utmost to help the trafficking victims; but in the face of severe budgetary constraints, it can only provide “limited, prioritized support.”
Fear, guilt and stigma
Humanitarian groups also warn of a high risk of victims being re-trafficked. This is a danger even for those who have somehow managed to return to their countries of origin.
In some instances, those who come back home are stigmatized as a failure — “a situation that is really unbearable,” says Ferrer.
Emmanuel David is a prime example: He feels obliged to to apologize to his family for not returning a success.
When asked about his little daughter, he simply says “Daddy can’t go home without money.” /dl

articles.title: Putin rejects mobilization rumors, many Russians unconvinced
articles.summary: Twice within the first week of September, Russian President Vladimir Putin publicly dismissed rumors of a looming mobilization campaign in the country. On September 1, Putin called the rumors…

blocks.text: Twice within the first week of September, Russian President Vladimir Putin publicly dismissed rumors of a looming mobilization campaign in the country. On September 1, Putin called the rumors “complete nonsense” and described them as an “information attack” against Russia.
Two days later, on September 3, at the Economic Forum in Vladivostok, Putin said that “there is no scenario today that would require mobilization.”
Summons are cause for unease among Russian DW users

DW’s Russian service asked readers in Russia, on condition of anonymity, whether they see signs of an impending mobilization. The most common response from DW readers concerned receiving summonses from military enlistments offices.
“My nephew received a summons for data verification,” wrote a reader from the industrial city of Naberezhnye Chelny.
“I received a summons ordering me to appear for data verification. I’m self-employed. What should I do?” wrote a user named Maxim.
“One of my friends, a school teacher, received a summons through the government services portal [Gosuslugi] on July 9 to update his records,” said another reader, Sergei.

People fear that they may be called up for military service or lose the ability to leave the country freely. As a result, some of those who have received draft notices are seeking to travel abroad as quickly as possible, while restrictions on leaving the country have not yet taken effect.
“One acquaintance of mine left Russia two months ago after receiving a summons for data verification from the military enlistment office,” one reader wrote.
Emigration as ‘a fantasy’
Not everyone, however, sees emigration as a realistic option in the event of mobilization.
“As for leaving, that’s a fantasy. Where would you go, and more importantly, with what money?” one DW reader wrote.

In June, reports emerged from Russia’s Penza region that men were forcibly taken to military enlistment offices and pressured into signing military contracts. According to local reports, the practice became widespread enough that residents organized protests in support of relatives and neighbors. Journalists reporting on the issue say such raids are continuing.

“People are being detained, particularly near the entrances to their apartment buildings,” Lena Lemyasova, a journalist with news outlet Important Stories [Vazhnye Istorii], told DW. “Often men who have been drinking. Unknown individuals approach them, or vehicles pull up — often cars provided by local authorities. The men are simply seized and taken away, then their families and neighbors hear nothing more. Later, information sometimes emerges that they were transported to military units. They are often held there before being sent to the front.”
Important Stories specializes in investigative journalism. Its publisher, Roman Anin, spent ten years as investigations editor at well-known independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta.
What do Russian lawyers say about the summonses?

Does receiving a military summons mean a person will be sent to war? According to lawyer Artem Klyga, a summons issued “for data verification” does not in itself mean that someone will be drafted, mobilized or deployed. Data verification notices are one of several legally established reasons for calling someone to a military enlistment office.

“These summonses only show that military enlistment offices have significantly improved their military registration procedures. If mobilization begins, such records would help authorities quickly summon the people they need,” Klyga explained to DW.

Russians have also increasingly reported receiving mobilization orders issued in advance. In peacetime, such orders do not oblige individuals to take any action. However, if mobilization is declared, recipients are required to report to their designated military enlistment office.

“They were issued before the war and during the war [against Ukraine] as well. But what changed in the first half of 2026 is that, judging by all indications, they began to be distributed in the hundreds of thousands,” Russian lawyer Timofei Vaskin told DW. “We do not know the exact figures because the information is classified. But judging from social media reports and the number of inquiries we and our colleagues received, the increase was dramatic, by dozens of times.”
At the same time, the 2022 decree on partial mobilization in Russia has never been formally revoked and technically remains in force.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has repeatedly described reports of a new mobilization wave as “fake stories.” Yet critics note that Peskov also denied reports of a possible mobilization beginning in May 2022.
Just eight days before the announcement of partial mobilization, he said: “At the moment, this is not being discussed.”
Growing demand for mobilization specialists

As of August 8, DW found several vacancies on the Russian job platform HeadHunter seeking specialists in “mobilization preparedness.” 40 such vacancies are available in Moscow and the surrounding region and 13 in St Petersburg.

For example, some companies are looking for specialists responsible for ensuring that the organization has a mobilization plan in place and knows how it would operate if the state were to place the economy on a wartime footing. Their duties also include preparing the company for emergencies and civil defense measures, as well as helping to transition the organization to a special operating regime in the event of wartime conditions.
The positions were advertised by both private companies and state institutions.
Summonses, military training exercises, the expansion of military registration systems and active recruitment efforts help explain why official denials have failed to put the rumors to rest.
Preparing for ‘any decision Putin might make’

“The way to look at this is that bureaucrats have been tasked with preparing the system for any decision Putin might make. And if that decision is mobilization, they are expected to be ready,” Artem Klyga said.

In late July, the independent outlet Agentstvo counted 197 vacancies around Russia containing the term “mobilization preparedness” and more than 2,600 vacancies related to “military registration” on the same recruitment platform. /dl

articles.title: Iran tightens social control with crackdown on cafes
articles.summary: Iranian authorities have launched a clampdown on cafes in the capital, Tehran, in recent months, suspecting them of fostering anti-government sentiment and facilitating protests. According to the…

blocks.text: Iranian authorities have launched a clampdown on cafes in the capital, Tehran, in recent months, suspecting them of fostering anti-government sentiment and facilitating protests.
According to the human rights organization HRANA, at least seven cafes and restaurants were shut down on July 19 alone for allegedly failing to comply with mandatory hijab rules.

Previously, some media outlets, including Javan, a newspaper affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), have described cafes as “gathering places for protesters” who, in their view, pose a threat to “national security.”
Most recently, the “Vanak Park” cafes in Tehran were sealed, resulting in at least 200 people losing their jobs.
Crackdown on cafes
Authorities believe cafes, because of their widespread presence and popularity, could play a role in organizing mass protests.
The government’s fears are rooted in the latest wave of protests in Iran, which began on December 28, 2025, and grew into the country’s largest uprising since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

Saediniya, a well-known cafe chain with 10 branches in Iran, closed its branches on this day in support of calls for strikes. It was subsequently accused of engaging in “propaganda against the state.”
Iran’s Supreme Court has now upheld the sentence of Sadegh Saedinia, the owner of the cafe chain, to 12 years and six months in prison, along with the confiscation of his assets.
He was arrested over his support for the protests, and all branches of his cafe chain were confiscated and shut down by judicial order.

Other cafes, including “Lamiz” and “Voria,” faced a broadly similar fate. Voria is owned by a prominent Iranian footballer. Both were sealed by judicial order because of their indirect support for calls to protest. Cafe closures have not been confined to periods of protest, however, and the practice continues.
The rise of the cafe culture
Tehran has seen a surge in the number of cafes over the past decade, rising from around 300 in the early 2010s to as many as 4,000 now, according to various estimates.

Some experts attribute the growing number to changes in urban lifestyles in recent years. They see this as more than the expansion of a particular type of business and describe it as a sign of wider social and cultural changes within Iranian society.

“The explosive growth of cafes in society can, to some extent, be seen as a social response to living in a state of chronic crisis,” Saba Alaleh, a clinical psychologist and psychoanalyst whose work focuses on political and social issues, told DW’s Persian service.
“In such circumstances, people are not simply looking to consume or be entertained. They are looking for a place to temporarily distance themselves from the pressures of everyday life,” she said.

“In this sense, the cafe becomes a third space. It is neither home nor the workplace, but a space between the two where people can briefly step away from their everyday roles and pressures, connect with others, and feel that life is still somewhat manageable and normal.”
The cafe trend has become particularly popular among Gen Z, who are bearing the brunt of runaway inflation and steep living costs in Iran.

“The young people who gather in these cafes do not necessarily come from affluent backgrounds,” Nasser, a cafe owner in Tehran, told DW. “In many parts of Tehran, young people from the middle class also meet at cafes, and many of our customers belong to this group.”
The political role of cafes
Even before the latest bout of nationwide protests that began at the end of last year, shutting down cafes was common practice for the Iranian government.
Most of these crackdowns and closures, however, were carried out under the pretext of enforcing compulsory hijab.
The protests that began in late December 2025 changed that, with cafes becoming the target more often and for varied reasons.
“They shut down our cafe on the pretext that we had served customers who were not wearing the hijab, but that is only an excuse,” Nasser said.
“Outside, on the streets of Tehran, women and girls have effectively abandoned the compulsory hijab, yet the government expects us not to allow them into the cafe,” he added.
Maintaining control over social spaces
Alaleh said the issue is no longer simply about cracking down on women for not wearing the hijab.

“Authoritarian governments generally seek to control the flow of information, social interactions and the organization of citizens,” she pointed out. “Any space beyond the direct supervision of those in power that allows trust, dialogue and social ties to develop can weaken part of the government’s monopoly over the social sphere.”
The expert said the crackdown on cafes and cafegoers is part of the government’s efforts to preserve its monopoly over social spaces.

She underlined that to a security apparatus, even a group of young people casually sitting together can represent the emergence of an independent social network outside the formal structures of power.
“The broader and more deeply rooted these independent networks become, the more difficult it is for the government to maintain exclusive control over the public sphere,” added Alaleh. /dl

articles.title: August of 2026 hottest month ever recorded globally – EU monitor
articles.summary: PARIS — The EU’s climate monitor said Thursday that August was the hottest single month ever recorded globally, with ocean temperatures also reaching unprecedented highs as western Europe…

blocks.text: PARIS — The EU’s climate monitor said Thursday that August was the hottest single month ever recorded globally, with ocean temperatures also reaching unprecedented highs as western Europe capped its warmest summer.
In response to the assessment by the Copernicus Climate Change Service, the UN warned that until humanity weaned off fossil fuels, the planet would only push deeper into uncharted territory.
Copernicus observations go back to 1940 but other evidence — such as ice cores, tree rings and coral skeletons — allow scientists to place today’s climate against a much longer historical context.

“Humans haven’t seen temperatures as hot as today for, arguably, at least the last 100,000 years,” Samantha Burgess from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, which oversees Copernicus, told AFP.

Global average air temperatures in August were 16.96C, Copernicus said — surpassing by 0.01C the previous all-time monthly record set in July 2023. Copernicus said it considered the two months joint-highest given the narrow difference.

Scientists say that human activity — primarily the burning of coal, oil and gas — has warmed the planet by roughly 1.4C since pre-industrial times and increased the severity and likelihood of extreme weather.
Yet heat-trapping greenhouse gas emissions rose to new highs in 2025.

“The evidence is irrefutable: this is the spiraling price of humanity’s fossil fuel addiction, and the global climate crisis it is fueling,” United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell said of the Copernicus report.
More ahead
Global sea surface temperatures also set a new daily high and tied equal-hottest for August, extending a three-month streak of record-breaking warmth across the world’s oceans.
More than 90 percent of excess heat trapped by greenhouse gas emissions has been absorbed by the oceans, sparing land from warming but at severe cost to marine life, reefs and coastal communities.
Records tumbled in overheated basins like the Atlantic and Mediterranean and also the tropical Pacific, where the strongest El Nino weather pattern in the modern era is fast accumulating strength.
These events are marked by unusually warm Pacific waters but raise the odds of wild weather thousands of miles away, from floods in Peru to droughts in Africa and wildfires in Australia.
The warmer phase of a natural climate cycle, El Nino episodes usually deliver a temporary spike in global temperatures already elevated by long-term background warming.

Scientists expect records to keep falling in the months ahead as this “super” El Nino approaches peak intensity around December and for 2027 — and maybe even 2026 — to become the hottest years ever observed.

“Climate change makes every El Nino hotter, and until we stop burning coal, oil, and gas these record-shattering months will simply keep on coming,” said Friederike Otto, a climate scientist from Imperial College London.
Sizzling summer
Copernicus also said that August “marked the end of western Europe’s warmest summer” that surpassed the long-standing record set in 2003.
The June to August season was defined by severe, back-to-back heatwaves that shut schools, dried up rivers and primed the land for devastating wildfires.
Between mid-July and mid-August, the continent’s EuroMomo monitoring platform estimated that Europe saw more than 32,000 excess deaths.
Scientists from the World Weather Attribution network concluded that a particularly strong heatwave in June would have been “virtually impossible” without the influence of climate change.
But extraordinary heat was felt around the globe.
On Wednesday, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration said the contiguous United States has endured its hottest summer on record.
And regions home to around 900 million people lived through the hottest July ever observed, according to AFP analysis of Copernicus data.

“We’ve had an exceptional summer — not only in Europe, but other parts of the world where records that have existed for close to a century have fallen,” said Burgess, an ocean scientist and strategic lead for at ECMWF.
The climate would “continue to get more extreme unless we turn off the tap to global emissions”, she added. /dl

articles.title: Thailand kindergarten shooting: Suspected gunman surrenders
articles.summary: BANGKOK — A police officer who allegedly gunned down his wife at the kindergarten where she was a teacher in eastern Thailand surrendered Thursday after an overnight standoff with authorities,…

blocks.text: BANGKOK — A police officer who allegedly gunned down his wife at the kindergarten where she was a teacher in eastern Thailand surrendered Thursday after an overnight standoff with authorities, officials said.

Tatsapong Tongthat, an officer at the Bang Lamung station in Chonburi province, allegedly killed his wife late Wednesday morning inside a building at the Nongplalai Municipal Kindergarten about 150 kilometers (93 miles) southeast of the capital Bangkok, according to the provincial government.
Authorities said he fled to his home after the shooting and police surrounded the house, where he remained until surrendering after an 18-hour standoff.

School safety and gun violence in Thailand have come under scrutiny after a 14-year-old opened fire at his high school and family home on Aug. 7, killing eight people and injuring more than 20 before apparently taking his own life.
Another 14-year-old student was arrested Sept. 2 after he fired several shots but failed to injure anyone at his school in Kamphaeng Phet province, 200 kilometers (120 miles) north of Bangkok.

Thailand has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in Asia despite fairly restrictive gun laws. While mass shootings are still rare, Thailand has seen an uptick in high-profile attacks in recent years. /dl

articles.title: Wall Street Journal publisher convicted in Hong Kong of deterring reporter from union role
articles.summary:
Dow Jones convicted of one count of deterring Selina Cheng from role at Hong Kong Journalist Association but cleared of second charge

A Hong Kong court has convicted the publisher of the…

blocks.text: A Hong Kong court has convicted the publisher of the Wall Street Journal of deterring a reporter from taking up a trade union role, in a case that raised concerns about press freedom in the city.

The newspaper dismissed Selina Cheng just weeks after she was appointed chair of the Hong Kong Journalist Association (HKJA) in 2024. She was told at the time her termination was officially due to restructuring.

Outside court on Thursday, Cheng said: “If reporters’ employment rights are not sufficiently safeguarded, or when their rights are violated and not enforced in law, then we can no longer work safely as reporters.”

Principal magistrate David Cheung ruled that Dow Jones Publishing, the parent company of the Wall Street journal, was guilty of “preventing or deterring an employee from exercising trade union rights,” but acquitted it of “dismissing or discriminating against an employee because she exercised those rights.”

Cheng, who covered China’s automobiles and energy sectors for the WSJ, said her editor had told her that employees should not be seen as advocating for press freedom in “places like Hong Kong”, saying it could be perceived as a conflict of interest. She alleged her employer had attempted to prevent her from taking up a role in the union.
She said the company told her that she needed to seek the firm’s approval for outside activities and requested her to leave her then-board position at the association.
Cheng launched the private prosecution against Dow Jones Publishing after losing her job in July 2024, weeks after taking up the position as chair of the union.
The company pleaded not guilty to both charges, which each carry a maximum fine of HK$100,000 (about $12,750).
Sentencing is expected to be handed down at a later date.

During the trial, the defence argued that Cheng was terminated because of redundancy and that the prosecution had not sufficiently proved that the firm’s management instructed Cheng’s supervisor. The defence also accused Cheng of acting in bad faith in a previous hearing.

But magistrate David Cheung said that Cheng’s termination “was motivated by wrongful and unjustified application of their code of conduct” when it insisted Cheng needed to seek prior approval to stand as chair of HKJA.
Cheung said he accepted Cheng’s explanation, describing the former WSJ reporter as “honest and reliable”, adding she and was clearly motivated by “the wish to see justice”.

Cheng’s termination alarmed journalists, who are already operating in an increasingly restricted media environment in the city, where foreign outlets have traditionally faced less pressure than local news outlets.

“The WSJ set a very bad precedent by punishing an employee who was exercising her constitutionally protected rights in Hong Kong,” said Eric Lai, a senior fellow at the Georgetown Center for Asian Law.

The WSJ maintained there was no link between Cheng’s role in the Hong Kong union and her termination. At the time of Cheng’s dismissal, it issued a statement saying: “The Wall Street Journal has been and continues to be a fierce and vocal advocate for press freedom in Hong Kong and around the world.”

HKJA is the oldest journalist union in Hong Kong. It was established in 1968 and is registered as a trade union representing journalists and workers in news. It has faced increasing pressure since the introduction of a Beijing-imposed national security law in 2020.

Hong Kong has fallen sharply in global press freedom rankings since the law’s introduction. In 2019 Reporters Without Borders ranked the city 73rd in the world. By 2026 it had fallen 67 places to 140th out of 180 countries and territories.

articles.title: Rubio says US will work with allies to stop drug-trafficking as three killed in latest boat strike
articles.summary:
Rubio visits Ecuador and welcomes cooperation after campaign of unilateral strikes on alleged ‘narco-terrorists’

US secretary of state Marco Rubio gave new clarity on the approach toward…

blocks.text: US secretary of state Marco Rubio gave new clarity on the approach toward combating drug trafficking in Latin American waters, saying the Trump administration was focused on working with allied countries and aligning with their laws but insisting the military will “still blow up ships if need be.”

The public acknowledgment of a shift in US strategy comes a year after Washington began a campaign of unilateral deadly strikes against those it calls “narco-terrorists” operating boats in international waters.

Late Wednesday, US Southern Command announced the latest such strike in the Caribbean Sea, saying it killed three people. That brought the number of people who have been killed in boat strikes by the US military to at least 230 in 69 strikes.

Still, the Trump administration is focused on building agreements for joint operations with allied countries in the region, including Colombia and Ecuador, that comply with their laws in their waters.

“I think its an incredible advance for the first time to have countries that are willing to participate in these efforts in their territorial waters,” Rubio told reporters on a trip to the Ecuadorian capital, Quito.
“The important point is that these routes are being disrupted. These routes are being ended,” he added.
He said the decision is “a strike-by-strike or operation-by-operation determination” that depends on the threat and location of the boat.

Recent US interdictions in Latin American waters are unlike the Trump administration’s initial strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats that began in September 2025. People onboard floating refueling stations said to be supporting drug trafficking have been removed and transferred to Ecuadorian authorities. Then the US military blows up the vessels.
The shift comes after a series of strikes on boats over the year on people the Trump administration accused of being “narco-terrorists” without providing evidence.
Rubio’s comments came during a three-nation tour of South America aimed at boosting security cooperation with conservative leaders who have cozied up to Donald Trump.

articles.title: Notorious Ecuadorian crime gang designated a terrorist group by US
articles.summary:
Trump administration to seek extra funding from Congress to ‘dismantle’ Los Tiguerones over narcotics trafficking

The US has designated Ecuador’s Los Tiguerones gang, which

blocks.text: The US has designated Ecuador’s Los Tiguerones gang, which stormed a television station during a live broadcast in 2024, as a terrorist organisation as the Trump administration expands its campaign against narcotics traffickers it says are destabilising Latin America.

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, made the announcement in Quito, where he met Ecuadorian president Daniel Noboa, one of several rightwing allies of Donald Trump whom Rubio is courting as a security partner during a three-nation tour through Latin America that began on Tuesday.
Rubio said the Los Tiguerones gang was linked to narcotics trafficking, as well as attacks on civilians, law enforcement officers and journalists.

“We are not talking about an ordinary mafia, nor are we talking about common criminals, we are talking about terrorists who, in many cases, possess weapons and equipment resembling the national armies of certain countries,” he said.

The heavily armed gang’s attack on the TC Televisión network in 2024 prompted Noboa to declare a state of “internal armed conflict”, amid claims foreign drug gangs had descended on Ecuador to take control of important routes for coca grown in neighbouring Colombia and Peru and then shipped to the US.

Live footage from the El Noticiero news programme showed men toting pistols, shotguns, machine guns, grenades and sticks of dynamite. The viral images quickly became a symbol of the drug violence destabilising the country.

In its efforts to fight against narcotics trafficking and illegal migration from Latin America, the Trump administration has also empowered a number of hardline leaders through its “Shield of the Americas” coalition that aims to tighten security cooperation with rightwing allies in the region.
During his trip, Rubio plans to visit several newly elected conservative leaders amid a significant political shift to the right in Latin America.

On Wednesday, Rubio hailed Ecuador as being the Trump administration’s most “aggressive” partner in its military campaign against alleged drug traffickers, including in the controversial strikes against boats that have killed at least 227 people whom the Trump administration has called drug traffickers without providing evidence.

Rubio said that he would seek $45m (£33m) in additional funding from Congress towards efforts aimed at “dismantling these terrorist groups”, although he did not go into details. He also told reporters that elite forces from both countries were “working jointly on a day-to-day basis in a way that has no precedent in order to try to dismantle these terrorist organisations”.

blocks.caption: Marco Rubio (left) is welcomed to Ecuador on Wednesday by its president, Daniel Noboa  Photograph: Dolores Ochoa/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Rubio visited Colombia on Tuesday, where he met its newly inaugurated president Abelardo De La Espriella, who narrowly won a June election against leftist leader Gustavo Petro with whom the Trump White House had cold relations.

During his remarks, Rubio took something of a victory lap, saying that the two sides would seek to “[confront] the mistakes of the past four years” and called Petro’s leadership of the country “unnatural”. Colombia joined the Shield of the Americas initiative only after its change in government.
During the meeting, the two men discussed security and counternarcotics policy, and signed memorandums of understanding on critical minerals and nuclear energy.

Rubio is expected to next travel to Peru, where he will meet Keiko Fujimori, who defeated a leftwing candidate by a margin of just 50,000 votes during a close election in July. She has promised to fight crime with an “iron fist” and adopt some controversial policies from neighbouring El Salvador, which has been a close ally of the US on security policies.

articles.title: Uganda to withdraw from Invictus Games ‘out of respect for King Charles’, says military chief
articles.summary:
Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba announces decision to pull out in post on X, citing tensions over ‘Harry-Meghan nonsense’

Uganda is withdrawing from the Duke of Sussex’s Invictus Games, the…

blocks.text: Uganda is withdrawing from the Duke of Sussex’s Invictus Games, the country’s military chief has said, out of respect for King Charles amid division over the “Harry-Meghan nonsense”.
Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, son of the Ugandan president, made the surprise announcement in a post on X on Wednesday.

Kainerugaba wrote: “In order not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III of the United Kingdom, whom we deeply revere, Uganda hereby withdraws from the Invictus Games. We shall not participate in anything that does not have His Majesty’s approval.”

The timing of the post suggests it may be in response to an official letter to UK senior government and military officials on behalf of Charles that reiterated the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were not working royals and would not use their HRH styles.

When asked by the Times about what had motivated the move, Kainerugaba is reported to have said: “I have factions in the Ministry of Defence that support that Harry-Meghan nonsense. I had to quash it straight away. I support the monarch. Period.”

The news, first reported by the Uganda Pulse news website, will be a blow to Harry, who two months ago stood alongside Uganda’s defence minister, Kiryowa Kiwanuka, at an Invictus Games event in London to announce that the East African nation would be the 26th country to enter the multisport event for wounded service personnel.

At the time, Kiwanuka praised the Ugandan president, Yoweri Museveni for his “visionary leadership” and Kainerugaba, a Sandhurst graduate, for “championing our team’s entry”, adding that their support “marks a new chapter for our servicemen and women”.

Ugandan government spokesperson Alan Kasujja confirmed to the BBC: “Gen Kainerugaba decides whether or not the UPDF [Uganda People’s Defence Force] participates in the Invictus Games. What you saw is his stated position. If it changes, he will let the world know.”

The decision to withdraw may be an unintended consequence of the official letter, issued on Monday by the head of the royal household, the lord chamberlain, Richard Benyon, at Charles’s behest, clarifying the position of the Sussexes after their return to the UK two weeks ago.

The letter directed that the couple were “no longer working members of the royal family”, that their charitable work “is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity” and “their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests”.

Kainerugaba was appointed army chief in 2024 and is widely seen as his 81-year-old father’s successor to the presidency. He has made several provocative posts on X, including threats to invade neighbouring Kenya, demands that Jay-Z hand over his wife, Beyoncé, so he could marry her, and threats against Bobi Wine, Museveni’s principal political rival.
The Invictus Games and representatives for the Duke of Sussex have been approached for comment.

articles.title: Family of British man found dead in Grenada ask local police to work with UK investigators
articles.summary:
Andrew Frederick’s body was found in property he was staying at in Grenada in January

The family of a British father who was found dead in the Caribbean in January is urging authorities in…

blocks.text: The family of a British father who was found dead in the Caribbean in January is urging authorities in Grenada to work with UK police to uncover the truth about his death.

Andrew Frederick’s body was found in the property he was staying at in Grenada on 4 January. An autopsy, performed in the same week by a privately hired pathologist, concluded that the 47-year-old’s death was a homicide.

In June, Grenada’s director of public prosecution, Howard Pinnock, said at a press conference that Frederick’s and another pending case would be sent to the coroner to determine the cause of death “because there is no basis in terms of both investigations that any homicide has occurred”.
After a sustained campaign by the family, British authorities became involved and Frederick’s body was repatriated to the UK last month, where a second autopsy was carried out.
The UK coroner has noted that Frederick’s organs are missing and the death is currently “unascertained”.
At the start of an inquest at West London coroner’s court last week, senior coroner Lydia Brown said the Metropolitan police are now investigating Frederick’s death.

The family, who attended the court hearing by video link, said the coroner’s “decision to suspend Andrew’s inquest to allow the Metropolitan police to conduct a criminal investigation marks a significant turning point”.
In statement to the Guardian, they urged Grenada and the UK to work together to find out what happened to Frederick.

“We are encouraged and grateful that the Metropolitan police investigation is now under way. Justice for Andrew depends on everyone with the power to act, on both sides of the Atlantic, doing what is right,” the statement said.

It added: “Andrew was a deeply loved member of a close-knit family; a son, brother, father and grandson. He leaves behind his cherished daughter, who should be growing up with him beside her, not learning to live without him.

“Our family remain determined to uncover the truth about what happened to Andrew and to see justice follow. We hope this ruling is the step that finally enables a complete, properly coordinated investigation and that everyone who can assist will now do so.”

Earlier this year, the family had called for an urgent review of the policies governing UK assistance to the loved ones of Britons killed abroad, after they were forced to launch their own public appeals for information, and commission an independent forensic pathologist and a private investigation.

“Eight months have passed since Andrew was taken from us. In that time, we have learned what no family should ever have to learn, and fought battles no family should ever face alone,” their statement said.

It added: “We have relentlessly sought answers and support while carrying the weight of Andrew’s loss and the horror of what was done to him. We still do not have a complete account of what happened, and important questions remain unanswered.

“We hope the Grenadian authorities with knowledge of the case will now share that information and work collaboratively with the Metropolitan police, allowing the investigation to proceed without further delay. We are also seeking urgent answers as to why Andrew’s organs were absent when his body was returned to the UK for further examination.”
In Grenada, the Office of the Commissioner told the Guardian that “the matter will be progressing to the coroner’s court for the parish of Saint George”.
A Met spokesperson said: “The Met is investigating the death of 47-year-old Andrew Donald Frederick, who died in Grenada on 4 January.
“Mr Frederick’s family are being supported by specialist officers.
“No arrests have been made at this stage and inquiries are ongoing.”
Officers have contacted the Royal Grenada Police Force (RGPF) to offer assistance and discuss how the investigation can be progressed.
Inquest proceedings have been suspended pending the outcome of police investigations.

articles.title: 3 suspects in Degamo slay found guilty of illegal possession of gun, bombs
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines—A Manila court has found three former Army soldiers, who were earlier linked to the killing of former Negros Oriental Governor Roel Degamo, guilty of illegal possession of…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines—A Manila court has found three former Army soldiers, who were earlier linked to the killing of former Negros Oriental Governor Roel Degamo, guilty of illegal possession of firearms and explosives.
Manila Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 40, in an Aug. 18 decision, convicted Joric Labrador of unlawful possession of a firearm and ammunition.
It also found Joven Javier and Benjie Rodriguez guilty of one count each of unlawful possession of explosives in connection with the assassination of Degamo in March 2023.
Labrador was sentenced to up to 10 years in prison, while Javier and Rodriguez were meted a prison term of reclusion perpetua or 20 years.

The court also directed that the firearm and explosives seized from the three accused be handed over to the Philippine National Police.These items include a .45 caliber pistol, two magazines, 14 rounds of live ammunition, and two hand grenades,
The three respondents are also facing multiple murder and frustrated murder and attempted murder charges before the Manila RTC for the killing of Degamo.
The 56-year-old governor was shot down inside his home in Pamploma town, Negros Oriental.
According to the Department of Justice, which brought the charges to the Manila RTC, the validity of warrantless arrests was upheld in these cases.
This is because the confiscated items were properly identified and handled, based on testimonies by the police and other witnesses. /apl

articles.title: DPWH chief Dizon to testify in graft trial of Zaldy Co, others
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Public Works and Highways Secretary Vince Dizon will testify in the trial of former lawmaker Zaldy Co and his co-accused on graft charges in connection with alleged anomalous…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Public Works and Highways Secretary Vince Dizon will testify in the trial of former lawmaker Zaldy Co and his co-accused on graft charges in connection with alleged anomalous flood control project in Mindoro, the Sandiganbayan said on Wednesday.

Associate Justice Maryann Corpuz-Mañalac made this announcement as the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division heard testimonies from two cashier officers of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) in Mimaropa (Mindoro, Marinduque, Romblon, and Palawan).
“As agreed upon, let the presentation of the next witness in the person of Secretary Vince Dizon proceed on September 23, at 8:30 in the morning,” Corpuz-Mañalac.
Corpuz-Mañalac also said the next witness’ judicial affidavit has been submitted online to the court.

In November 2025, the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division issued arrest warrants against Co and his co-accused from the DPWH and Sunwest Corporation in connection with a P289.9 million road dike project in Naujan, Oriental Mindoro, which was flagged as substandard and found to have structural deficiencies.
Co was linked to Sunwest Corporation, which was among the top 15 contractors awarded with the most flood control projects worth P100 billion from July 2022 to May 2025. /gsg

articles.title: NPA leader killed in clash with Army troops in Leyte
articles.summary: TACLOBAN CITY- A ranking New People’s Army (NPA) leader was killed in a brief clash with government troops on Tuesday afternoon in the hinterlands of Barangay Caridad, Baybay City, Leyte, the…

blocks.text: TACLOBAN CITY- A ranking New People’s Army (NPA) leader was killed in a brief clash with government troops on Tuesday afternoon in the hinterlands of Barangay Caridad, Baybay City, Leyte, the military reported.

The Army’s 8th Infantry Division(ID), which is based in Catbalogan City, Samar, said the encounter occurred on Sept. 8 after soldiers received information from a resident about the presence of armed men allegedly collecting money and food from communities in the area.
Troops from the 802nd Infantry Brigade(IB) proceeded to the area to verify the report, resulting in a firefight that lasted about five minutes, according to the military.
Killed was Erwin Murillo Maceda, alias “Romnick,” who was identified by the Army as the vice team leader of the NPA’s Island Committee Levox under the Eastern Visayas Regional Party Committee.
An M16 rifle was also recovered from the encounter site, the 8th ID said.

Brig. Gen. Pompeyo Jason Almagro, commander of the 802nd IB, said Maceda and his group had allegedly been involved in extortion, threats against residents and business owners, and attacks on government security installations in Leyte.

“The people of Leyte have endured years of fear, intimidation, and disruption caused by armed groups. We will not allow these conditions to return to communities that have worked hard to achieve peace,” Almagro said in a statement released on Wednesday.

The military said the encounter followed reports of armed NPA members attempting to regain their presence in communities where government authorities have declared stable peace and security conditions.
The Army also credited residents’ cooperation and timely reporting for enabling government forces to respond to the reported presence of armed men.
“The cooperation of our communities is critical. Their timely reporting allows government forces to respond before threats can escalate,” Almagro said.
The 8th ID renewed its call for remaining NPA members to abandon armed struggle and surrender, saying government programs are available to assist former rebels who return to civilian life.
The military said it would continue operations in areas where armed groups are reported to be operating while encouraging NPA members to return peacefully to their families and communities./coa

articles.title: INQToday: Romualdez ordered to appear in court, Panelo joins VP’s team
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – Here are INQToday’s top stories this afternoon: Former House Speaker Martin Romualdez has been ordered to appear before the Sandiganbayan on September 10 as the anti-graft…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Here are INQToday’s top stories this afternoon:Former House Speaker Martin Romualdez has been ordered to appear before the Sandiganbayan on September 10 as the anti-graft court hears his plea to remain hospitalized while facing a non-bailable plunder case.
Meanwhile, Vice President Sara Duterte has appointed lawyer Paolo Panelo as her assistant spokesperson, adding a new voice to her communications team amid her ongoing legal and impeachment battles.
And 14 Filipino seafarers who survived an attack on a Saudi Arabia-flagged oil tanker near the Strait of Hormuz are now back in the Philippines. /dp

articles.title: P1.79-M shabu confiscated from high-value suspects in Taguig, Valenzuela
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Police on Wednesday confiscated suspected shabu or methamphetamine hydrochloride with a combined value of P1.79 million, and arrested five suspects during separate…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Police on Wednesday confiscated suspected shabu or methamphetamine hydrochloride with a combined value of P1.79 million, and arrested five suspects during separate buy-bust operations in Taguig and Valenzuela cities.
The confiscated substances had a combined weight of 263.6 grams, the National Capital Region Police Office said.
According to law enforcement, the arrest happened after an undercover police officer purchased alleged shabu from a 37-year-old newly identified high-value suspect.
Police also arrested his other accomplices, including two newly identified high-value individuals aged 35 and 20, and a 28-year-old high-value individual.
Seized during the operation were six heated-sealed plastic sachets of suspected shabu, a mobile phone, and other personal items.

The authorities also confiscated a Glock 14 Gen 5 pistol with one magazine and seven rounds of live ammunition from the 37-year-old suspect, facing another charge aside from drug trafficking for violating the Republic Act No. 10591, or the Comprehensive Firearms and Ammunition Regulation Act.
The four suspects arrested in Taguig were taken into police custody and are expected to face charges for violations of the Republic Act No. 9165, or the Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002.
The seized drugs and other evidence will be subjected to forensic examination.
Anotherbuy-bust operation in Barangay Punturin, Valenzuela City, at 4:49 a.m. resulted in the arrest of a 45-year-old high-value individual and the confiscation of P432,480 worth of alleged shabu.
Authorities recovered two plastic sachets allegedly containing 63.6 grams of suspected shabu.
Under police custody, the suspect faces charges of violating Sections 5 and 11 of Republic Act No. 9165 and will be referred to the City Prosecutor’s Office for inquest proceedings.

NCR Officer-in-ChargePolice Brig. Gen. Christopher Abrahano said that the back-to-back operations show the NCRPO’s efforts to disrupt illegal drug activities and prevent firearms from being used in further criminal acts.

“We will continue to focus our operations on high‑value individuals and areas being used for illegal drug activities. The recovery of a firearm in one of these operations further underscores the need for sustained, intelligence‑driven police actions to prevent more serious crimes and protect our communities,” Abrahano said in a statement. Martina Nieyandra Calica. Inquirer.net trainee /mr

articles.title: Mimaropa cops plant over 31,000 trees under environmental project
articles.summary: CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — Police planted 31,592 trees across the Mimaropa region since launching an environmental initiative in July, the regional police office said in a statement on…

blocks.text: CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — Police planted 31,592 trees across the Mimaropa region since launching an environmental initiative in July, the regional police office said in a statement on Wednesday.

The latest tree-planting activity was held on Sept. 8 in Barangay Sta. Isabel, Pinamalayan town in Oriental Mindoro, where nearly 300 participants planted more than 100 narra seedlings and over 100 fruit-bearing trees.

Oriental Mindoro Police Provincial Office (ORMIN PPO) led the activity, bringing together police personnel, firefighters, local government representatives, civic organizations, and other community partners.

Brig. Gen. Christopher Dela Cruz, MIMAROPA police director, joined the activity and said environmental protection forms part of the police’s broader responsibility to help build safe and resilient communities.
“Hindi lamang tayo nagtipon para magtanim ng puno. Nandito tayo upang magtanim ng pag-asa, malasakit, at pananagutan para sa kinabukasan,” Dela Cruz said.
(We did not just gather to plant trees. We are here to plant hope, compassion, and accountability for the future.)

The police regreening initiative, called Project T.R.E.E. (Take Responsibility for the Enhancement of the Environment), was launched on July 6 as part of Dela Cruz’s F.I.G.H.T. C.R.I.M.E.S. framework./coa

articles.title: Intent to nab dela Rosa not waning amid ‘negotiations’ – PNP
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) maintained that its efforts to arrest Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa were not waning despite purported ongoing negotiations with “protectors”…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) maintained that its efforts to arrest Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa were not waning despite purported ongoing negotiations with “protectors” for his surrender.
“It will take as long as it will take,” PNP public information chief Col. Allen Rae Co said in a press briefing in Camp Crame on Wednesday.
“Our efforts did not wane, will not wane, and we will not deviate from serving the warrant of arrest,” he insisted.
Dela Rosa was ordered arrested by the International Criminal Court in a warrant issued last November.
The warrant was only publicized in May and it was in connection with his alleged involvement in former President Rodrigo Duterte’s war against illegal drugs.
On Tuesday, Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla said that the government was in negotiations with dela Rosa’s “protectors,” whom he only identified as “powerful people.”
The senator’s legal counsel, Israelito Torreon, however, denied any personal knowledge of the supposed negotiations nor the protectors.
For its part, Co said the PNP’s search for dela Rosa are continuous, but the spokesperson refused to provide further details, citing operational matters.
He further noted that 91 of the 117 firearms registered to dela Rosa are still unaccounted for.
“Our FEO is continuously coordinating with the family for the surrender of the guns. Legal police action will be initiated,” Co explained.
The PNP FEO revoked dela Rosa’s firearms license and gun registrations in June as part of the bid to capture him.
Dela Rosa was last seen leaving the Senate premises and was supposedly dropped off in Makati City in the early hours of May 14, after a shooting in the chamber.
Remulla previously said dela Rosa’s last known location was in Mindanao. /apl

articles.title: Zamboanga City marks ‘Day of Remembrance’ for bloody 2013 siege
articles.summary: PAGADIAN CITY, Zamboanga del Sur – The Zamboanga City government observed a “Day of Remembrance” on Wednesday for the 2013 bloody Zamboanga Siege that killed hundreds and displaced tens of thousands…

blocks.text: PAGADIAN CITY, Zamboanga del Sur – The Zamboanga City government observed a “Day of Remembrance” on Wednesday for the 2013 bloody Zamboanga Siege that killed hundreds and displaced tens of thousands of residents.
Mayor Khymer Adan Olaso issued Executive Order KHYM 183- 2026 on Tuesday, declaring Wednesday a “Day of Remembrance” to honor the lives lost and the sacrifices made during the 2013 Zamboanga Siege.
The order recognizes the heroism of the security forces who defended the city and remembers the civilians caught in the crossfire during the three-week conflict 13 years ago.
Olaso highlighted the selflessness of the military, police, and emergency personnel who stood on the frontlines to safeguard the city’s democratic ideals and way of life.
Pursuant to Sangguniang Panlungsod Resolution No. 1019, dated Sept. 2, 2014, the declaration formalizes Sept. 9 as an annual day of commemoration.

The mayor urged local businesses—including major department stores, restaurants, public conveyances, entertainment centers, and resorts—to observe the occasion by offering customers a 20% discount every September 9, with special emphasis on active security personnel, as a gesture of solidarity and appreciation.
The September 2013 siege remains one of the darkest chapters in the city’s history.

Sparked by an influx of Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) fighters identified with the Nur Misuari faction, the three-week standoff directly affected six barangays and displaced 22,196 families—or 122,226 individuals.

The urban armed conflict claimed the lives of 25 military and police personnel, alongside 13 civilians, while 266 others were wounded. Rebel casualties were reported at 153 killed in action, with 278 individuals arrested.
The physical and economic destruction was massive.

At least 9,722 homes were burned or destroyed, causing an estimated P200.83 million in damages, while the closure of the city’s airport and seaport paralyzed trade links across Basilan, Sulu, Tawi-Tawi, and the broader Zamboanga Peninsula, resulting in an estimated P331 million in daily economic losses.

Despite the lingering scars, local officials emphasized the resilience of the city’s constituents. Rebuilding and recovery efforts have relied heavily on support from the national government, non-governmental organizations, civil society groups, and international partners.

In his declaration, Olaso offered eternal prayers and condolences to the families of the victims, reassuring residents that the memory and heroism of those who served—including prosecutors from the Department of Justice who pursued legal accountability—will remain permanently etched in the hearts of every Zamboangueño./ca

articles.title: 68 Itogon families evacuate amid prolonged rains in Benguet
articles.summary: BAGUIO CITY – Sixty-eight families (351 people) have voluntarily evacuated their homes in the Benguet municipality of Itogon as prolonged rains from a succession of weather disturbances and the…

blocks.text: BAGUIO CITY – Sixty-eight families (351 people) have voluntarily evacuated their homes in the Benguet municipality of Itogon as prolonged rains from a succession of weather disturbances and the enhanced southwest monsoon raised safety concerns in several communities.

As of Monday, a total of 227 families, or 874 individuals, have been affected by the continued rains across Itogon’s nine barangays, according to the Municipal Social Welfare and Development Office (MSWDO). It said 81 houses were also reported damaged.

The evacuations were carried out as residents in high-risk areas responded to government advisories to seek safer locations amid weeks of rainfall brought by weather disturbances Luis, Maymay, Neneng, Obet, and Pilandok, as well as the monsoon.

Barangay Ampucao recorded the highest number of affected families at 65 (256 individuals, followed by Loacan with 47 families (211 people). Gumatdang reported 46 affected families, while Poblacion had 44 families (134 individuals).

The MSWDO distributed 238 family food packs and hygiene kits to affected residents. The provincial government also provided 200 five-kilogram rice packs, while the Office of Civil Defense in the Cordillera provided nonfood items and fuel assistance for emergency response operations.

The Department of Social Welfare and Development also extended cash assistance to affected families in Gumatdang, Virac, Tuding, and Tolibeng in Loacan. The Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office provided additional nonfood items to families in Tolibeng.

Mayor Bernard Waclin, together with the MSWDO and disaster risk reduction councils, led the assessment and relief efforts. The municipal government said no casualties had been reported in Itogon amid the prolonged rains and successive weather disturbances. Maureen Matayew / Contributor/coa

articles.title: ‘It’s hell’: father of slain Australian surfers tells Mexico homicide trial about identifying sons’ bodies
articles.summary:
Three men are on trial over the death of brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and their friend, US citizen Jack Carter Rhoad, in Ensenada

The father of two Australian surfers killed in Mexico…

blocks.text: The father of two Australian surfers killed in Mexico two years ago testified in court on Tuesday that his life had been turned into hell, as the high-profile trial continued into its second day.

Three men are charged in the killing of Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, respectively, and their 30-year-old American friend Jack Carter Rhoad, who were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast in April 2024.
Authorities say the three were killed in an attempted robbery, and their bodies were found dumped in a cliff-top shaft with gunshot wounds to their heads.
“It’s hell,” the victims’ father Martin Robinson told the court. “It’s hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons.”
“It’s not just the loss, but also the potential they had the dreams that lay ahead of them, the places they travelled, and the love they had for others,” he said.
Robinson described the ordeal of having to identify his sons’ bodies: Callum by a tattoo on his forearm, while identifying Jake was more difficult and required photographs.
Rhoad’s mother Page compared the crime to an execution.
“I miss my son every day, and I don’t know if I will ever be able to regain my balance,” she testified. “Carter loved Mexico. He spoke fluent Spanish and loved dancing, Mexican food and its people.”
Authorities say the men were killed during an attempt to steal their pickup truck, which was later found burned near their bodies.
A protected witness testified Monday that they accompanied one of the defendants to the crime scene and fled after hearing gunshots, and were later threatened into silence.
The surfers’ disappearances and deaths sparked widespread outrage and grief in Australia and the United States, prompting a major social media search for their bodies.
“We hold no resentment toward the people who did this, but we cannot understand how they could have taken the lives of two beautiful people,” Martin Robinson told the court.
The trial is expected to run until the end of September.
Rhoad’s widow, Natalie, is scheduled to testify on Wednesday.

articles.title: ‘No executive suite for Romualdez if transferred to PNP hospital’
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Former House Speaker and incumbent Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez will not be confined in an executive suite if he is transferred to the Philippine National Police General Hospital…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Former House Speaker and incumbent Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez will not be confined in an executive suite if he is transferred to the Philippine National Police General Hospital (PNPGH) in Camp Crame.
“May room nang naka-ready sa kanya,” PNP public information chief Col. Allen Rae Co explained in a press briefing in Camp Crame.
(There is a room waiting for him already.)
“Wala ditong executive suite. Rooms are rooms. Ordinary rooms,” he stressed.
(There is no executive suite here. Rooms are rooms. Ordinary rooms.)
Romualdez was arrested on plunder charges on Monday night while confined at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City for various purported ailments.

On Tuesday, however, Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla said the PNP will ask the Sandiganbayan to transfer Romualdez to the PNPGH to show that the former speaker is not receiving special treatment.
“Our doctors have been coordinating with the doctors of Cardinal Santos for practicing rights so we can assess him independently,” Co said.
“And then, they will confer for us to be able to assess if the former Speaker will be physically fit to face the Sandiganbayan,” he added.
Romualdez has since requested the Sandiganbayan to allow his continued hospital confinement.
But earlier on Wednesday, the Office of the Ombudsman opposed the motion while asking that another team of government doctors assess whether he needed to be confined.
“We welcome them to erase any doubts or suspicions of special treatment,” Co said.
“The more, the merrier. We very much welcome additional doctors to assess the situation or the health status of our former speaker,” he added.
Romualdez is charged in connection with over P7 billion in alleged kickbacks in various government projects from 2022 to 2025. /gsg

articles.title: Iloilo City mayor secures power pledges to strengthen local grid
articles.summary: ILOILO CITY — In response to recurring power interruptions across Panay Island, Iloilo City Mayor Raisa Treñas has secured critical commitments from energy providers to boost power capacity and build…

blocks.text: ILOILO CITY — In response to recurring power interruptions across Panay Island, Iloilo City Mayor Raisa Treñas has secured critical commitments from energy providers to boost power capacity and build grid redundancy for the fast-growing city.

In a statement released on Wednesday from South Korea, where she is currently on official travel, Treñas said the city government is proactively pursuing long-term solutions to safeguard local power stability despite regional supply challenges.
“We know how frustrating these continuing interruptions and rotational brownouts are for our people,” Treñas noted.

She added: “Even while the manual load shedding implemented by the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) is not directly within the control of the city government, we will not just wait around.”
To address Panay Island’s vulnerability as it sits at the tail end of the national power grid, the mayor outlined three major power generation projects to strengthen the island’s electricity supply.

The mayor said Panay Energy Development Corporation (PEDC) has committed to expanding its generation capacity, with the additional power targeted to become fully operational by 2028. Meanwhile, cleaner energy provider PH Natural Gas is preparing to establish operations in Iloilo City, which is expected to help diversify the local energy mix.

In nearby Guimaras, MORE Power is also set to operate a 40-megawatt (MW) floating power barge by the first quarter of 2027. The facility is expected to provide immediate backup power and help improve the reliability of electricity supply in Panay.
Treñas noted that building redundancy—having multiple, independent sources of electricity—is essential to sustaining Iloilo’s rapid economic expansion and insulating it from wider grid failures.

“These are the investments we must continuously pursue because we cannot depend on just one source of power,” Treñas stressed. “Especially here in Panay, being at the tail end of the grid, having more generation, more sources, and more redundancy is vital.”

To ensure these projects proceed without unnecessary delays, the mayor called on the national government and regulatory bodies to fast-track the required permits and approval processes so construction can begin immediately.

She reaffirmed that the city administration will continue engaging with power utilities, private investors, and regional stakeholders to build a more resilient energy infrastructure for Iloilo City./coa

articles.title: DTI-Bukidnon cracks down on social media promos, flags 5 firms
articles.summary: MALAYBALAY CITY, Bukidnon — Five business establishments in the cities of Valencia and Malaybalay have been slapped with show-cause orders by the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) Bukidnon…

blocks.text: MALAYBALAY CITY, Bukidnon — Five business establishments in the cities of Valencia and Malaybalay have been slapped with show-cause orders by the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) Bukidnon provincial office for allegedly running unauthorized sales promotions on social media.

The DTI-Bukidnon, through its Consumer Protection Division (CPD), intensified its monitoring after noticing a spike in online promotional offers, including contests and discounts advertised digitally.
Junar Merla, DTI-Bukidnon CPD chief, said that digital campaigns must not bypass regulatory frameworks.

Operating a sales promotion without a valid DTI permit violates Article 116 of Republic Act No. 7394. Violators face potential administrative fines ranging from P500 to P300,000 under Article 164, alongside penalties upon conviction under Article 123(b).

While the show cause orders demand formal explanations from the establishments to ensure due process, DTI-Bukidnon emphasized that the enforcement actions aim to uphold fair marketplace transparency and protect consumers from unlawful practices.
It did not name the five business establishments ordered to explain.
The provincial office plans to sustain its monitoring efforts across online and physical platforms./coa

items: Metro Manila: Caloocan, Malabon, Navotas, Valenzuela, Quezon City, Makati, Mandaluyong, San Juan, Pasay, Marikina, and Manila
Bataan
Rizal: Rodriguez and San Mateo
